results.src_text:
My line of work

Four people talk about their jobs.
Lisa - Exhibition Programmes Organiser, Science Museum
I'm responsible for putting temporary exhibitions together. This includes planning and designing the exhibition and promoting it. I have to read up about the subject of the exhibition beforehand and then talk to important people in the area so that I can establish the main themes and aims of the exhibition, and plan what objects and pictures should be displayed. I have to make sure the public can understand the thinking behind the exhibition, which means planning interactive displays, workshops and theatre. I also have to bring in engineers and electricians to make sure the final display is not dangerous to visitors. Before the exhibition opens, I help design and write the brochures and leaflets that we'll use to tell people about it.

Janet - Teacher of London Taxi Drivers
The first thing I do when I get here at 7.30 a.m. is check the accounts. Then I see what new maps and documents need to be produced in order to learn the 'runs' or routes necessary to pass the London taxi-driver test. By midday, about 50 students are in school, working out how to make the journeys. They work out the most direct route, using the correct one-way streets, and right- and left- hand turns. I get involved when there's a difference of opinion - like whether you can do a right turn at a particular junction. When they're close to the test, I'll give them a simple route and no matter what way they say they'll go, I'll tell them they have to use another route because the road is closed. The next student will have to find a third route and again I'll come up with a reason why they can't go that way. It's just to make them think.

Sarah - Marine Conservationist
I live by the coast and work from home. This involves responding to telephone enquiries, producing educational resources and setting up training courses. Occasionally, I go into our main office but generally I am on the coast. I also work with schools and study centres and run courses for coastal managers and those involved in making decisions about the fate of the seas.I do things like take them out to sea in a boat in an attempt to make them think more about the life underneath them. This often changes their views as it's very different from making decisions using a computer screen. I am extremely lucky because conservation is my hobby, so the job has many highs for me. The downside of the job is that I work for a charity, so there is a constant need for more money. This means I'm always looking for more resources and I'm not able to achieve everything I want.

Chris - Map and Atlas Publisher
My work is pretty varied. I have to make sure that the publishing programme matches market requirements, and ensure that we keep stocks of 300 or so of the books that we publish. We have very high standards of information and content. We receive many letters from readers on issues such as the representation of international boundaries and these in particular require a careful response. I discuss future projects and current sales with co-publishers. I work as part of an enthusiastic group which makes the job that much more enjoyable. The negative side, as with many jobs, is that there is far too much administration to deal with, which leaves less time to work on the more interesting tasks such as product development and design.
results.tgt_text:
Mon métier

Quatre personnes parlent de leur travail.

Lisa - Organisatrice de programmes d’expositions, Musée des Sciences
Je suis chargée de monter des expositions temporaires. Cela comprend la planification et la conception de l’exposition, ainsi que sa promotion. Je dois me documenter sur le sujet de l’exposition à l’avance, puis parler à des personnes importantes dans ce domaine afin de définir les principaux thèmes et objectifs de l’exposition, et prévoir quels objets et quelles images doivent être présentés. Je dois veiller à ce que le public puisse comprendre la réflexion qui sous-tend l’exposition, ce qui signifie prévoir des présentations interactives, des ateliers et du théâtre. Je dois aussi faire appel à des ingénieurs et à des électriciens pour m’assurer que l’exposition finale ne présente aucun danger pour les visiteurs. Avant l’ouverture de l’exposition, j’aide à concevoir et à rédiger les brochures et les dépliants que nous utiliserons pour en parler au public.

Janet - Formatrice de chauffeurs de taxi londoniens
La première chose que je fais quand j’arrive ici à 7 h 30, c’est vérifier les comptes. Ensuite, je regarde quelles nouvelles cartes et quels documents doivent être préparés afin d’apprendre les « runs » ou itinéraires nécessaires pour réussir l’examen de chauffeur de taxi londonien. À midi, environ 50 élèves sont à l’école, en train de trouver comment effectuer les trajets. Ils déterminent l’itinéraire le plus direct, en utilisant les rues à sens unique appropriées, ainsi que les virages à droite et à gauche corrects. J’interviens lorsqu’il y a un désaccord, par exemple pour savoir si l’on peut tourner à droite à un carrefour précis. Lorsqu’ils approchent de l’examen, je leur donne un itinéraire simple et, quel que soit le trajet qu’ils disent emprunter, je leur dis qu’ils doivent en utiliser un autre parce que la route est fermée. L’élève suivant devra trouver un troisième itinéraire et, de nouveau, je trouverai une raison pour laquelle il ne peut pas passer par là. C’est simplement pour les faire réfléchir.

Sarah - Spécialiste de la conservation marine
J’habite au bord de la mer et je travaille depuis chez moi. Cela consiste à répondre aux demandes de renseignements par téléphone, à produire des ressources pédagogiques et à mettre en place des stages de formation. Il m’arrive d’aller dans notre bureau principal, mais en général je suis sur la côte. Je travaille aussi avec des écoles et des centres d’études et j’organise des formations pour les gestionnaires du littoral et les personnes impliquées dans la prise de décisions concernant le sort des mers. Je fais des choses comme les emmener en mer sur un bateau afin de les amener à réfléchir davantage à la vie sous-marine qui se trouve sous eux. Cela change souvent leur point de vue, car c’est très différent de prendre des décisions devant un écran d’ordinateur. J’ai énormément de chance parce que la protection de la nature est mon hobby, donc ce travail m’apporte beaucoup de satisfactions. Le mauvais côté du métier, c’est que je travaille pour une association caritative, donc il y a constamment besoin de plus d’argent. Cela signifie que je suis toujours à la recherche de nouvelles ressources et que je ne peux pas réaliser tout ce que je souhaite.

Chris - Éditeur de cartes et d’atlas
Mon travail est assez varié. Je dois m’assurer que le programme de publication correspond aux exigences du marché, et veiller à ce que nous conservions des stocks d’environ 300 livres que nous publions. Nous avons des normes très élevées en matière d’information et de contenu. Nous recevons de nombreuses lettres de lecteurs sur des questions telles que la représentation des frontières internationales, et celles-ci exigent en particulier une réponse soignée. Je discute des projets futurs et des ventes actuelles avec des coéditeurs. Je travaille au sein d’une équipe enthousiaste, ce qui rend le travail d’autant plus agréable. Le côté négatif, comme dans beaucoup de métiers, c’est qu’il y a beaucoup trop d’administration à gérer, ce qui laisse moins de temps pour travailler sur les tâches les plus intéressantes, comme le développement et la conception de produits.

results.src_text:
P. D. James

Barbara Michaels meets the acclaimed crime writer, whose innocent exterior hides a complex and brilliant imagination.

Best-selling crime writer P.D. James - the initials stand for Phyllis Dorothy - exudes an air of quiet authority. It is easy to envisage her, had she not become a creator of detective stories with more twists and turns than a spiral staircase, as a headmistress of a girls' school. But it is soon apparent from what she says that the authoritative mien is, in fact, a cloak for shyness. She reluctantly admits that Adam Dalgliesh, the detective in her novels, ‘is, I suppose, modelled on myself - or rather, the way I would have turned out if I had been a man'. Dalgliesh prefers to unravel the complexities of crimes solo, as does his creator. 'I need time on my own, particularly when I am writing. I can write more or less anywhere as long as I have total privacy.'
She is too modest to concur with the view that she is Britain's best-known crime writer, even though her books - 12 major detective novels - are read avidly by millions all over the world. She herself is a great fan of the works of close friend Ruth Rendell. 'I particularly enjoy her psychological works, written under the name of Barbara Vine.' Books beside her bed are most likely to be by women writers such as Iris Murdoch, Anita Brookner and Penelope Lively, although not to the total exclusion of male authors like Graham Greene and Evelyn Waugh, whom she considers to have been the greatest novelists of their generation.
Success came to P.D. James late in life. Now in her seventies, she was 42 when her first crime novel, Cover Her Face, was published. Born in Oxford, the eldest of three children, Phyllis grew up mainly in Cambridge, where her family moved when she was 11 years old. ‘I met my husband there - he was a student at the university, and I have always loved the place. That is why I chose it as the setting for An Unsuitable Job For A Woman.'
Reluctantly, she reveals that from a promising start, life has been hard, even tragic at times. Her Irish doctor husband, Connor Bantry White, returned from the Second World War, during which he served with the Royal Army Medical
Corps, a very sick man. 'I had to work long hours to support him and our two young daughters, Clare and Jane. The ideas were teeming in my head, but I could do practically nothing about it - I simply hadn't the time. My husband's parents, however, were marvellous, and took my daughters under their wing, giving them a sense of security throughout those difficult years.'
While working full-time in administration for the National Health Service, she made good use of her enviable organisational skills. At one point, five psychiatric outpatients' clinics came under her jurisdiction. Then followed 11 years at the Home Office, first in the Police Department, doing administration for forensic science research, and then in the Criminal Law section, in the juvenile crime division. It was while working in forensic science that she became 'quite accustomed’ to the sight of corpses. But it was not fascination with death itself that inspired her. ‘It was, rather, the shape and construction involved in the writing of a crime novel that appealed. I have always enjoyed reading detective stories, and I always knew that I wanted to be a writer.'
‘I didn’t want to use the traumatic events of my own life in a work of fiction. The writing of a detective story appealed as a wonderful apprenticeship for someone setting out to be a serious novelist, and it was suitably remove from my own experience. As I went on, I became increasingly aware that one could stay within the constraints and indeed within the so-called formula of the classic detective story and still write a good, serious and revealing novel about human beings. Writing detective stories', she says, 'is a way of bringing order out of disorder. The solution of a crime confirms the sanctity of life - even If that life ls unlovable. Nobody really likes violence.'
results.tgt_text:
P. D. James

Barbara Michaels rencontre la célèbre auteure de romans policiers, dont l’apparence innocente dissimule une imagination complexe et brillante.

L’auteure de best-sellers policiers P.D. James — ces initiales signifient Phyllis Dorothy — dégage une impression d’autorité tranquille. Il est facile de l’imaginer, si elle n’était pas devenue créatrice d’histoires policières aux rebondissements plus nombreux qu’un escalier en colimaçon, en directrice d’une école de jeunes filles. Mais ce qu’elle dit révèle bientôt que cette allure autoritaire n’est en réalité qu’un manteau jeté sur sa timidité. Elle admet à contrecœur qu’Adam Dalgliesh, le détective de ses romans, « est, je suppose, calqué sur moi — ou plutôt sur ce que je serais devenue si j’avais été un homme ». Dalgliesh préfère élucider seul la complexité des crimes, tout comme sa créatrice. « J’ai besoin de temps pour moi, surtout quand j’écris. Je peux écrire à peu près n’importe où, du moment que je bénéficie d’une intimité totale. »

Elle est trop modeste pour souscrire à l’idée qu’elle est l’auteure de romans policiers la plus connue de Grande-Bretagne, bien que ses livres — douze grands romans policiers — soient lus avec avidité par des millions de personnes dans le monde entier. Elle-même admire beaucoup l’œuvre de son amie proche Ruth Rendell. « J’apprécie particulièrement ses romans psychologiques, écrits sous le nom de Barbara Vine. » Les livres posés près de son lit sont le plus souvent dus à des auteures comme Iris Murdoch, Anita Brookner et Penelope Lively, sans exclure totalement des écrivains tels que Graham Greene et Evelyn Waugh, qu’elle considère comme les plus grands romanciers de leur génération.

Le succès est venu tard dans la vie de P.D. James. Aujourd’hui septuagénaire, elle avait quarante-deux ans lorsque son premier roman policier, Cover Her Face, a été publié. Née à Oxford, aînée de trois enfants, Phyllis a grandi principalement à Cambridge, où sa famille s’est installée lorsqu’elle avait onze ans. « C’est là que j’ai rencontré mon mari — il était étudiant à l’université — et j’ai toujours aimé cet endroit. C’est pourquoi je l’ai choisi comme cadre d’An Unsuitable Job For A Woman. »

Avec réticence, elle révèle qu’après des débuts prometteurs, la vie a été dure, parfois même tragique. Son mari, Connor Bantry White, médecin irlandais, est revenu de la Seconde Guerre mondiale, durant laquelle il avait servi dans le Royal Army Medical Corps, gravement malade. « J’ai dû travailler de longues heures pour subvenir à ses besoins et à ceux de nos deux petites filles, Clare et Jane. Les idées fourmillaient dans ma tête, mais je ne pouvais pratiquement rien en faire — je n’en avais tout simplement pas le temps. Les parents de mon mari, en revanche, ont été merveilleux et ont pris mes filles sous leur aile, leur donnant un sentiment de sécurité durant toutes ces années difficiles. »

Tout en travaillant à plein temps dans l’administration du National Health Service, elle a su tirer bon parti de ses remarquables capacités d’organisation. À un moment donné, cinq consultations externes de psychiatrie relevaient de sa responsabilité. Puis ont suivi onze années au Home Office, d’abord au département de la police, où elle assurait l’administration de la recherche en science forensique, puis à la section de droit pénal, dans la division de la délinquance juvénile. C’est en travaillant dans le domaine de la médecine légale qu’elle s’est « assez habituée » à la vue des cadavres. Mais ce n’est pas une fascination pour la mort elle-même qui l’a inspirée. « C’était plutôt la forme et la construction propres à l’écriture d’un roman policier qui me séduisaient. J’ai toujours aimé lire des histoires de détectives, et j’ai toujours su que je voulais devenir écrivain. »

« Je ne voulais pas utiliser les événements traumatisants de ma propre vie dans une œuvre de fiction. L’écriture d’un roman policier me paraissait être un merveilleux apprentissage pour quelqu’un qui aspirait à devenir un romancier sérieux, et c’était suffisamment éloigné de ma propre expérience. Au fil du temps, j’ai pris de plus en plus conscience qu’on pouvait rester dans les limites, et même dans la soi-disant formule du roman policier classique, tout en écrivant un roman bon, sérieux et révélateur sur les êtres humains. Écrire des histoires policières, dit-elle, c’est une manière de faire surgir l’ordre du désordre. La résolution d’un crime confirme le caractère sacré de la vie — même si cette vie est celle de quelqu’un qu’on ne peut aimer. Au fond, personne n’aime vraiment la violence. »

P. D. James

Barbara Michaels meets the famous crime novelist whose innocent appearance conceals a complex and brilliant imagination.

Best-selling crime writer P. D. James—those initials stand for Phyllis Dorothy—gives an impression of quiet authority. It is easy to imagine her, had she not become the creator of detective stories with more twists than a spiral staircase, as the headmistress of a girls’ school. But what she says soon reveals that this authoritative bearing is really only a cloak thrown over her shyness. She admits reluctantly that Adam Dalgliesh, the detective in her novels, “is, I suppose, modeled on me—or rather on what I would have become if I had been a man.” Dalgliesh prefers to unravel the complexities of crime on his own, just like his creator. “I need time to myself, especially when I’m writing. I can write almost anywhere, provided I have complete privacy.”

She is too modest to subscribe to the idea that she is Britain’s best-known crime novelist, although her books—twelve major detective novels—are read avidly by millions of people all over the world. She herself greatly admires the work of her close friend Ruth Rendell. “I particularly enjoy her psychological novels, written under the name Barbara Vine.” The books by her bedside are most often by women writers such as Iris Murdoch, Anita Brookner, and Penelope Lively, though without entirely excluding writers such as Graham Greene and Evelyn Waugh, whom she considers the greatest novelists of their generation.

Success came late in P. D. James’s life. Now in her seventies, she was forty-two when her first detective novel, Cover Her Face, was published. Born in Oxford, the eldest of three children, Phyllis grew up mainly in Cambridge, where her family moved when she was eleven. “It was there that I met my husband—he was a university student—and I have always loved the place. That is why I chose it as the setting for An Unsuitable Job For A Woman.”

Reluctantly, she reveals that after a promising start, life was hard, sometimes even tragic. Her husband, Connor Bantry White, an Irish doctor, returned from the Second World War, during which he had served in the Royal Army Medical Corps, seriously ill. “I had to work long hours to support him and our two little daughters, Clare and Jane. Ideas were teeming in my head, but I could do practically nothing with them—I simply didn’t have the time. My husband’s parents, on the other hand, were wonderful and took my daughters under their wing, giving them a sense of security throughout all those difficult years.”

While working full-time in the administration of the National Health Service, she managed to make good use of her remarkable organizational abilities. At one point, five outpatient psychiatric clinics were under her responsibility. Then came eleven years at the Home Office, first in the police department, where she handled the administration of forensic science research, then in the criminal law section, in the juvenile delinquency division. It was while working in the field of forensic medicine that she became “quite used” to the sight of dead bodies. But it was not a fascination with death itself that inspired her. “It was rather the form and structure inherent in writing a detective novel that appealed to me. I have always enjoyed reading detective stories, and I have always known that I wanted to become a writer.”

“I did not want to use the traumatic events of my own life in a work of fiction. Writing a detective novel seemed to me a wonderful apprenticeship for someone who aspired to become a serious novelist, and it was sufficiently removed from my own experience. Over time, I became increasingly aware that one could remain within the bounds, and even within the so-called formula of the classic detective novel, while still writing a good, serious, and revealing novel about human beings. Writing detective stories,” she says, “is a way of bringing order out of disorder. The solving of a crime confirms the sacredness of life—even if that life is someone’s whom one cannot love. Deep down, no one really likes violence.”

However, most of the problems were small and most of the guests at the conference were amazed by the network. After this, the ARPAnet began to grow even more rapidly. But now it was not the world's only network of computers.
After the ARPAnet had shown that a computer network could be built and that it could be useful, other networks began to appear. Universities, government departments and other organizations saw that networking could multiply the power of their computers - and the power of the people who used them.
But these new networks created their own rules. A system that was best for the ARPAnet did not necessarily suit other organizations with different needs, different styles of work and different hardware.
So, once again, there were many different computer systems that could not talk to each other. Now, just a few years after the ARPAnet was invented, the appearance of new networks had once again created the problem that had caused Bob Taylor to imagine the world's first computer network.
By this time, Bob Kahn was in charge of the ARPAnet project. He was very familiar with the new problem because he had worked on some of the newer networks. They were all designed to deal with different circumstances. For example, the Alohanet network in Hawaii used radio waves to deal with the problem of communicating over mountains and between different islands.
The network in the San Francisco area was not even fixed: it was on lorries which moved around from place to place. The Atlantic Packet Satellite Network used another system, sending messages up to satellites in space to communicate across half the world.

HOWARD BONNIER

Bray is a beautiful village about fifty kilometres west of London. A young Englishman named Howard Bonnier opened a restaurant called The Palace there about three and a half months ago. Not many people in Britain know Mr Bonnier's name yet, but he's already quite famous in France. This is because he has written in French magazines about almost all the best restaurants in that country. He's only 29 years old.
When Howard was a teenager, he often went to restaurants with his mother and father. He liked doing this so much that he decided not to buy lots of clothes and CDs; instead, he used his money to visit France and eat in good restaurants. He also bought a lot of French and English cookbooks - he says he has more than two hundred and fifty!
So why did he decide to open a restaurant? Simply because he loves cooking. Has it been an easy thing to do? He says it's expensive to start your own restaurant and it's much more difficult to cook for fifty people than to cook for your family, but he's sure he's done the right thing.

Photography

When a photographer takes a photograph, he or she makes a selection of visual information that is determined by his or her technical and aesthetic skills, personal views and experience, together with a set of social and cultural norms. And in the course of this book we shall see how these factors not only affect the style, content and expression of a photograph, but also how those images are perceived and responded to by the viewer. For example, we might consider that the casual reader of a newspaper will have an implicit understanding of the photographic images reproduced on the page. But rather than accepting the photograph at face value, we might question whether it accurately recorded the scene as it would have looked at the time. Or, in contrast, does it communicate the photographer’s point of view? Is it the precise instant recorded that is of particular importance, or should the photograph on the page be understood as a symbol to represent a state of affairs in the world?

More than a game

Sport for me has always been more than just a game. The most successful people in sport have total self-belief. You need tunnel vision if you want to succeed in sport. There’s only one route to being the best and you have to put everything else to one side. Sport is ruthless and no one else is going to do it for you. It’s sink or swim.
Sport has taught me personal discipline and determination, but it can also teach you the benefits of working as one of a team. My sport allows and encourages you to excel individually, yet it is a team game and you have to balance these two aspects. It’s very much like life - you can succeed as an individual, but you must never forget there are others around you.
Sport has given me a great deal - and not just financially. It has opened doors for me and opened my eyes, and I’ve seen things around the world that others will never see. But you also have to give up a lot for those perks.

Tuning in

Some experiences etch themselves so sharply on our memory that they form islands of clarity in our recollection. For me, such a momentous occasion took place one night in California many years ago, when I lay awake listening to the rapturous strains of a mockingbird singing from an invisible location in one of the tall trees that were dotted around the suburban neighbourhood. I don’t suffer from insomnia - it was the exquisite artistry of the singer that kept me awake. As I followed his intricately woven melodies, I found myself drawn into an unexpected aesthetic environment. In order to follow the patterns that issued from the bird, I had to call on my experience of jazz and Indian classical music. The bird had me convinced that I was being treated to an ad lib performance of the most breathtaking improvisational acrobatics. I groaned and I cheered as one improbable musical variation followed another through the open window where I lay listening, until finally I fell asleep.
results.tgt_text:
Photographie

Lorsqu’un photographe prend une photographie, il ou elle opère une sélection d’informations visuelles déterminée par ses compétences techniques et esthétiques, ses opinions personnelles et son expérience, ainsi que par un ensemble de normes sociales et culturelles. Et, au fil de cet ouvrage, nous verrons comment ces facteurs influent non seulement sur le style, le contenu et l’expression d’une photographie, mais aussi sur la manière dont ces images sont perçues et accueillies par le spectateur. Par exemple, on pourrait considérer que le lecteur occasionnel d’un journal a une compréhension implicite des images photographiques reproduites sur la page. Mais, plutôt que d’accepter la photographie telle quelle, nous pourrions nous demander si elle a fidèlement enregistré la scène telle qu’elle apparaissait à ce moment-là. Ou bien, au contraire, communique-t-elle le point de vue du photographe ? Est-ce l’instant précis saisi qui revêt une importance particulière, ou faut-il comprendre la photographie sur la page comme un symbole représentant un état de choses dans le monde ?

Plus qu’un jeu

Pour moi, le sport a toujours été bien plus qu’un simple jeu. Les personnes qui réussissent le mieux dans le sport ont une confiance absolue en elles-mêmes. Il faut avoir une vision étroite et déterminée si l’on veut réussir dans le sport. Il n’existe qu’une seule voie pour être le meilleur, et il faut tout le reste mettre de côté. Le sport est impitoyable et personne d’autre ne le fera à votre place. C’est réussir ou sombrer.
Le sport m’a appris la discipline personnelle et la détermination, mais il peut aussi vous enseigner les avantages du travail en équipe. Mon sport vous permet et vous encourage à exceller individuellement, et pourtant c’est un sport d’équipe, et il faut trouver un équilibre entre ces deux aspects. C’est très semblable à la vie : on peut réussir en tant qu’individu, mais il ne faut jamais oublier qu’il y a d’autres personnes autour de soi.
Le sport m’a énormément apporté, et pas seulement sur le plan financier. Il m’a ouvert des portes et m’a ouvert les yeux, et j’ai vu à travers le monde des choses que d’autres ne verront jamais. Mais il faut aussi renoncer à beaucoup de choses pour obtenir ces avantages.

Être à l’écoute

Certaines expériences s’impriment si fortement dans notre mémoire qu’elles forment des îlots de clarté dans nos souvenirs. Pour moi, un moment aussi marquant eut lieu une nuit en Californie, il y a de nombreuses années, lorsque je restai éveillé à écouter les accents ravissants d’un moqueur polyglotte chantant depuis un endroit invisible dans l’un des grands arbres disséminés dans le quartier résidentiel. Je ne souffre pas d’insomnie : c’est l’art exquis du chanteur qui me maintenait éveillé. En suivant ses mélodies finement entrelacées, je me suis trouvé entraîné dans un univers esthétique inattendu. Pour suivre les motifs émis par l’oiseau, j’ai dû faire appel à mon expérience du jazz et de la musique classique indienne. L’oiseau m’avait convaincu que j’assistais à une performance improvisée, ad libitum, faite des acrobaties d’improvisation les plus époustouflantes. Je gémissais et j’acclamais tandis qu’une variation musicale improbable en suivait une autre à travers la fenêtre ouverte près de laquelle j’étais allongé à écouter, jusqu’à ce que je finisse par m’endormir.

I also moved some guns and other things to this bigger cave. I wanted to have guns near me when I was at my country house. I was more intelligent than 500 cannibals !
Every morning, I took some guns and walked about three miles to my place on the hill. I watched and waited for the cannibals. But nobody came. Nothing happened. I watched every morning for months, but I didn't see anybody.
Then I went back to my old life and looked for food in the mornings. I didn't visit that hill for a long time. I tried to forget about the mark on the beach and the bones. I tried, but I couldn't forget.
It was now the end of the summer of my twenty-third year on this island. I had a lot of work in my garden. I looked at the corn every morning very early. One morning, before it was light, I saw a fire on the beach. It was about two miles away, near the hill. I ran quickly to the hill and looked for the fire.
I saw nine men on the beach below me. They wore no clothes. They sat round a small fire. The weather was very hot, so the fire was for food. They danced - they moved their arms and legs quickly up and down. After an hour, the water in the sea was high on the beach. The nine men got into their boats and began to leave.
I ran back to my cave for my gun. When I came to the hill again, I saw their two boats on the sea. Then I saw three other boats. The five boats went north.

John's sixteen-year-old daughter, Christine, was sitting at the table doing her homework. His son Andrew, who was thirteen, was watching television.
'Thanks, Christine,' John said. 'I'm sorry I'm late. Is everything OK?'
'Fine, thanks.' Christine gave him a quick smile, then got on with her work. John got his food from the kitchen, Fried fish and chips. The food was dry and didn't taste very good. But he didn't say anything about that. John was not a good cook himself and his children were no better. His wife had been a good cook, he remembered.
John tried to eat the terrible supper and looked around the small, miserable flat. The furniture was twenty years old, the wallpaper and carpets were cheap and dirty. The rooms were all small, and he could see no trees or gardens from the windows - just the lights from hundreds of other flats. And there were books, clothes, and newspapers on the floor.
Once, when his wife had been alive, he had had a fine house. A beautiful big house in the country, with a large garden. They had had lots of new furniture, two cars, expensive holidays - everything they needed. He had had a good job. They hadn't needed to think about money. And then he had started the boat-building company, and his luck had ended.
When Rachel had died, John had been terribly unhappy - much too unhappy to think about business. A few months later his company had closed, and he had lost all his money. John had had to sell his beautiful house in the country, and move to this miserable flat.

Hi, Dad. Your dinner is in the kitchen.
Christine, John’s sixteen-year-old daughter, was sitting at the table doing her homework. His son Andrew, who was thirteen, was watching television.
“Thanks, Christine,” said John. “I’m sorry I’m late. Is everything all right?”
“Very well, thank you.” Christine gave him a quick smile, then went back to her work. John went to get his meal from the kitchen: fried fish and chips. The meal was dry and didn’t taste very good. But he said nothing. John wasn’t a good cook himself, and his children were no better. His wife had been a good cook, he remembered.
John tried to eat the awful dinner and looked around him at the small miserable apartment. The furniture was twenty years old, the wallpaper and carpets were cheap and dirty. The rooms were all very small, and from the windows he could see neither trees nor gardens—only the lights of hundreds of other apartments. And there were books, clothes, and newspapers on the floor.
Once, when his wife was still alive, he had had a beautiful house. A large and beautiful house in the country, with a big garden. They had had lots of new furniture, two cars, expensive holidays—everything they needed. He had had a good job. They had not needed to think about money. And then he had started his boat-building business, and his luck had changed.
When Rachel died, John had been terribly unhappy—far too unhappy to think about business. A few months later, his company had closed, and he had lost all his money. John had had to sell his beautiful house in the country and move into this miserable apartment.

Volunteer tourism 

Four academic writers discuss the topic of international voluntary work. 
 
A.
It is hard to argue that the actual contribution to development amounts to a great deal directly. Whilst volunteer tourists can get involved in building homes or schools, they have usually paid a significant fee for the opportunity to be involved in this work: money that, if donated to a local community directly, could potentially pay for a greater amount of labour than the individual volunteer could ever hope to provide. This is especially so in the case of gap years, in which the level of technical skill or professional experience required of volunteers is negligible. Hence, it is unsurprising that many academic studies allude to the moral issue of whether gap year volunteering is principally motivated by altruism – a desire to benefit the society visited – or whether young people aim to generate ‘cultural capital’ which benefits them in their careers. However, the projects may play a role in developing people who will, in the course of their careers and lives, act ethically in favour of those less well-off. 

B.
Volunteering may lead to greater international understanding; enhanced ability to solve conflicts; widespread and democratic participation in global affairs through global civic society organisations; and growth of international social networks among ordinary people. In this scenario, the whole is greater than the sum of its parts, an outcome where benefits accrue to volunteers and host communities, and contribute to the global greater good. However, if volunteering is largely limited to individuals of means from wealthier areas of the world, it may give these privileged volunteers an international perspective, and a career boost, but it will do little for people and communities who currently lack access to international voluntary work. Those who volunteer will continue to reap its benefits, using host organisations and host communities as a rung on the ladder of personal advancement. 

C.
At its worst, international volunteering can be imperialist, paternalistic charity, volunteer tourism, or a self-serving quest for career and personal development on the part of well-off Westerners. Or it can be straightforward provision of technical assistance for international development. At its best, international volunteering brings benefits (and costs) to individual volunteers and the organisations within which they work, at the same time as providing the space for an exchange of technical skills, knowledge, and cross-cultural experience in developing communities. Most significantly, volunteering can raise awareness of, and a lifelong commitment to combating, existing unequal power relations and deep-seated causes of poverty, injustice, and unsustainable development. 
 
 
D.
Volunteer tourism seems to fit well with the growth of life strategies to help others. Such limited strategies, aimed at a humble ‘making a difference’, can appear positive and attractive in an anti-political climate. The personal element appears positive – it bypasses big government and eschews big business. Yet it also bypasses the democratic imperative of representative government and reduces development to individual acts of charity, most often ones that seek to work around rather than transform the situations of poor, rural societies. Cynicism at the act of volunteering is certainly misplaced. The act of volunteer tourism may involve only simple, commendable charity. However, where volunteer tourism is talked up as sustainable development and the marketing of the gap-year companies merges into development thinking, this is symptomatic of a degradation of the discourse of development. The politics of volunteer tourism represents a retreat from a social understanding of global inequalities and the poverty lived by so many in the developing word.
results.tgt_text:
Le tourisme volontaire

Quatre auteurs universitaires discutent du thème du volontariat international.

A.
Il est difficile de soutenir que la contribution réelle au développement représente directement quelque chose de considérable. Bien que les touristes volontaires puissent participer à la construction de maisons ou d’écoles, ils ont généralement payé des frais importants pour avoir l’occasion de prendre part à ce travail : un argent qui, s’il était donné directement à une communauté locale, pourrait potentiellement rémunérer une quantité de main-d’œuvre supérieure à ce que le volontaire individuel pourrait jamais espérer fournir. C’est particulièrement vrai dans le cas des années de césure, où le niveau de compétence technique ou d’expérience professionnelle exigé des volontaires est négligeable. Il n’est donc pas surprenant que de nombreuses études universitaires évoquent la question morale de savoir si le volontariat pendant une année de césure est principalement motivé par l’altruisme — le désir d’apporter un bénéfice à la société visitée — ou si les jeunes cherchent à acquérir un « capital culturel » qui leur sera utile dans leur carrière. Cependant, ces projets peuvent jouer un rôle dans la formation de personnes qui, au cours de leur carrière et de leur vie, agiront de manière éthique en faveur des plus démunis.

B.
Le volontariat peut conduire à une meilleure compréhension internationale ; à une capacité accrue de résoudre les conflits ; à une participation étendue et démocratique aux affaires mondiales par l’intermédiaire d’organisations de la société civile mondiale ; et au développement de réseaux sociaux internationaux parmi les gens ordinaires. Dans ce scénario, le tout est supérieur à la somme de ses parties, un résultat où les bénéfices reviennent aux volontaires comme aux communautés d’accueil, et contribuent au bien commun mondial. Cependant, si le volontariat est largement réservé à des individus aisés issus des régions les plus riches du monde, il peut offrir à ces volontaires privilégiés une perspective internationale, ainsi qu’un avantage pour leur carrière, mais il apportera peu aux personnes et aux communautés qui n’ont actuellement pas accès au volontariat international. Ceux qui font du volontariat continueront d’en récolter les bénéfices, en utilisant les organisations d’accueil et les communautés d’accueil comme un échelon sur l’échelle de leur avancement personnel.

C.
Dans sa pire forme, le volontariat international peut relever d’une charité impérialiste et paternaliste, du tourisme volontaire, ou d’une quête intéressée de carrière et de développement personnel de la part d’Occidentaux aisés. Ou bien il peut consister tout simplement en une prestation d’assistance technique au service du développement international. Dans sa meilleure forme, le volontariat international apporte des bénéfices (et des coûts) aux volontaires individuels ainsi qu’aux organisations au sein desquelles ils travaillent, tout en offrant un espace d’échange de compétences techniques, de connaissances et d’expériences interculturelles dans les communautés en développement. Plus important encore, le volontariat peut sensibiliser aux rapports de pouvoir inégaux existants et aux causes profondes de la pauvreté, de l’injustice et d’un développement non durable, et susciter un engagement à vie pour les combattre.

D.
Le tourisme volontaire semble bien s’accorder avec l’essor de stratégies de vie visant à aider les autres. De telles stratégies limitées, orientées vers le modeste objectif de « faire une différence », peuvent paraître positives et attrayantes dans un climat antipolitique. La dimension personnelle semble positive — elle contourne l’État central et évite les grandes entreprises. Pourtant, elle contourne aussi l’impératif démocratique du gouvernement représentatif et réduit le développement à des actes individuels de charité, le plus souvent à des actes qui cherchent à contourner, plutôt qu’à transformer, la situation des sociétés rurales pauvres. Le cynisme à l’égard de l’acte de volontariat est certainement mal placé. L’acte de tourisme volontaire peut n’impliquer qu’une charité simple et louable. Cependant, lorsque le tourisme volontaire est présenté comme du développement durable et que le discours marketing des entreprises spécialisées dans les années de césure se confond avec la réflexion sur le développement, cela est symptomatique d’une dégradation du discours sur le développement. La politique du tourisme volontaire représente un recul par rapport à une compréhension sociale des inégalités mondiales et de la pauvreté vécue par tant de personnes dans le monde en développement.

results.src_text:
Amateur Astronomy

Many things have changed in astronomy over the past half-century. Until about 30 years ago, there was a great shortage of charts and catalogues. Telescopic equipment was limited and there were few books on practical astronomy. Today, the range of off-the-shelf telescopes and equipment covers almost everything one could need. Electronic calculators and computers have revolutionised almanacs and chart production, and facilitated the analysis of observations and the publication of results.
All this must surely make this the golden age of amateur astronomy. Well, perhaps, but a great deal has been lost as well. Now one may have to travel 80 km to find a sky comparable to that found in urban areas 50 years ago. The daytime skies are now plagued by aircraft condensation trails which can persist for hours and often spread out to form amorphous clouds, making solar observations impossible and hampering night-time observation too.

Too Much Choice

Society is becoming ‘overchoiced’. There are too many things to do, too many options, too many opportunities. In the new economy, the desire for the new product, service or next big thing is an addiction, and technology simply accelerates the pace of change: the noise, the proliferation of new goods and services, offering more and more choice. No sooner has the new product emerged off this virtual production line than the next one is about to be launched. The head spins, the brain races, the fatigue sets in; the disconnection from life begins.
Choice is the mantra of the new economy, but more choice means more stress, less time and more complexity. Hence a new trend is afoot. The search is on for ‘simplexity’ - the simple things that give meaning in an increasingly complex world. But simplifying your life is not easy in an age of economic excess. There are more basic brands of detergent and breakfast cereals than we can ever need or want, more software upgrades, features and calling plans than we can keep track of.

McAndrews Hotel

Every summer we spend a fortnight in McAndrews Hotel in North Mayo, Ireland. It is a family tradition, instigated by my grandmother, and by now it has achieved a certain sacredness. Nothing is allowed to interfere with the ritual. We are of a kind, McAndrews clientele: old-fashioned, odd perhaps, some would say snobbish. I do not like the bad manners, the insolence of shop assistants which passes for egalitarianism in this present age; I resent chummy overtures from waiters who sometimes appear to restrain themselves with difficulty from slapping one on the back. I know most of my fellow-guests’ names - like me they have been coming here since they were children - yet can rest assured that when I meet any of them in any part of the hotel, I shall be spared all social intercourse apart from a civil word of greeting. Such respect for dignity and personal privacy is hard to come by in commercial establishments these days.
results.tgt_text:
Astronomie amateur

Bien des choses ont changé en astronomie au cours du dernier demi-siècle. Il y a encore une trentaine d’années, on manquait cruellement de cartes et de catalogues. Le matériel télescopique était limité et il existait peu d’ouvrages sur l’astronomie pratique. Aujourd’hui, la gamme de télescopes et d’équipements disponibles dans le commerce couvre presque tout ce dont on pourrait avoir besoin. Les calculatrices électroniques et les ordinateurs ont révolutionné la production des almanachs et des cartes, et facilité l’analyse des observations ainsi que la publication des résultats.
Tout cela devrait certainement faire de notre époque l’âge d’or de l’astronomie amateur. Eh bien, peut-être, mais beaucoup a été perdu aussi. Désormais, il faut parfois parcourir 80 km pour trouver un ciel comparable à celui que l’on trouvait dans les zones urbaines il y a 50 ans. Les ciels diurnes sont maintenant infestés de traînées de condensation d’avions qui peuvent persister pendant des heures et s’étaler souvent jusqu’à former des nuages amorphes, rendant les observations solaires impossibles et gênant aussi les observations nocturnes.

Trop de choix

La société est en train de devenir victime d’un « excès de choix ». Il y a trop de choses à faire, trop d’options, trop d’occasions. Dans la nouvelle économie, le désir du nouveau produit, du nouveau service ou de la prochaine grande nouveauté est une addiction, et la technologie ne fait qu’accélérer le rythme du changement : le bruit, la prolifération de nouveaux biens et services, offrant toujours plus de choix. À peine le nouveau produit sort-il de cette chaîne de production virtuelle que le suivant est déjà sur le point d’être lancé. La tête tourne, le cerveau s’emballe, la fatigue s’installe ; la déconnexion d’avec la vie commence.
Le choix est le mantra de la nouvelle économie, mais davantage de choix signifie davantage de stress, moins de temps et plus de complexité. D’où l’émergence d’une nouvelle tendance. La recherche s’oriente vers la « simplexité » — les choses simples qui donnent du sens dans un monde de plus en plus complexe. Mais simplifier sa vie n’est pas facile à l’ère de l’excès économique. Il existe plus de marques élémentaires de lessive et de céréales du petit déjeuner que nous n’en aurons jamais besoin ou envie, plus de mises à jour logicielles, de fonctionnalités et de forfaits téléphoniques que nous ne pouvons en suivre.

L’hôtel McAndrews

Chaque été, nous passons une quinzaine de jours à l’hôtel McAndrews, dans le nord du comté de Mayo, en Irlande. C’est une tradition familiale, instaurée par ma grand-mère, et elle a désormais acquis un certain caractère sacré. Rien n’est autorisé à troubler ce rituel. Nous sommes d’une certaine espèce, la clientèle du McAndrews : à l’ancienne, peut-être excentriques, certains diraient snobs. Je n’aime pas les mauvaises manières, l’insolence des vendeurs qui passe pour de l’égalitarisme à notre époque ; je supporte mal les familiarités des serveurs qui semblent parfois se retenir à grand-peine de vous donner une tape dans le dos. Je connais le nom de la plupart de mes compagnons de séjour — comme moi, ils viennent ici depuis leur enfance — et pourtant je peux être assuré que, lorsque j’en rencontre un dans n’importe quelle partie de l’hôtel, je serai dispensé de toute interaction sociale en dehors d’un mot de salut poli. Un tel respect de la dignité et de la vie privée est rare, de nos jours, dans les établissements commerciaux.

The Eden Project 

Since it opened, the Eden Project in the south-west of England has become one of the UK’s most popular tourist attractions. At first sight, the huge ‘biospheres’ on this former industrial site look like a scene from a science-fiction movie. 

Each biosphere contains a different climate zone, showing visitors just how important the relationship between people and plants is. It is amazing to see just how many products that we use every day come from plants: wood, rubber, fruit, rice, sugar, coffee and chocolate, for example. Over 135,000 different types of plant are grown here. However cold the weather is outside, computer-controlled electric heaters keep the plants at the right temperature. 
In the Rainforest Zone, the atmosphere is always damp because of a huge waterfall. Another zone reproduces the environment of the Mediterranean, California and South Africa, and there are plans to build a desert zone in the near future.
results.tgt_text:
Le projet Eden

Depuis son ouverture, le projet Eden, dans le sud-ouest de l’Angleterre, est devenu l’une des attractions touristiques les plus populaires du Royaume-Uni. À première vue, les immenses « biosphères » de cet ancien site industriel ressemblent à une scène tirée d’un film de science-fiction.

Chaque biosphère contient une zone climatique différente, montrant aux visiteurs à quel point la relation entre les êtres humains et les plantes est importante. Il est étonnant de voir combien de produits que nous utilisons chaque jour proviennent des plantes : le bois, le caoutchouc, les fruits, le riz, le sucre, le café et le chocolat, par exemple. Plus de 135 000 types de plantes différents y sont cultivés. Quelle que soit la rigueur du froid à l’extérieur, des chauffages électriques commandés par ordinateur maintiennent les plantes à la bonne température.
Dans la zone de la forêt tropicale, l’atmosphère est toujours humide grâce à une immense cascade. Une autre zone reproduit l’environnement de la Méditerranée, de la Californie et de l’Afrique du Sud, et il est prévu de construire une zone désertique dans un avenir proche.

The Eden Project

Since it opened, the Eden Project, in the southwest of England, has become one of the most popular tourist attractions in the United Kingdom. At first glance, the immense “biospheres” of this former industrial site look like a scene from a science-fiction film.

Each biosphere contains a different climate zone, showing visitors just how important the relationship between human beings and plants is. It is amazing to see how many products we use every day come from plants: wood, rubber, fruit, rice, sugar, coffee, and chocolate, for example. More than 135,000 different types of plants are grown there. No matter how bitterly cold it is outside, computer-controlled electric heaters keep the plants at the right temperature.
In the tropical rainforest zone, the atmosphere is always humid thanks to a huge waterfall. Another zone reproduces the environment of the Mediterranean, California, and South Africa, and there are plans to build a desert zone in the near future.

Henry was acutely aware of the importance of securing a male heir during his reign. He was worried that he had only one surviving child, Mary, to show for his marriage to Catherine, who was now in her 40s. So the king asked Cardinal Wolsey to appeal to Pope Clement VII for an annulment and it soon became clear he wanted to marry Anne Boleyn, who had been a lady-in-waiting to his first wife.
But, unwilling to anger Catherine of Aragon's nephew – the most powerful ruler in Europe, the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V – the Pope refused. Thomas Wolsey's ascendancy was cut short by this failure.
In 1533, Henry VIII broke with the church and married the now pregnant Anne Boleyn in a secret ceremony. Henry was excommunicated by the Pope. The English reformation had begun.
After Wolsey's downfall, Thomas Cromwell became Henry's chief minister and earned the confidence of the King by helping him to break with Rome and establish Henry VIII as head of the Church of England. This act also brought him much needed wealth through the dissolution of the well-funded monasteries. Over four years Cromwell ordered that 800 monasteries be disbanded and their lands and treasures taken for the crown.
The cultural and social impact was significant, as much of the land was sold to the gentry and churches and monasteries were gutted and destroyed. Henry's personal religious beliefs remained Catholic, despite the growing number of people at court and in the nation who had adopted Protestantism.

Schnauzer Dogs

There are three sizes of Schnauzer dog.
The two smaller sizes first came to England over 50 years ago, but the Giant Schnauzer has not been here very long. The name Giant is a good one because the dogs are 65 to 67.5 cm high.
All the dogs have long hair, which should be cut quite often. Most smaller Schnauzers are grey in colour, but the Giant Schnauzer is usually black.
Schnauzers come from Germany, where farmers use the dogs to help them with their sheep, and they are also used by the police, because Schnauzer dogs are very intelligent.
A Schnauzer makes a nice family dog. It is friendly and very good with young children.

The next day in the school library, Buffy was doing her exercises with Giles. She had to do them every day. A Vampire Slayer had to be strong.
Giles was holding a big soft ball. Buffy was hitting it as hard as she could. Xander was watching.
Buffy wanted to go to the World Culture Dance at the Bronze the next evening. But she was always busy at night. She walked around the streets of Sunnydale and looked for vampires.
'So,' she said to Giles, 'can I go?' She hit the ball very hard with her foot.
Giles almost fell. 'No,' he answered.
'Why not?' Buffy hit it again.
'Because you're the Slayer,' Giles said. 'You're not like other girls. You have a job, an important job. You haven't got time for dances.'
Another hit. 'Blah, blah, blah!' said Buffy. She was angry. It just wasn't fair.
Giles tried again. They often had this kind of conversation. 'Buffy - listen to me. You can't go to the dance. Your exchange student mustn't find out about you. You have to be careful while he's living with you.'
'He's living in the same house as her - he's not living with her,' Xander said quickly. No one seemed to understand the difference except him.
'So I have to go to the dance,' Buffy said. 'Like an ordinary person.' Hit!
'I didn't mean that,' said Giles. He was tired.
Buffy knew that she was winning. 'Come on, Giles!'
She got ready to hit the ball again.
'OK, OK!' Giles said quickly. 'That's enough for today. Go to your dance.'

results.title: 8120c2b8-1cfd-407a-b6c9-95d0a455fd05.txt
results.src_text:
Science flying in the face of gravity

Journalist Tom Mumford joins students using weightlessness to test their theories.

It looked like just another aircraft from the outside. The pilot told his young passengers that it was built in 1964, a Boeing KC-135 refuelling tanker, based on the Boeing 707 passenger craft.
But appearances were deceptive and the 13 students from Europe and America who boarded were in for the flight of their lives. Inside, it had become a long white tunnel.
There were almost no windows, but it was eerily illuminated by lights along the padded walls. Most of the seats had been ripped out, apart from a few at the back, where the pale-faced, budding scientists took their places with the air of condemned men.
For 12 months, they had competed with other students from across the continent to participate in the flight. The challenge, offered by the European Space Agency, had been to suggest imaginative experiments to be conducted in weightless conditions.
Those with the best ideas won a place on this unusual flight, which is best described as the most extraordinary roller-coaster ride yet devised. For the next two hours the Boeing's flight would resemble that of an enormous bird which had lost its reason, shooting upwards towards the heavens before hurtling towards Earth.
The intention was to achieve a kind of state of grace at the top of each curve. As the pilot cuts the engines at 3,000 metres, the aircraft throws itself still higher by virtue of its own momentum before gravity takes over and it plummets earthwards again.
In the few silent seconds between ascending and falling, the aircraft and everything inside it become weightless, and the 13 students would, in theory, feel themselves closer to the moon than the Earth. The aircraft took off smoothly enough, but any lingering illusions the young scientists and I had that we were on anything like a scheduled passenger service were quickly dispelled when the pilot put the Boeing into a 45-degree climb which lasted around 20 seconds. The engines strained wildly, blood drained from our heads, and bodies were scattered across the cabin floor.
Then the engines cut out and the transition to weightlessness was nearly instantaneous. For 20 seconds we conducted a ghostly dance in the unreal silence:the floor had become a vast trampoline, and one footstep was enough to launch us headlong towards the ceiling.
We floated aimlessly; the idea of going anywhere was itself confusing. Left or right, up or down, no longer had any meaning. Only gravity, by rooting us somewhere, permits us to appreciate the possibility of going somewhere else.
After ten seconds of freefall descent, the pilot pulled the aircraft out of its nose dive. The return of gravity was less immediate than its loss, but was still sudden enough to ensure that some of the students came down with a bump.
Our first curve completed, there were those who turned green at the thought of the 29 to follow. Thirty curves added up to ten minutes 'space time’ for experiments and the Dutch students were soon studying the movements of Leonardo, their robotic cat, hoping to discover how it is that cats always land on their feet.
At the appropriate moment the device they had built to investigate this was released, floating belly-up, and one of the students succeeded in turning it belly-down with radio-controlled movements. The next curve was nearly its last, however, when another student landed on top of it during a less well managed return to gravitational pull.
Next to the slightly stunned acrobatic robocat, a German team from the University of Aachen investigated how the quality of joins in metal is affected by the absence of gravity, with an eye to the construction of tomorrow's space stations.
Another team of students, from Utah State University, examined the possibility of creating solar sails from thin liquid films hardened in ultra-violet sunlight. Their flight was spent attempting to produce the films under microgravity. They believe that once the process is perfected, satellites could be equipped with solar sails that use the sun's radiation just as a yacht's sails use the wind. 
After two hours spent swinging between heaven and Earth, that morning’s breakfast felt unstable, but the predominant sensation was exhilaration, not nausea.
This was a feeling that would stay with us for a long time. ‘It was an unforgettable experience,’ said one of the students. 'I was already aiming to become an astronaut, but now I want to even more.’

La science défiant la gravité

Le journaliste Tom Mumford accompagne des étudiants qui utilisent l’apesanteur pour tester leurs théories.

De l’extérieur, cela ressemblait à un avion comme un autre. Le pilote expliqua à ses jeunes passagers qu’il avait été construit en 1964 : un Boeing KC-135 ravitailleur, dérivé de l’avion de ligne Boeing 707.
Mais les apparences étaient trompeuses, et les 13 étudiants venus d’Europe et d’Amérique qui montèrent à bord allaient vivre le vol de leur vie. À l’intérieur, l’appareil avait été transformé en un long tunnel blanc.
Il n’y avait presque pas de hublots, mais l’intérieur était baigné d’une lumière étrange diffusée par des lampes fixées le long des parois capitonnées. La plupart des sièges avaient été arrachés, à l’exception de quelques-uns au fond, où les jeunes scientifiques en herbe, le visage pâle, prirent place avec l’air de condamnés.
Pendant 12 mois, ils avaient affronté d’autres étudiants de tout le continent pour obtenir le droit de participer à ce vol. Le défi, lancé par l’Agence spatiale européenne, consistait à proposer des expériences originales à mener en conditions d’apesanteur.
Ceux qui avaient les meilleures idées remportaient une place à bord de ce vol inhabituel, que l’on pourrait décrire comme les montagnes russes les plus extraordinaires jamais conçues. Pendant les deux heures suivantes, la trajectoire du Boeing allait ressembler à celle d’un oiseau gigantesque ayant perdu la raison, s’élançant vers les cieux avant de replonger vers la Terre.
L’objectif était d’atteindre une sorte d’état de grâce au sommet de chaque courbe. Lorsque le pilote coupe les moteurs à 3 000 mètres, l’avion continue de monter grâce à son propre élan, avant que la gravité ne reprenne le dessus et qu’il ne retombe vers la Terre.
Pendant les quelques secondes silencieuses entre la montée et la chute, l’avion et tout ce qu’il contient deviennent en apesanteur, et les 13 étudiants devaient, en théorie, se sentir plus proches de la Lune que de la Terre. L’avion décolla assez doucement, mais les dernières illusions que les jeunes scientifiques et moi pouvions encore nourrir, en croyant voyager à bord de quelque chose ressemblant à un vol régulier, furent rapidement dissipées lorsque le pilote fit grimper le Boeing à 45 degrés pendant une vingtaine de secondes. Les moteurs rugissaient, le sang quittait nos têtes et les corps étaient projetés sur le plancher de la cabine.
Puis les moteurs furent coupés et le passage à l’apesanteur fut presque instantané. Pendant 20 secondes, nous exécutâmes une danse fantomatique dans un silence irréel : le sol était devenu un immense trampoline, et un simple pas suffisait à nous propulser tête la première vers le plafond.
Nous flottions sans but ; l’idée même d’aller quelque part devenait déroutante. À gauche ou à droite, en haut ou en bas, tout cela n’avait plus de sens. Seule la gravité, en nous assignant un lieu, nous permet d’apprécier la possibilité d’aller ailleurs.
Après dix secondes de chute libre, le pilote redressa l’appareil pour le sortir de son piqué. Le retour de la gravité fut moins immédiat que sa disparition, mais suffisamment brusque pour que certains étudiants retombent lourdement.
Notre première courbe achevée, certains devinrent verts à l’idée des 29 autres qui allaient suivre. Trente courbes représentaient au total dix minutes de « temps spatial » pour les expériences, et les étudiants néerlandais se mirent bientôt à étudier les mouvements de Leonardo, leur chat robotique, espérant découvrir pourquoi les chats retombent toujours sur leurs pattes.
Au moment voulu, l’appareil qu’ils avaient construit pour étudier ce phénomène fut lâché, flottant le ventre en l’air, et l’un des étudiants réussit à le retourner ventre en bas grâce à des commandes radio. La courbe suivante faillit pourtant lui être fatale, lorsqu’un autre étudiant retomba dessus lors d’un retour à la gravité moins bien maîtrisé.
À côté de ce chat acrobate robotique quelque peu sonné, une équipe allemande de l’université d’Aix-la-Chapelle étudiait comment l’absence de gravité affecte la qualité des assemblages métalliques, dans la perspective de construire les stations spatiales de demain.
Une autre équipe d’étudiants, de l’université d’État de l’Utah, examinait la possibilité de créer des voiles solaires à partir de minces films liquides durcis par la lumière ultraviolette du soleil. Leur vol fut consacré à tenter de produire ces films en microgravité. Ils pensent qu’une fois le procédé perfectionné, on pourrait équiper les satellites de voiles solaires utilisant le rayonnement du soleil comme les voiles d’un yacht utilisent le vent.
Après deux heures passées à osciller entre le ciel et la Terre, le petit déjeuner de ce matin-là semblait peu stable, mais la sensation dominante était l’exaltation, non la nausée.
C’était un sentiment qui resterait longtemps avec nous. « Ce fut une expérience inoubliable », déclara l’un des étudiants. « Je voulais déjà devenir astronaute, mais maintenant je le veux encore davantage. »

Science Defying Gravity

Journalist Tom Mumford accompanies students who use weightlessness to test their theories.

From the outside, it looked like any other airplane. The pilot explained to his young passengers that it had been built in 1964: a Boeing KC-135 tanker aircraft, derived from the Boeing 707 airliner.
But appearances were deceptive, and the 13 students from Europe and America who boarded it were about to experience the flight of their lives. Inside, the aircraft had been transformed into a long white tunnel.
There were almost no windows, but the interior was bathed in a strange light cast by lamps fixed along the padded walls. Most of the seats had been ripped out, except for a few at the back, where the pale-faced young aspiring scientists took their places with the air of people condemned.
For 12 months, they had competed against other students from across the continent for the right to take part in this flight. The challenge, launched by the European Space Agency, was to propose original experiments to be carried out under conditions of weightlessness.
Those with the best ideas won a place on board this unusual flight, which could be described as the most extraordinary roller coaster ever devised. For the next two hours, the Boeing’s trajectory would resemble that of a gigantic bird gone mad, soaring toward the heavens before plunging back toward Earth.
The goal was to reach a kind of state of grace at the top of each curve. When the pilot cuts the engines at 3,000 meters, the plane continues to climb on its own momentum before gravity takes over again and it falls back toward Earth.
During the few silent seconds between the climb and the fall, the plane and everything in it become weightless, and the 13 students were, in theory, supposed to feel closer to the Moon than to Earth. The plane took off gently enough, but any lingering illusions that the young scientists and I may still have had, imagining we were traveling on something resembling a regular flight, were quickly swept away when the pilot sent the Boeing climbing at a 45-degree angle for about twenty seconds. The engines roared, the blood drained from our heads, and our bodies were hurled onto the cabin floor.
Then the engines were cut and the shift to weightlessness was almost instantaneous. For 20 seconds, we performed a ghostly dance in an unreal silence: the floor had become a giant trampoline, and a single step was enough to send us headfirst toward the ceiling.
We floated aimlessly; the very idea of going anywhere became bewildering. Left or right, up or down, none of it made any sense anymore. Only gravity, by assigning us a place, allows us to appreciate the possibility of going elsewhere.
After ten seconds of free fall, the pilot pulled the plane out of its dive. The return of gravity was less immediate than its disappearance, but sudden enough for some students to crash back down heavily.
With our first arc completed, some turned green at the thought of the 29 others still to come. Thirty arcs represented a total of ten minutes of “space time” for the experiments, and the Dutch students soon began studying the movements of Leonardo, their robot cat, hoping to discover why cats always land on their feet.
At the right moment, the device they had built to study this phenomenon was released, floating belly-up, and one of the students managed to turn it belly-down using radio controls. Yet the next arc nearly proved fatal for it, when another student fell on top of it during a less well-controlled return to gravity.
Next to this somewhat stunned acrobatic robot cat, a German team from Aachen University was studying how the absence of gravity affects the quality of metal joints, with a view to building the space stations of tomorrow.
Another student team, from Utah State University, was examining the possibility of creating solar sails from thin liquid films hardened by the sun’s ultraviolet light. Their flight was devoted to trying to produce these films in microgravity. They believe that once the process is perfected, satellites could be equipped with solar sails that use the sun’s radiation in the same way a yacht’s sails use the wind.
After two hours spent oscillating between the sky and the Earth, that morning’s breakfast seemed rather unsteady, but the dominant feeling was exhilaration, not nausea.
It was a feeling that would stay with us for a long time. “It was an unforgettable experience,” said one of the students. “I already wanted to become an astronaut, but now I want it even more.”

He started walking down to the village. It was difficult because he was very tired. He went carefully because he didn't want to fall again. By the end of the day he was at the river, and he stopped for a drink. 
There were beautiful flowers near the river. 'This is a lovely place,' Nunez thought. There were a lot of small houses in the centre of the village. They looked very strange to him, because they didn't have any windows. 
He could see men and women at work in the village. Some were in the fields with their children. He could see gardens near the houses and there were fine vegetables in them. When Nunez was near the village, he shouted to some men. 
'Hello!' he shouted. 'Hello ... hello!' and he waved his arms. The men heard him and they turned their heads. They looked one way, and then the other way. They looked past Nunez, but they didn't look at him. 'Why can't they see me?' he thought. 
Nunez moved nearer and shouted again. He was now quite near three men. He waved again, but they didn't wave back to him. 'What's wrong with them?' he thought. 'Are they blind?' He walked down to the men, and then he saw their faces. 
He was right - the men were all blind. They had no eyes. 'Who is this?' one man asked his friend. 'A man? Or is it a spirit?' 'It's a man,' said the second man. 'I think it's a man.'

Il commença à descendre vers le village. C’était difficile parce qu’il était très fatigué. Il avançait prudemment parce qu’il ne voulait pas retomber. À la fin de la journée, il arriva à la rivière et s’arrêta pour boire.

Il y avait de belles fleurs près de la rivière. « C’est un endroit charmant », pensa Nunez. Il y avait beaucoup de petites maisons au centre du village. Elles lui paraissaient très étranges, parce qu’elles n’avaient pas de fenêtres.

Il pouvait voir des hommes et des femmes au travail dans le village. Certains étaient dans les champs avec leurs enfants. Il voyait des jardins près des maisons et il y avait de beaux légumes. Quand Nunez fut près du village, il cria à des hommes :

« Bonjour ! » cria-t-il. « Bonjour… bonjour ! » et il agita les bras. Les hommes l’entendirent et tournèrent la tête. Ils regardèrent d’un côté, puis de l’autre. Ils regardèrent au-delà de Nunez, mais ils ne le regardèrent pas. « Pourquoi ne peuvent-ils pas me voir ? » pensa-t-il.

Nunez s’approcha et cria de nouveau. Il était maintenant tout près de trois hommes. Il agita encore la main, mais ils ne lui répondirent pas par un geste. « Qu’est-ce qu’ils ont ? » pensa-t-il. « Sont-ils aveugles ? » Il descendit vers les hommes, puis il vit leurs visages.

Il avait raison : les hommes étaient tous aveugles. Ils n’avaient pas d’yeux. « Qui est-ce ? » demanda un homme à son ami. « Un homme ? Ou est-ce un esprit ? » « C’est un homme, dit le deuxième homme. Je crois que c’est un homme. »

Life was getting out of hand

Susan Harr unplugs her gadgets and rediscovers the joys of manual labour.

Everyone is in love with technology. It gives us all those marvellous gadgets that make life easier and leave us so much more time to do other things. A gradual, though not particularly subtle, form of brainwashing has persuaded us that technology rules, and that it is OK.
These implications are obvious. The movement of my fingers uses nothing from the previous power supply being eaten up by our greedy race. A craft executed by hand does not pollute the environment.
However, a recent unhappy experience with my malfunctioning word processor -
a £48 call-out fee, a labour charge of £15 per quarter of an hour, plus parts and replacements costs - has confirmed a suspicion that gadgets are often not worth the expense or the trouble. Are we as dependent on technology as we imagine? Bit by bit, I have been letting the household technology fall by the wayside as its natural and often short life expires.
This makes me wonder just what 'time' technology gives us. The time to take up more activities for which we must buy more gadgets? If so, hats off to the marketing experts: but I think they are conning us.
So when the thing started making curious noises, which continued even when it was disconnected by a puzzled service agent, I abandoned it to the backyard, where it whispers damply to itself like some robot ghost.
I am not tied to a noisy, whirring machine, with my head bent and my back turned on the world, and I can take my time over the garment. In any case, I was always slightly alarmed by those electric machines that dash across the fabric towards your fingers. Best of all, I can pop the whole lot into a carrier bag and take it with me wherever I go.
Of course, there are some gadgets I would not like to be without. A year living without a washing machine convinced me of the value of the electric washtub. But there are others whose loss has brought unexpected delight. Feeling that we were becoming too apt to collapse in front of the television, or slot in a video, I sent back the rented colour equipment and we returned to the small black-and-white portable.
It is a real strain on the eyes and concentrates the mind on what is really worth watching. We now spend a lot more time walking the dog (who never liked television anyway), reading, talking or pursuing other hobbies.
One of these, in my own case, is sewing; and here is another gadget that went by the board. My old Singer sewing machine is now an ornamental plant table, and as l cannot afford to replace it, I have taken to sewing by hand.
We have come to believe that we could not do without it, and if we do resist the notion that our lives would be unmanageable without the appliances of science we certainly do not want to relinquish them. Pity the generations whose lives were blighted by tedious and blister inducing toil. Even our brains are relieved of exertion by computers that not only perform miraculous calculations with amazing speed but now provide entertainment.
In fact, the time I now spend placidly stitching is anything but tedious, and the advantages are numerous. For a start, I can sew and listen to the radio - another rediscovered pleasure - or I can talk with family and friends. If it is a simple task, I can watch the programmes I do want to see on television, and alleviate my puritanical guilt at sitting in front of the box by doing something useful at the same time. And what a lovely, cosy feeling it is to sit by the fire and sew with a pot of tea for company.
Quite wrongly, I had tended to think with horror of the women who sewed elaborate garments, robes, linen and household items by hand. I thought of those long hours, the strain on the eyes and so on. 
There is a wonderfully soothing quality about executing a craft by hand, a great satisfaction in watching one's work become neater, more assured. I find things get done surprisingly quickly, and the pace of life suddenly slows down to the rhythm of my own hands. I am also freed from one of the most detestable aspects of late 20th century life the need to rush to finish an activity so that I can rush to the next.
Meanwhile I have regained control of my sink, where I plunge my hands into the suds and daydream while doing the washing up agreeable, if temporarily forgotten, activity.
The result of all this brooding is that I now prowl the house with a speculative eye. Do we really need the freezer, the microwave oven, that powered lawnmower? Come to think of it, we could save an awful lot of money by doing without electric lights!

48 livres de frais de déplacement, 15 livres de main-d’œuvre par quart d’heure, plus le prix des pièces et des remplacements — a confirmé un soupçon : les gadgets ne valent souvent ni la dépense ni les ennuis.
