Looking after the countryside 

THE NATIONAL TRUST 

The National Trust is an organisation whose aim is to conserve the British countryside. Gill Page visits the Lleyn Peninsula in North Wales and talks to one of the wardens employed by the Trust to look after the beautiful areas it owns. 

Common sense. That's what a National Trust Warden needs, according to Gareth Roberts. 'And you definitely need to be good at handling people, because you're continually dealing with farmers, visitors, conservationists and building firms.' 
Gareth was born and bred on the Lleyn Peninsula and worked on his parents' farm until he married. About 80 people applied for the post as National Trust Warden for the Lleyn Peninsula. In the end, Gareth's local knowledge and farming experience won him the job, despite his lack of formal training. 
'I find it particularly helpful that I still farm with my parents and that I can deal with farmers on the same level and be aware of their problems. Also, they can't take me in about anything!' he says. His farming life also means he is well able to cope with the physical demands of the job - erecting fences, planting trees, building walls. 
Since he has been with the Trust, Gareth says he has come to understand more about nature conservation. 'When I was a youngster,' he recalls, 'I used to pick and press flowers, collect butterfly larvae and old birds' nests. And I thought to myself recently, where would I find all those flowers, the birds' nests, the grasshoppers now? It's really become clear to me that farming has affected the countryside. It's not the farmers' fault - they were just doing what the government told them.' 
Gareth says that, when he started his job, farmers and conservationists were set against each other. Both sides wanted things done their way.Now they are talking and can see each other's point of view. 'We're at the crossroads and there's just a small step needed to join them together,' says Gareth. 
Conservation is one of the main aspects of Gareth's work, along with public entry to the Trust's land, tree planting and maintenance, and meeting the Trust's tenant farmers. 'My role is to make sure jobs get finished, with as little fuss and as economically as possible. What I enjoy most is seeing projects completed, although about half my time is spent on reports, signing bills and so on.' 
Gareth is certainly keen on his job and despite never being off duty, he obviously enjoys every minute of his work, especially talking to the public. Most of them, anyway. 'It's the attitude of some people I dislike,' he admits. 'They just walk into the area, demand everything, then walk out again as if it's their absolute right. Having to be nice to those people gets on my nerves!' 
But as Gareth says, it's all down to common sense really.So if you've got plenty of that, and you like the idea of an outdoor job, you might think of applying to become a warden like Gareth - but don't expect a job to be available on the Lleyn Peninsula for a good many years!
results.tgt_text:
Prendre soin de la campagne

LE NATIONAL TRUST

Le National Trust est une organisation dont le but est de préserver la campagne britannique. Gill Page visite la péninsule de Llŷn, dans le nord du pays de Galles, et s’entretient avec l’un des gardes employés par le Trust pour veiller sur les magnifiques régions dont il est propriétaire.

Du bon sens. Voilà ce dont un garde du National Trust a besoin, selon Gareth Roberts. « Et il faut absolument savoir bien s’y prendre avec les gens, parce qu’on est constamment en contact avec des agriculteurs, des visiteurs, des écologistes et des entreprises de construction. »

Gareth est né et a grandi sur la péninsule de Llŷn et a travaillé dans la ferme de ses parents jusqu’à son mariage. Environ 80 personnes ont posé leur candidature au poste de garde du National Trust pour la péninsule de Llŷn. Finalement, ce sont ses connaissances locales et son expérience agricole qui lui ont permis d’obtenir le poste, malgré son absence de formation officielle.

« Je trouve particulièrement utile de continuer à travailler à la ferme avec mes parents, car cela me permet de traiter avec les agriculteurs d’égal à égal et de comprendre leurs problèmes. Et puis, ils ne peuvent rien me faire croire de faux ! », dit-il. Sa vie d’agriculteur signifie aussi qu’il est tout à fait capable de faire face aux exigences physiques du travail : poser des clôtures, planter des arbres, construire des murs.

Depuis qu’il travaille pour le Trust, Gareth dit qu’il comprend mieux la protection de la nature. « Quand j’étais jeune, se souvient-il, je cueillais et faisais sécher des fleurs, je collectionnais des larves de papillons et de vieux nids d’oiseaux. Et récemment, je me suis demandé : où trouverais-je aujourd’hui toutes ces fleurs, ces nids d’oiseaux, ces sauterelles ? Il est vraiment devenu évident pour moi que l’agriculture a eu un effet sur la campagne. Ce n’est pas la faute des agriculteurs : ils faisaient simplement ce que le gouvernement leur disait de faire. »

Gareth explique que, lorsqu’il a commencé son travail, les agriculteurs et les écologistes s’opposaient les uns aux autres. Les deux camps voulaient que les choses se fassent à leur manière. Aujourd’hui, ils se parlent et peuvent comprendre le point de vue de l’autre. « Nous sommes à la croisée des chemins et il ne manque qu’un petit pas pour les réunir », dit Gareth.

La protection de la nature est l’un des principaux aspects du travail de Gareth, avec l’accès du public aux terres du Trust, la plantation et l’entretien des arbres, ainsi que les rencontres avec les fermiers locataires du Trust. « Mon rôle consiste à m’assurer que les travaux soient terminés, avec le moins de complications possible et de la manière la plus économique possible. Ce que j’aime le plus, c’est voir les projets achevés, même si environ la moitié de mon temps est consacrée aux rapports, à la signature des factures, etc. »

Gareth tient certainement beaucoup à son travail et, bien qu’il ne soit jamais vraiment de repos, il apprécie manifestement chaque minute de ce qu’il fait, surtout lorsqu’il parle au public. Enfin, à la plupart des gens. « C’est l’attitude de certaines personnes que je n’aime pas, reconnaît-il. Elles entrent simplement dans la région, exigent tout, puis repartent comme si c’était leur droit absolu. Devoir être aimable avec ces gens-là m’agace ! »

Mais comme le dit Gareth, tout cela relève vraiment du bon sens. Donc, si vous en avez à revendre et que l’idée d’un travail en plein air vous plaît, vous pourriez envisager de poser votre candidature pour devenir garde comme Gareth — mais ne vous attendez pas à ce qu’un poste se libère sur la péninsule de Llŷn avant de très nombreuses années !
results.back_text:
Taking Care of the Countryside

THE NATIONAL TRUST

The National Trust is an organization whose aim is to preserve the British countryside. Gill Page visits the Llŷn Peninsula in North Wales and talks to one of the wardens employed by the Trust to look after the beautiful areas it owns.

Common sense. That is what a National Trust warden needs, according to Gareth Roberts. “And you absolutely have to know how to deal well with people, because we are constantly in contact with farmers, visitors, environmentalists, and construction companies.”

Gareth was born and raised on the Llŷn Peninsula and worked on his parents’ farm until he got married. About 80 people applied for the job of National Trust warden for the Llŷn Peninsula. In the end, it was his local knowledge and farming experience that enabled him to get the job, despite his lack of formal training.

“I find it especially useful to keep working on the farm with my parents, because it allows me to deal with farmers on equal terms and understand their problems. And besides, they can’t make me believe anything that isn’t true!” he says. His life as a farmer also means that he is perfectly capable of coping with the physical demands of the job: putting up fences, planting trees, building walls.

Since he started working for the Trust, Gareth says he has come to understand nature conservation better. “When I was young,” he recalls, “I used to pick and dry flowers, collect butterfly larvae and old birds’ nests. And recently I asked myself: where would I find all those flowers, those birds’ nests, those grasshoppers today? It has really become obvious to me that farming has had an effect on the countryside. It isn’t the farmers’ fault: they were simply doing what the government told them to do.”

Gareth explains that when he began the job, farmers and environmentalists were opposed to each other. Both sides wanted things done their own way. Today, they talk to each other and can understand the other’s point of view. “We are at a crossroads and only one small step is needed to bring them together,” says Gareth.

Nature conservation is one of the main aspects of Gareth’s work, along with public access to Trust land, planting and maintaining trees, and meeting the Trust’s tenant farmers. “My job is to make sure that the work gets done, with as few complications as possible and in the most economical way possible. What I enjoy most is seeing projects completed, even though about half my time is spent on reports, signing invoices, and so on.”

Gareth certainly cares deeply about his work and, although he is never really off duty, he clearly enjoys every minute of what he does, especially when he is talking to the public. Well, most people. “It’s the attitude of some people that I don’t like,” he admits. “They simply come into the area, demand everything, and then leave as if it were their absolute right. Having to be nice to people like that annoys me!”

But as Gareth says, it all really comes down to common sense. So if you have plenty of that and the idea of an outdoor job appeals to you, you might consider applying to become a warden like Gareth—but do not expect a position on the Llŷn Peninsula to become available for many years to come!

Monsieur Firmin was right. All Paris talked about the new Margarita in Faust, the girl with the beautiful voice, the girl with the voice of an angel. People loved her. They laughed and cried and called for more. Daae was wonderful, the best singer in the world!
Behind the stage Meg Giry looked at Annie Sorelli. 'Christine Daae never sang like that before,' she said to Annie. 'Why was she so good tonight?'
'Perhaps she's got a new music teacher,' Annie said.
The noise in the Opera House went on for a long time. In Box 14, Philippe, the Comte de Chagny, turned to his younger brother and smiled.
'Well, Raoul, what did you think of Daae tonight?'
Raoul, the Vicomte de Chagny, was twenty-one years old. He had blue eyes and black hair, and a wonderful smile. The Chagny family was old and rich, and many girls in Paris were in love with the young Vicomte. But Raoul was not interested in them.
He smiled back at his brother. 'What can I say? Christine is an angel, that's all. I'm going to her dressing-room to see her tonight.'
Philippe laughed. He was twenty years older than Raoul, and was more like a father than a brother.
'Ah, I understand,' he said. 'You are in love! But this is your first night in Paris, your first visit to the opera. How do you know Christine Daae?'
'You remember four years ago, when I was on holiday by the sea, in Brittany?' Raoul said. 'Well, I met Christine there. I was in love with her then, and I'm still in love with her today!'

The cop saw the car stop on the bridge but didn't think too much about it. People often stopped their cars on the bridge late at night, when there was not much traffic. The bridge was over the deep river that cut the city neatly in two, and the center of the bridge provided the best view of the city.
Suicides liked the bridge, too. The cop didn't think of that until he saw the man get out of the car, walk slowly along the footpath at the edge, and put a hand on the rail. There was something about that lonely figure, something about the grayness of the night, the fog coming off the river. The cop looked at him and swore, and wondered if he could get to him in time.
He didn't want to shout or blow his whistle because he knew what surprise could do to a probable suicide. Then the man lit a cigarette, and the cop knew he had time. They always smoked all of that last cigarette before they went over the edge.
When the cop was within ten yards of him, the man turned, gave a slight jump, then nodded as if accepting that the moment had passed. He appeared to be in his middle thirties, tall with a long narrow face and thick black eyebrows.
'Looking at the city?' said the cop. 'I saw you here, and thought I'd come and have a talk with you. It can get lonely at this hour of the night.' He patted his pockets, pretending to look for his cigarettes and not finding them. 'Got a spare cigarette on you?' he asked.
The man gave him a cigarette and lit it for him. The cop thanked the man and looked out at the city.

Le policier a vu la voiture s’arrêter sur le pont, mais il n’y a pas prêté grande attention. Les gens arrêtaient souvent leur voiture sur le pont tard dans la nuit, quand la circulation était faible. Le pont enjambait la rivière profonde qui coupait nettement la ville en deux, et le centre du pont offrait la meilleure vue sur la ville.

Les suicidaires aimaient aussi le pont. Le policier n’y pensa pas jusqu’à ce qu’il voie l’homme sortir de la voiture, marcher lentement le long du trottoir au bord du pont et poser une main sur la rambarde. Il y avait quelque chose dans cette silhouette solitaire, quelque chose dans la grisaille de la nuit, dans le brouillard qui montait de la rivière. Le policier le regarda et jura, se demandant s’il pourrait arriver jusqu’à lui à temps.

Il ne voulait ni crier ni siffler, parce qu’il savait ce que la surprise pouvait provoquer chez un suicidaire probable. Puis l’homme alluma une cigarette, et le policier sut qu’il avait du temps. Ils fumaient toujours entièrement cette dernière cigarette avant de basculer dans le vide.

Quand le policier fut à une dizaine de mètres de lui, l’homme se retourna, fit un léger bond, puis hocha la tête comme s’il acceptait que l’instant fût passé. Il paraissait dans le milieu de la trentaine, grand, avec un visage long et étroit et d’épais sourcils noirs.

— Vous regardez la ville ? dit le policier. Je vous ai vu ici, et je me suis dit que je viendrais bavarder un peu avec vous. On peut se sentir seul à cette heure de la nuit.  
Il se tapota les poches, faisant semblant de chercher ses cigarettes sans les trouver.  
— Vous n’auriez pas une cigarette de trop ? demanda-t-il.

L’homme lui donna une cigarette et la lui alluma. Le policier le remercia et regarda la ville.

Steve Jobs met engineering student Steve Wozniak through a mutual friend. Jobs was surprised to find Wozniak “knew more about electronics than I did.”
Their first joint venture was building devices that enabled people to make illegal free calls. Wozniak later said it was a “bad idea” to sell them, but it gave the duo “a taste of what we could do with my engineering skills and Jobs’ vision.” They then worked on a game for Atari, where Jobs convinced Wozniak to work round the clock to produce the game in four days – something Wozniak considered to be impossible. Jobs was paid a bonus for delivering on time that he kept secret from Wozniak.
Steve Jobs insisted on attending Reed College, Oregon, an expensive liberal arts university, despite his parents telling him they couldn’t afford it.
However, he soon dropped out. He had an on-off relationship with Chrisann Brennan and lived in a cabin in Los Gatos, California. His passion for good design led him to drop into a calligraphy class back at Reed which later inspired him to include a selection of fonts on his computers. He visited India, shaved his head and wore traditional Indian clothes. Eastern philosophy influenced him. He said: “I saw the craziness of the Western world as well as its capacity for rational thought.”
Jobs and Wozniak formed Apple Computer and built their first machine, the Apple I. It was sold without a case, screen, power supply or keyboard.

results.src_text:
It's true - we're all getting too big for our boots

Chris Greener was fourteen when he told his careers teacher he wanted to join the navy when he left school. 'What do you want to be?' asked the teacher. 'The flagpole on a ship?' The teacher had a point - because Chris, though still only fourteen, was already almost two metres tall. Today, at 228 cm, he is Britain's tallest man.
Every decade, the average height of people in Europe grows another centimetre. Every year, more and more truly big people are born. Intriguingly, this does not mean humanity is producing a new super race. In fact, we are returning to what we were like as cavemen. Only now are we losing the effects of generations of poor diet - with dramatic effects. 'We are only now beginning to fulfil our proper potential,' says palaeontologist Professor Chris Stringer. 'We are becoming Cro-Magnons again - the people who lived on this planet 40,000 years ago.'
For most of human history, our ancestors got their food from a wide variety of sources: women gathered herbs, fruits and berries, while men supplemented these with occasional kills of animals (a way of life still adopted by the world's few remaining tribes of hunter- gatherers). One research study found that they based their diet on 85 different wild plants, for example. Then about 9,000 years ago, agriculture was invented - with devastating consequences. Most of the planet's green places have been gradually taken over by farmers, with the result that just three carbohydrate-rich plants - wheat, rice and maize - provide more than half of the calories consumed by the human race today.
This poor diet has had a disastrous effect on human health and physique. Over the centuries we have lived on soups, porridges and breads that have left us underfed and underdeveloped. In one study in Ohio, scientists discovered that when they began to grow corn, healthy hunter-gatherers were turned into sickly, underweight farmers. Tooth decay increased, as did diseases. Far from being one of the blessings of the New World, corn was a public health disaster, according to some anthropologists.
Nevertheless, from then on agriculture spread because a piece of farmed land could support ten times the number of people who had previously lived off it as hunter-gatherers. The fact that most people relying on this system are poorly nourished and stunted has only recently been tackled, even by the world's wealthier nations. Only in Europe, the US and Japan are diets again reflecting the richness of our ancestors' diets.
As a result, the average man in the US is now 179cm, in Holland 180 cm, and in Japan 177 cm. It is a welcome trend, though not without its own problems. Heights may have risen, but the world has not moved on, it seems. A standard bed-length has remained at 190cm since 1860. Even worse, leg-room in planes and trains seems to have shrunk rather than grown, while clothes manufacturers are constantly having to revise their range of products.
The question is: where will it all end? We cannot grow for ever. We must have some programmed upper limit. But what is it? According to Robert Fogel, of University, it could be as much as 193 cm - and we are likely to reach it some time this century.
However, scientists add one note of qualification. Individuals may be growing taller because of improved nutrition, but as a species we are actually shrinking. During the last ice age, 10,000 years ago, members of the human race were slightly rounder and taller - an evolutionary response to the cold. (Large, round bodies are best at keeping in heat.) Since the climate warmed, we appear to have got slightly thinner and smaller, even when properly fed. And as the planet continues to heat up, we may shrink even further. In other words, the growth of human beings could be offset by global warming.
results.tgt_text:
C’est vrai : nous prenons tous trop de place

Chris Greener avait quatorze ans lorsqu’il a dit à son conseiller d’orientation qu’il voulait entrer dans la marine en quittant l’école. « Que veux-tu devenir ? » demanda l’enseignant. « Le mât d’un navire ? » Le professeur n’avait pas tort : Chris, bien qu’il n’ait alors que quatorze ans, mesurait déjà presque deux mètres. Aujourd’hui, avec ses 228 cm, c’est l’homme le plus grand de Grande-Bretagne.

Tous les dix ans, la taille moyenne des Européens augmente d’un centimètre supplémentaire. Chaque année, il naît de plus en plus de personnes réellement très grandes. Fait intriguant, cela ne signifie pas que l’humanité est en train de produire une nouvelle super-race. En réalité, nous revenons à ce que nous étions à l’époque des hommes des cavernes. Ce n’est que maintenant que nous nous débarrassons des effets de générations de mauvaise alimentation — avec des conséquences spectaculaires. « Ce n’est que maintenant que nous commençons à réaliser pleinement notre véritable potentiel », affirme le paléontologue Chris Stringer. « Nous redevenons des Cro-Magnons — les hommes qui vivaient sur cette planète il y a 40 000 ans. »

Pendant la majeure partie de l’histoire humaine, nos ancêtres tiraient leur nourriture d’une grande diversité de sources : les femmes cueillaient des herbes, des fruits et des baies, tandis que les hommes complétaient cela par des prises occasionnelles d’animaux (un mode de vie encore adopté par les quelques tribus de chasseurs-cueilleurs qui subsistent dans le monde). Une étude a ainsi montré que leur alimentation reposait sur 85 plantes sauvages différentes. Puis, il y a environ 9 000 ans, l’agriculture a été inventée — avec des conséquences dévastatrices. La plupart des espaces verts de la planète ont été progressivement occupés par les agriculteurs, si bien qu’aujourd’hui seulement trois plantes riches en glucides — le blé, le riz et le maïs — fournissent plus de la moitié des calories consommées par l’humanité.

Cette alimentation pauvre a eu un effet désastreux sur la santé et la constitution physique de l’être humain. Au fil des siècles, nous avons vécu de soupes, de bouillies et de pains qui nous ont laissés sous-alimentés et insuffisamment développés. Dans une étude menée dans l’Ohio, des scientifiques ont découvert que lorsque l’on a commencé à cultiver le maïs, des chasseurs-cueilleurs en bonne santé se sont transformés en agriculteurs malingres et de faible poids. Les caries dentaires ont augmenté, tout comme les maladies. Loin d’être l’une des bénédictions du Nouveau Monde, le maïs a été, selon certains anthropologues, une catastrophe de santé publique.

Néanmoins, à partir de ce moment-là, l’agriculture s’est répandue parce qu’une parcelle de terre cultivée pouvait faire vivre dix fois plus de personnes que lorsqu’elle était exploitée auparavant par des chasseurs-cueilleurs. Le fait que la plupart des gens dépendant de ce système soient mal nourris et aient une croissance ralentie n’a été pris en compte que récemment, même dans les nations les plus riches du monde. Ce n’est qu’en Europe, aux États-Unis et au Japon que les régimes alimentaires recommencent à refléter la richesse de ceux de nos ancêtres.

En conséquence, la taille moyenne des hommes est aujourd’hui de 179 cm aux États-Unis, de 180 cm aux Pays-Bas et de 177 cm au Japon. C’est une évolution bienvenue, bien qu’elle ne soit pas sans poser certains problèmes. La taille a peut-être augmenté, mais le monde, lui, ne semble pas avoir suivi. La longueur standard d’un lit est restée à 190 cm depuis 1860. Pire encore, l’espace pour les jambes dans les avions et les trains semble avoir diminué plutôt qu’augmenté, tandis que les fabricants de vêtements doivent constamment revoir leur gamme de produits.

La question est la suivante : où tout cela s’arrêtera-t-il ? Nous ne pouvons pas grandir éternellement. Nous devons bien avoir une limite supérieure programmée. Mais laquelle ? Selon Robert Fogel, de l’Université, elle pourrait atteindre 193 cm — et nous sommes susceptibles de l’atteindre au cours de ce siècle.

Cependant, les scientifiques ajoutent une réserve. Les individus grandissent peut-être davantage grâce à une meilleure nutrition, mais en tant qu’espèce, nous sommes en réalité en train de rapetisser. Durant la dernière période glaciaire, il y a 10 000 ans, les membres de l’espèce humaine étaient légèrement plus trapus et plus grands — une réponse évolutive au froid. (Les corps grands et ronds conservent mieux la chaleur.) Depuis que le climat s’est réchauffé, nous semblons être devenus légèrement plus minces et plus petits, même lorsque nous sommes correctement nourris. Et à mesure que la planète continue de se réchauffer, nous pourrions rapetisser encore davantage. En d’autres termes, la croissance des êtres humains pourrait être compensée par le réchauffement climatique.

It’s true: we all take up too much space

Chris Greener was fourteen when he told his careers adviser that he wanted to join the navy when he left school. “What do you want to become?” asked the teacher. “A ship’s mast?” The teacher was not wrong: Chris, although he was only fourteen at the time, was already almost two metres tall. Today, at 228 cm, he is the tallest man in Britain.

Every ten years, the average height of Europeans increases by an extra centimetre. Each year, more and more truly very tall people are being born. Intriguingly, this does not mean that humanity is producing a new super-race. In reality, we are returning to what we were in the time of the cavemen. Only now are we shedding the effects of generations of poor diet — with spectacular consequences. “Only now are we beginning to fully realize our true potential,” says the paleontologist Chris Stringer. “We are becoming Cro-Magnons again — the humans who lived on this planet 40,000 years ago.”

For most of human history, our ancestors got their food from a great variety of sources: women gathered herbs, fruit, and berries, while men supplemented this with occasional catches of animals (a way of life still followed by the few hunter-gatherer tribes that remain in the world). One study showed that their diet was based on 85 different wild plants. Then, about 9,000 years ago, agriculture was invented — with devastating consequences. Most of the planet’s green spaces were gradually taken over by farmers, so that today only three carbohydrate-rich plants — wheat, rice, and maize — provide more than half of the calories consumed by humanity.

This poor diet had a disastrous effect on human health and physique. Over the centuries, we have lived on soups, porridges, and breads that left us undernourished and underdeveloped. In a study carried out in Ohio, scientists discovered that when maize began to be cultivated, healthy hunter-gatherers turned into scrawny, underweight farmers. Tooth decay increased, as did disease. Far from being one of the blessings of the New World, maize was, according to some anthropologists, a public health catastrophe.

Nevertheless, from that point on, agriculture spread because a plot of cultivated land could support ten times more people than when it had previously been used by hunter-gatherers. The fact that most people dependent on this system were poorly nourished and stunted was only taken into account recently, even in the richest nations in the world. It is only in Europe, the United States, and Japan that diets are once again beginning to reflect the richness of those of our ancestors.

As a result, the average height of men today is 179 cm in the United States, 180 cm in the Netherlands, and 177 cm in Japan. It is a welcome development, although it is not without certain problems. Height may have increased, but the world itself does not seem to have kept up. The standard length of a bed has remained 190 cm since 1860. Worse still, legroom on planes and trains seems to have shrunk rather than increased, while clothing manufacturers have to constantly revise their product ranges.

The question is this: where will it all stop? We cannot keep growing forever. There must be some programmed upper limit. But what is it? According to Robert Fogel, of the University, it could be as much as 193 cm — and we are likely to reach it during this century.

However, scientists add a qualification. Individuals may be growing taller thanks to better nutrition, but as a species, we are actually shrinking. During the last Ice Age, 10,000 years ago, members of the human species were slightly stockier and taller — an evolutionary response to the cold. (Large, round bodies retain heat better.) Since the climate warmed, we seem to have become slightly slimmer and shorter, even when properly nourished. And as the planet continues to warm, we may shrink even further. In other words, the growth of human beings could be offset by global warming.

results.src_text:
The Cabinet-Maker
Charles Hurst makes a living from perfectly crafted furniture Joanna Watt meets him
Charles Hurst gives the impression of being a man in a hurry. I arrive at his workshop, tucked under a railway arch in East London, and am greeted with a quick handshake and the words: 'Well, fire away then!' Whether this brusqueness is real or a front hiding a shy streak is not immediately apparent. But a glance around the workshop reveals that Hurst is obviously busy, with good reason not to waste a minute of his time.
The arched space is full of half-made pieces of furniture and planks of wood in an amazing array of natural colours. Hurst has been a cabinet-maker for ten years and has built up a very nice reputation for himself. His order book is always full for several months in advance, despite the fact that he does not really promote himself. Word has spread that if you want a decent cupboard or table, bookcase or kitchen units, Hurst is your man.
Of course, finding a furniture-maker is not that taxing a task. Wherever you live in the countryside, the craft is alive and well. But finding a cabinet- maker who prides himself on making beautifully crafted furniture with clean, simple lines is less easy. 'There are few real cabinet-makers now. People call themselves furniture-makers,' Hurst says wearily. As a craftsman who sets himself exacting standards, he is continually disappointed by some contemporary furniture. 'I am amazed by what some furniture-makers get away with, and saddened by what people will put up with.' He rails against shoddy, mass-produced furniture, and craftsmen who churn out second-rate pieces.
Such a quest for perfection is obviously a key to Hurst's success. That and his talent. This man is not coy about his ability. Indeed, his blatant self- confidence is as surprising as his initial brusque manner. 'I have a huge natural ability,' he says, with a deadpan expression. 'I have always been good at making things.' If it were not for the self-deprecating mood into which he slipped towards the end of our interview, I would have believed his conceit to be wholly genuine.
Hurst is self-taught. So how did he learn his craft? 'I asked the right questions and picked it all up,' he says nonchalantly. Almost all of his commissions come from private individuals ('l used to do some commercial work for companies but it was soul-destroying'). Some clients have returned time and again. 'You end up doing the whole of their house. That is very satisfying.' But he is honest enough to admit that relationships with clients do not always run smoothly. 'The most infuriating clients are those who don't know what they want, and then decide they do when it's too late ... my favourite clients are the exacting ones.'
If Hurst has every reason to be pleased with himself, he is also gracious in his praise for others - where it is due. With a sudden shot of modesty, he says: 'There are people far better than me. I can admire other people. After all, I wasn't trained at Parnham' (the leading college of furniture design). However, he is also unremittingly critical of those craftsmen who 'are trying to be artists and take a year to make one piece.' He also has little time for degree shows, in which students exhibit their work but at the same time are 'trying to make fashion statements. That can be pretentious. A piece of furniture is not about making a statement. It has to be something that people really can use.'
Confident Hurst may be, even brusque, but you could never call him or his work pretentious. Indeed, his parting shot displays a welcome down- to-earth approach to his craft and a streak of humility strangely at odds with his earlier self- confidence. 'After all, I am only making furniture,' he says as I make my exit.

L’ébéniste

Charles Hurst gagne sa vie en fabriquant des meubles à la finition irréprochable. Joanna Watt l’a rencontré.

Charles Hurst donne l’impression d’être un homme pressé. J’arrive à son atelier, blotti sous une arche de chemin de fer dans l’est de Londres, et il m’accueille par une poignée de main expéditive et ces mots : « Bon, allez-y, posez vos questions ! » Il n’est pas immédiatement évident de savoir si cette brusquerie est authentique ou si elle dissimule une certaine timidité. Mais un coup d’œil autour de l’atelier révèle que Hurst est manifestement occupé, et qu’il a de bonnes raisons de ne pas perdre une minute de son temps.

L’espace voûté est rempli de meubles à moitié terminés et de planches de bois déclinant une étonnante palette de couleurs naturelles. Hurst est ébéniste depuis dix ans et s’est forgé une très belle réputation. Son carnet de commandes est toujours plein plusieurs mois à l’avance, malgré le fait qu’il ne fasse pas vraiment sa propre promotion. Le bouche-à-oreille a fait son œuvre : si vous voulez un buffet ou une table de qualité, une bibliothèque ou des éléments de cuisine, Hurst est l’homme qu’il vous faut.

Bien sûr, trouver un fabricant de meubles n’est pas une tâche si difficile. Où que l’on vive à la campagne, cet artisanat se porte très bien. Mais trouver un ébéniste qui se fasse un point d’honneur de fabriquer des meubles superbement réalisés, aux lignes épurées et simples, est moins facile. « Il y a peu de vrais ébénistes aujourd’hui. Les gens se disent fabricants de meubles », dit Hurst avec lassitude. En tant qu’artisan qui s’impose des exigences très élevées, il est continuellement déçu par certains meubles contemporains. « Je suis stupéfait de voir ce que certains fabricants de meubles se permettent, et attristé par ce que les gens sont prêts à tolérer. » Il s’emporte contre les meubles de mauvaise qualité produits en série, et contre les artisans qui débitent des pièces médiocres.

Une telle quête de perfection est manifestement l’une des clés du succès de Hurst. Cela, et son talent. Cet homme n’est pas modeste quant à ses capacités. En effet, sa confiance en soi affichée est presque aussi surprenante que sa brusquerie initiale. « J’ai un talent naturel immense », dit-il d’un air impassible. « J’ai toujours été doué pour fabriquer des choses. » Si ce n’avait été l’humeur d’autodérision dans laquelle il est tombé vers la fin de notre entretien, j’aurais cru que sa suffisance était entièrement sincère.

Hurst est autodidacte. Alors, comment a-t-il appris son métier ? « J’ai posé les bonnes questions et j’ai tout assimilé », dit-il avec désinvolture. Presque toutes ses commandes viennent de particuliers (« Avant, je faisais quelques travaux commerciaux pour des entreprises, mais c’était destructeur pour l’âme »). Certains clients sont revenus encore et encore. « On finit par aménager toute leur maison. C’est très gratifiant. » Mais il est assez honnête pour admettre que les relations avec les clients ne se passent pas toujours sans heurts. « Les clients les plus exaspérants sont ceux qui ne savent pas ce qu’ils veulent, puis décident qu’ils le savent quand il est trop tard… mes clients préférés sont les plus exigeants. »

Si Hurst a toutes les raisons d’être satisfait de lui-même, il sait aussi louer les autres avec élégance — quand ils le méritent. Pris d’un soudain élan de modestie, il dit : « Il y a des gens bien meilleurs que moi. Je peux admirer le travail des autres. Après tout, je n’ai pas été formé à Parnham » (la principale école de design de mobilier). Cependant, il se montre aussi implacablement critique envers ces artisans qui « essaient d’être des artistes et mettent un an à faire une seule pièce ». Il n’a pas non plus beaucoup de considération pour les expositions de fin d’études, où les étudiants présentent leur travail tout en « essayant de faire des déclarations de mode. Cela peut être prétentieux. Un meuble n’est pas là pour faire passer un message. Il faut que ce soit quelque chose dont les gens puissent réellement se servir. »

Hurst a peut-être confiance en lui, il est peut-être même brusque, mais on ne pourrait jamais qualifier ni lui ni son travail de prétentieux. D’ailleurs, sa dernière remarque révèle une approche heureusement terre-à-terre de son métier et un trait d’humilité en étrange contradiction avec l’assurance qu’il affichait plus tôt. « Après tout, je ne fais que des meubles », dit-il au moment où je prends congé.

But a glance around the workshop reveals that Hurst is plainly busy, and that he has good reason not to waste a minute of his time.

His order book is always full several months in advance, despite the fact that he does not really promote himself. Of course, finding a furniture maker is not such a difficult task. Wherever one lives in the countryside, this craft is thriving. Indeed, his openly displayed self-confidence is almost as surprising as his initial brusqueness. “I have immense natural talent,” he says impassively. “I’ve always been good at making things.” Had it not been for the self-mocking mood he fell into towards the end of our interview, I would have thought his conceit entirely sincere.

Hurst is self-taught. So how did he learn his trade? “I asked the right questions and took everything in,” he says casually. Almost all his commissions come from private clients (“I used to do some commercial work for companies, but it was soul-destroying”). Some clients have come back again and again. “You end up fitting out their whole house. If Hurst has every reason to be pleased with himself, he also knows how to praise others graciously—when they deserve it. The Elephant Show 

by Daniel Allsop, age 14 

Last summer, I went to Thailand for a beach holiday with my family. One day, we took a trip to a park not far from our hotel. It had beautiful flower gardens but we were only interested in the elephant show. 
We went straight to a large square with seats on three sides. Three elephants came in with their keepers and stood in front of a large piece of white card. Each elephant was given a paintbrush and started to paint on its own card. From time to time, the keepers put a new brush full of paint into each elephant's trunk and took the old one away. Slowly, following their keepers' instructions, the elephants drew pictures on the cards. I couldn't believe what I was seeing! One picture showed a river, one a tree and the third a bunch of flowers. When the keepers held up the paintings, everyone wanted to buy one. We gave the elephants the bananas we brought for our lunch. 
Twenty years ago, elephants worked in the forest. Now, they no longer work there, but the cleverest of these animals live in special centres where visitors can watch them.

Le spectacle des éléphants

par Daniel Allsop, 14 ans

L’été dernier, je suis allé en Thaïlande pour passer des vacances à la plage avec ma famille. Un jour, nous avons fait une excursion dans un parc non loin de notre hôtel. Il y avait de magnifiques jardins fleuris, mais nous ne nous intéressions qu’au spectacle des éléphants.
Nous sommes allés directement vers une grande place avec des sièges sur trois côtés. Trois éléphants sont entrés avec leurs soigneurs et se sont placés devant un grand panneau blanc. On a donné un pinceau à chaque éléphant, et chacun a commencé à peindre sur son propre carton. De temps en temps, les soigneurs mettaient un nouveau pinceau plein de peinture dans la trompe de chaque éléphant et emportaient l’ancien. Lentement, en suivant les instructions de leurs soigneurs, les éléphants ont dessiné des images sur les cartons. Je n’en croyais pas mes yeux ! Une image représentait une rivière, une autre un arbre et la troisième un bouquet de fleurs. Quand les soigneurs ont montré les peintures, tout le monde a voulu en acheter une. Nous avons donné aux éléphants les bananes que nous avions apportées pour notre déjeuner.
Il y a vingt ans, les éléphants travaillaient dans la forêt. Aujourd’hui, ils n’y travaillent plus, mais les plus intelligents de ces animaux vivent dans des centres spéciaux où les visiteurs peuvent les regarder.

Paul Simon

Rock and roll in the 1950s was primarily a youth cult, but its lasting importance lay in the seismic impact it had on the middle class and the middle-aged. It also paved the way for the next generation of rock idols, who listened to it awestruck and aware that this strange, unsettling sound would somehow, irrevocably, be linked with their destinies.
For Paul Simon, as for other youngsters in the US, the chief opportunity for hearing this new and invigorating type of music that was sweeping the country was courtesy of Alan Freed's radio show, Moondog Rock'n'Roll Party. Freed's show was required listening for a whole generation of fledgling rock idols. Like the young John Lennon, 3,000 miles away in Liverpool, with his ear glued to Radio Luxembourg - the only European outlet for the new rock and roll - Paul Simon was fascinated by the sounds pouring from Freed's show, and prepared himself for the next big step for a rock and roll obsessed teenager, the switch from listening to others' music to making his own.

Snow

No path was visible, but I thought that I would be all right if I walked with due caution. The wind hammered down from the heights, knocking me over as I slid and slithered on the slippery ice. Suddenly the innocent-looking snow gave way beneath me. I dropped, startled, into a hole some four feet deep. The snow had formed a roof over the gap between two rocks, melting away to leave nothing but a thin crust through which I had plunged. I hauled myself out, shaken and unnerved, wondering what I would have done if the hole had been thirty feet deep. I sat back against the top of a pine tree that protruded from the snow to take stock of the situation. In an hour I had covered about half a mile. It was perfectly clear that I would have to abandon my plan.

Qualitative Research

There are now numerous books which attempt to give guidance to researchers about qualitative research. While much has been written about the collection of data, the books are often silent about the processes and procedures associated with data analysis. Indeed, much mystery surrounds the way researchers analyse their data. Accordingly, we invited a range of social scientists who have engaged in qualitative projects to discuss the approaches that they used. The idea was to share insight and understanding of the process of qualitative data analysis rather than to produce a guidebook for the intending researcher. Such a task involves a process of demystification, of making implicit procedures more explicit. While this may sound straightforward, we have found it far from simple. We have therefore given our contributors the opportunity to present their work in a range of styles, which include autobiographical narratives and more impersonal forms.

This poor diet has had a disastrous effect on human health and physique. Over the centuries we have lived on soups, porridges and breads that have left us underfed and underdeveloped. In one study in Ohio, scientists discovered that when they began to grow corn, healthy hunter-gatherers were turned into sickly, underweight farmers. Tooth decay increased, as did diseases. Far from being one of the blessings of the New World, corn was a public health disaster, according to some anthropologists.
Nevertheless, from then on agriculture spread because a piece of farmed land could support ten times the number of people who had previously lived off it as hunter-gatherers. The fact that most people relying on this system are poorly nourished and stunted has only recently been tackled, even by the world's wealthier nations. Only in Europe, the US and Japan are diets again reflecting the richness of our ancestors' diets.
As a result, the average man in the US is now 179cm, in Holland 180 cm, and in Japan 177 cm. It is a welcome trend, though not without its own problems. Heights may have risen, but the world has not moved on, it seems. A standard bed-length has remained at 190cm since 1860. Even worse, leg-room in planes and trains seems to have shrunk rather than grown, while clothes manufacturers are constantly having to revise their range of products.
The question is: where will it all end? We cannot grow for ever. We must have some programmed upper limit. But what is it? According to Robert Fogel, of University, it could be as much as 193 cm - and we are likely to reach it some time this century.
However, scientists add one note of qualification. Individuals may be growing taller because of improved nutrition, but as a species we are actually shrinking. During the last ice age, 10,000 years ago, members of the human race were slightly rounder and taller - an evolutionary response to the cold. (Large, round bodies are best at keeping in heat.) Since the climate warmed, we appear to have got slightly thinner and smaller, even when properly fed. And as the planet continues to heat up, we may shrink even further. In other words, the growth of human beings could be offset by global warming.

C'est vrai : nous sommes tous en train de devenir trop grands pour nos bottes

Chris Greener avait quatorze ans lorsqu'il a dit à son conseiller d'orientation qu'il voulait entrer dans la marine en quittant l'école. « Que veux-tu devenir ? » demanda le professeur. « Le mât d'un navire ? » Le professeur n'avait pas tort, car Chris, bien qu'il n'ait alors que quatorze ans, mesurait déjà presque deux mètres. Aujourd'hui, avec ses 228 cm, il est l'homme le plus grand de Grande-Bretagne.

Chaque décennie, la taille moyenne des Européens augmente d'un centimètre supplémentaire. Chaque année, de plus en plus de personnes vraiment grandes naissent. Fait intriguant, cela ne signifie pas que l'humanité est en train de produire une nouvelle super-race. En réalité, nous revenons à ce que nous étions à l'époque des hommes des cavernes. Ce n'est que maintenant que nous nous débarrassons des effets de générations de mauvaise alimentation — avec des effets spectaculaires. « Ce n'est que maintenant que nous commençons à réaliser notre véritable potentiel », affirme le paléontologue, le professeur Chris Stringer. « Nous redevenons des Cro-Magnons — les êtres humains qui vivaient sur cette planète il y a 40 000 ans. »

Pendant la plus grande partie de l'histoire humaine, nos ancêtres tiraient leur nourriture d'une grande variété de sources : les femmes cueillaient des herbes, des fruits et des baies, tandis que les hommes complétaient cela par des prises occasionnelles d'animaux (un mode de vie encore adopté par les quelques tribus de chasseurs-cueilleurs qui subsistent dans le monde). Une étude a montré, par exemple, qu'ils fondaient leur alimentation sur 85 plantes sauvages différentes. Puis, il y a environ 9 000 ans, l'agriculture a été inventée — avec des conséquences dévastatrices. La plupart des espaces verts de la planète ont progressivement été accaparés par les agriculteurs, si bien que trois plantes riches en glucides seulement — le blé, le riz et le maïs — fournissent aujourd'hui plus de la moitié des calories consommées par l'humanité.

Cette mauvaise alimentation a eu un effet désastreux sur la santé et la constitution physique humaines. Au fil des siècles, nous avons vécu de soupes, de bouillies et de pains qui nous ont laissés sous-alimentés et sous-développés. Dans une étude menée dans l'Ohio, des scientifiques ont découvert qu'au moment où ils se sont mis à cultiver le maïs, de sains chasseurs-cueilleurs se sont transformés en agriculteurs chétifs et maigres. Les caries ont augmenté, tout comme les maladies. Loin d'être l'une des bénédictions du Nouveau Monde, le maïs a constitué une catastrophe de santé publique, selon certains anthropologues.

Néanmoins, à partir de ce moment-là, l'agriculture s'est répandue parce qu'une parcelle cultivée pouvait faire vivre dix fois plus de personnes que lorsqu'elle servait auparavant de territoire à des chasseurs-cueilleurs. Le fait que la plupart des gens dépendant de ce système soient mal nourris et de petite taille n'a été pris en compte que récemment, même par les nations les plus riches du monde. Ce n'est qu'en Europe, aux États-Unis et au Japon que les régimes alimentaires recommencent à refléter la richesse de ceux de nos ancêtres.

En conséquence, l'homme moyen mesure désormais 179 cm aux États-Unis, 180 cm aux Pays-Bas et 177 cm au Japon. C'est une tendance bienvenue, bien qu'elle n'aille pas sans poser ses propres problèmes. Les tailles ont peut-être augmenté, mais le monde, lui, ne semble pas avoir suivi. La longueur standard d'un lit est restée de 190 cm depuis 1860. Pire encore, l'espace pour les jambes dans les avions et les trains semble avoir diminué au lieu d'augmenter, tandis que les fabricants de vêtements doivent sans cesse revoir leur gamme de produits.

La question est la suivante : où cela s'arrêtera-t-il ? Nous ne pouvons pas grandir éternellement. Nous devons avoir une limite supérieure programmée. Mais laquelle ? Selon Robert Fogel, de l'université, elle pourrait atteindre 193 cm — et nous devrions l'atteindre au cours de ce siècle.

Cependant, les scientifiques ajoutent une réserve. Les individus grandissent peut-être grâce à une meilleure nutrition, mais en tant qu'espèce, nous sommes en réalité en train de rapetisser. Durant la dernière période glaciaire, il y a 10 000 ans, les membres de l'espèce humaine étaient légèrement plus trapus et plus grands — une réponse évolutive au froid. (Les corps grands et ronds conservent mieux la chaleur.) Depuis le réchauffement du climat, nous semblons être devenus légèrement plus minces et plus petits, même lorsque nous sommes correctement nourris. Et à mesure que la planète continue de se réchauffer, nous pourrions rétrécir davantage encore. En d'autres termes, la croissance des êtres humains pourrait être compensée par le réchauffement climatique.

results.src_text:
The Young Achiever of the Year

Kal Kaur Rai has always been interested in fashion and has just won the title of Young Achiever of the Year at the Asian Business Awards. Ever since she was a child, she has drawn clothes and designed patterns. She never told her hard-working parents, who own a supermarket, that she wanted to turn her hobby into a career. She thought they expected her to go into a more established business, so she went to university to do a management degree.

After university, she moved to London and worked in an advertising agency. She had to attend industry events but couldn't afford the designer clothes she liked. She started making skirts and tops for herself. When her friends saw her clothes, they asked her to make things for them. She then found a small shop in London willing to take her designs on a sale-or- return basis. They were very popular and nothing came back. This encouraged her to leave her advertising job, take out a PS20,000 loan and begin her own womenswear label.

Kal's parents were not angry about her career change and said they would support her, which really pleased her. Her clothes are now on sale in over 70 stores and her business has an income of over PS500,000. Her clothes appear in fashion magazines, she designs for pop stars and she has just gained public recognition by winning this award. Her business has come a long way and she knows she is extremely lucky. 'What I do is my hobby - and I get paid for it! But remember, I've worked hard for this.'

BURGLARS LOVE THE AFTERNOON

Most house burglaries happen between 2 p.m. and 6 p.m.,say the police.
Inspector Ian Saunders told our newspaper that the number of house burglaries has gone up by more than 30% compared with last year. He also said that 67% of burglaries happen when people have gone out and forgotten to dose a door or a window.
He went on to report that night-time burglaries are unusual because families are usually at home at that time. But he said that winter afternoons are the best time for burglars because it is dark and they can't be seen easily. Also many houses are empty at that time, because people are often still at work.

results.src_text:
Life was getting out of hand

Susan Harr unplugs her gadgets and rediscovers the joys of manual labour.

Everyone is in love with technology. It gives us all those marvellous gadgets that make life easier and leave us so much more time to do other things. A gradual, though not particularly subtle, form of brainwashing has persuaded us that technology rules, and that it is OK.
These implications are obvious. The movement of my fingers uses nothing from the previous power supply being eaten up by our greedy race. A craft executed by hand does not pollute the environment.
However, a recent unhappy experience with my malfunctioning word processor -
a PS48 call-out fee, a labour charge of PS15 per quarter of an hour, plus parts and replacements costs - has confirmed a suspicion that gadgets are often not worth the expense or the trouble. Are we as dependent on technology as we imagine? Bit by bit, I have been letting the household technology fall by the wayside as its natural and often short life expires.
This makes me wonder just what 'time' technology gives us. The time to take up more activities for which we must buy more gadgets? If so, hats off to the marketing experts: but I think they are conning us.
So when the thing started making curious noises, which continued even when it was disconnected by a puzzled service agent, I abandoned it to the backyard, where it whispers damply to itself like some robot ghost.
I am not tied to a noisy, whirring machine, with my head bent and my back turned on the world, and I can take my time over the garment. In any case, I was always slightly alarmed by those electric machines that dash across the fabric towards your fingers. Best of all, I can pop the whole lot into a carrier bag and take it with me wherever I go.
Of course, there are some gadgets I would not like to be without. A year living without a washing machine convinced me of the value of the electric washtub. But there are others whose loss has brought unexpected delight. Feeling that we were becoming too apt to collapse in front of the television, or slot in a video, I sent back the rented colour equipment and we returned to the small black-and-white portable.
It is a real strain on the eyes and concentrates the mind on what is really worth watching. We now spend a lot more time walking the dog (who never liked television anyway), reading, talking or pursuing other hobbies.
One of these, in my own case, is sewing; and here is another gadget that went by the board. My old Singer sewing machine is now an ornamental plant table, and as l cannot afford to replace it, I have taken to sewing by hand.
We have come to believe that we could not do without it, and if we do resist the notion that our lives would be unmanageable without the appliances of science we certainly do not want to relinquish them. Pity the generations whose lives were blighted by tedious and blister inducing toil. Even our brains are relieved of exertion by computers that not only perform miraculous calculations with amazing speed but now provide entertainment.
In fact, the time I now spend placidly stitching is anything but tedious, and the advantages are numerous. For a start, I can sew and listen to the radio - another rediscovered pleasure - or I can talk with family and friends. If it is a simple task, I can watch the programmes I do want to see on television, and alleviate my puritanical guilt at sitting in front of the box by doing something useful at the same time. And what a lovely, cosy feeling it is to sit by the fire and sew with a pot of tea for company.
Quite wrongly, I had tended to think with horror of the women who sewed elaborate garments, robes, linen and household items by hand. I thought of those long hours, the strain on the eyes and so on. 
There is a wonderfully soothing quality about executing a craft by hand, a great satisfaction in watching one's work become neater, more assured. I find things get done surprisingly quickly, and the pace of life suddenly slows down to the rhythm of my own hands. I am also freed from one of the most detestable aspects of late 20th century life the need to rush to finish an activity so that I can rush to the next.
Meanwhile I have regained control of my sink, where I plunge my hands into the suds and daydream while doing the washing up agreeable, if temporarily forgotten, activity.
The result of all this brooding is that I now prowl the house with a speculative eye. Do we really need the freezer, the microwave oven, that powered lawnmower? Come to think of it, we could save an awful lot of money by doing without electric lights!
results.tgt_text:
La vie devenait incontrôlable

Susan Harr débranche ses appareils et redécouvre les joies du travail manuel.

Tout le monde est amoureux de la technologie. Elle nous offre tous ces merveilleux gadgets qui facilitent la vie et nous laissent tellement plus de temps pour faire autre chose. Une forme progressive, quoique pas particulièrement subtile, de lavage de cerveau nous a persuadés que la technologie règne en maître, et que cela est parfaitement acceptable.
Les conséquences de cette idée sont évidentes. Le mouvement de mes doigts n’utilise rien de l’approvisionnement énergétique antérieur que notre race avide est en train d’épuiser. Un travail artisanal exécuté à la main ne pollue pas l’environnement.
Cependant, une récente et fâcheuse expérience avec mon traitement de texte en panne — 48 livres de frais de déplacement, 15 livres de main-d’œuvre par quart d’heure, plus le coût des pièces et des remplacements — a confirmé un soupçon : les gadgets ne valent souvent ni la dépense ni les ennuis qu’ils causent. Sommes-nous aussi dépendants de la technologie que nous l’imaginons ? Peu à peu, j’ai laissé tomber la technologie domestique à mesure que sa vie naturelle, souvent brève, arrivait à son terme.
Cela me fait me demander exactement quel « temps » la technologie nous donne. Le temps de nous lancer dans davantage d’activités pour lesquelles il nous faut acheter encore plus de gadgets ? Si c’est le cas, chapeau bas aux experts du marketing ; mais je pense qu’ils nous roulent.
Alors, quand l’appareil s’est mis à émettre d’étranges bruits, qui ont continué même après qu’un technicien perplexe l’eut débranché, je l’ai abandonné au fond du jardin, où il murmure humide à lui-même comme une sorte de fantôme robotique.
Je ne suis pas attachée à une machine bruyante et vrombissante, la tête baissée et le dos tourné au monde, et je peux prendre mon temps pour confectionner le vêtement. En tout cas, ces machines électriques qui foncent sur le tissu en direction de vos doigts m’ont toujours légèrement effrayée. Mieux encore, je peux glisser tout le nécessaire dans un sac et l’emporter partout avec moi.
Bien sûr, il y a certains appareils dont je ne voudrais pas me passer. Une année passée sans machine à laver m’a convaincue de la valeur du baquet électrique. Mais il en est d’autres dont la disparition a apporté un plaisir inattendu. Ayant le sentiment que nous étions devenus trop enclins à nous affaler devant la télévision, ou à mettre une cassette vidéo, j’ai rendu le téléviseur couleur en location et nous sommes revenus au petit poste portable en noir et blanc.
C’est une véritable épreuve pour les yeux et cela oblige à se concentrer sur ce qui vaut vraiment la peine d’être regardé. Nous passons maintenant beaucoup plus de temps à promener le chien (qui, de toute façon, n’a jamais aimé la télévision), à lire, à parler ou à nous adonner à d’autres passe-temps.
L’un d’eux, dans mon cas, est la couture ; et voici un autre gadget qui a été abandonné. Ma vieille machine à coudre Singer sert désormais de table pour plantes ornementales, et comme je n’ai pas les moyens de la remplacer, je me suis mise à coudre à la main.
Nous en sommes venus à croire que nous ne pourrions pas nous en passer, et même si nous résistons à l’idée que notre vie serait ingérable sans les appareils de la science, nous ne voulons certainement pas y renoncer. Plaignons les générations dont l’existence a été gâchée par un labeur fastidieux qui donnait des ampoules. Même notre cerveau est soulagé de l’effort grâce aux ordinateurs qui non seulement effectuent des calculs miraculeux à une vitesse stupéfiante, mais nous fournissent désormais aussi des distractions.
En réalité, le temps que je passe maintenant à coudre paisiblement est tout sauf fastidieux, et les avantages sont nombreux. D’abord, je peux coudre et écouter la radio — un autre plaisir retrouvé — ou bien parler avec ma famille et mes amis. Si c’est une tâche simple, je peux regarder à la télévision les émissions que j’ai vraiment envie de voir, et atténuer ma culpabilité puritaine d’être assise devant l’écran en faisant en même temps quelque chose d’utile. Et quelle sensation délicieuse et douillette que de s’asseoir près du feu pour coudre avec une théière pour compagne.
À tort, j’avais eu tendance à penser avec horreur à ces femmes qui cousaient à la main des vêtements élaborés, des robes, du linge et des objets ménagers. Je pensais à ces longues heures, à la fatigue des yeux, etc.
Il y a dans l’exécution manuelle d’un travail artisanal une qualité merveilleusement apaisante, une grande satisfaction à voir son ouvrage devenir plus net, plus assuré. Je trouve que les choses se font étonnamment vite, et que le rythme de la vie ralentit soudain pour s’accorder à celui de mes propres mains. Je suis aussi libérée de l’un des aspects les plus détestables de la fin du XXe siècle : la nécessité de se dépêcher de finir une activité pour pouvoir se précipiter vers la suivante.
Pendant ce temps, j’ai repris le contrôle de mon évier, où je plonge les mains dans l’eau savonneuse et rêve tout éveillée en faisant la vaisselle, activité agréable quoique temporairement oubliée.
Le résultat de toutes ces réflexions, c’est qu’à présent je rôde dans la maison d’un œil spéculatif. Avons-nous vraiment besoin du congélateur, du four à micro-ondes, de cette tondeuse à gazon motorisée ? À bien y penser, nous pourrions économiser énormément d’argent en nous passant de l’éclairage électrique !

Susan Harr unplugs her appliances and rediscovers the joys of manual work.

Everyone is in love with technology. It offers us all these wonderful gadgets that make life easier and leave us so much more time to do other things. A gradual, though not particularly subtle, form of brainwashing has persuaded us that technology reigns supreme, and that this is perfectly acceptable.

The consequences of this idea are obvious. The movement of my fingers uses none of the dwindling energy supplies that our greedy race is exhausting. Handcrafted work done by hand does not pollute the environment.

However, a recent nasty experience with my broken word processor — £48 call-out charge, £15 labor for every quarter hour, plus the cost of parts and replacements — confirmed a suspicion: gadgets are often neither worth the expense nor the trouble they cause. Are we really as dependent on technology as we imagine? Little by little, I have let domestic technology go as it reached the end of its natural, often brief, life.

It makes me wonder exactly what “time” technology gives us. Time to launch into even more activities for which we need to buy still more gadgets? If so, hats off to the marketing experts; but I think they are taking us for a ride.

So when the machine began making strange noises, which continued even after a puzzled technician had unplugged it, I abandoned it at the bottom of the garden, where it mutters damply to itself like some kind of robotic ghost.

I am not tied to a noisy, whirring machine, hunched over with my head down and my back turned to the world, and I can take my time making the garment. In any case, those electric machines that race across the fabric toward your fingers have always slightly frightened me. Better still, I can slip everything I need into a bag and take it with me anywhere.

Of course, there are some appliances I would not want to do without. A year spent without a washing machine convinced me of the value of the electric washtub. But there are others whose disappearance has brought unexpected pleasure. Feeling that we had become too inclined to flop down in front of the television, or put on a video cassette, I returned the rented color television and we went back to the little portable black-and-white set.

It is a real strain on the eyes and it forces one to concentrate on what is really worth watching. We now spend much more time walking the dog (who, in any case, never liked television), reading, talking, or pursuing other hobbies.

One of them, in my case, is sewing; and here is another gadget that has been abandoned. My old Singer sewing machine now serves as a table for ornamental plants, and since I cannot afford to replace it, I have taken to sewing by hand.

We have come to believe that we could not do without these things, and even if we resist the idea that our lives would be unmanageable without the products of science, we certainly do not want to give them up. Let us pity the generations whose lives were spoiled by tedious, blister-raising toil. Even our brains are relieved of effort by computers which not only perform miraculous calculations at astonishing speed, but now also provide us with distractions.

In fact, the time I now spend sewing peacefully is anything but tedious, and the advantages are many. First of all, I can sew and listen to the radio — another rediscovered pleasure — or talk with my family and friends. If it is a simple task, I can watch on television the programs I really want to see, and ease my puritanical guilt about sitting in front of the screen by doing something useful at the same time. And what a deliciously cozy feeling it is to sit by the fire sewing, with a teapot for company.

Wrongly, I had tended to think with horror of those women who sewed elaborate clothes, dresses, linens, and household items by hand. I thought of those long hours, the eye strain, and so on.

There is in the manual execution of handicraft a wonderfully soothing quality, a great satisfaction in seeing one’s work become neater and more assured. I find that things get done surprisingly quickly, and that the pace of life suddenly slows to match that of my own hands. I am also freed from one of the most detestable aspects of the late twentieth century: the need to hurry to finish one activity so as to rush on to the next.

Meanwhile, I have regained control of my sink, where I plunge my hands into the soapy water and daydream while doing the dishes, an enjoyable activity though one temporarily forgotten.

The result of all these reflections is that I now prowl around the house with a speculative eye. Do we really need the freezer, the microwave oven, that motorized lawn mower? Come to think of it, we could save an enormous amount of money by doing without electric lighting!

Enough Sleep?

Tiredness, it is often claimed, has become the modern condition. As the richer, busier countries have grown, so sleeplessness and anxiety have also grown in the popular psyche. Research in the USA has found 40 million Americans to be chronically affected, and some recent best-selling novels in Britain have featured insomniacs as protagonists, or sleep-research laboratories as their settings.
Part of this interest is in sleep in general: in its rhythms, its uses and in problems with sleeping. But a central preoccupation remains. 'People need more sleep,' says one leading sleep researcher. 'People cut back on sleep when they're busy. They get up too early to avoid the rush hour.'
Recently, a sleep researcher tried an experiment. He offered his subjects the opposite of the modern routine. 'I allowed them to sleep for up to 14 hours a night for a month. It took them three weeks to reach an equilibrium of eight-and-a-quarter hours. That indicates a great rebound of sleep - sleep that they hadn't been getting!'
In Europe, such propositions are perhaps most thoroughly tested in a small unassuming building on a university campus in the English Midlands. The university sleep research laboratory has investigated, among many subjects, the effects of fatigue on sailors, the effects of airpot noise on sleepers, and the dangers of motorway driving for flagging drivers.
For guinea pigs, they advertise in the student newspapers. Subjects are picked up by taxi, paid PS5 an hour, and asked to adjust their sleeping patterns according to instructions. Dr Louise Reyner provides reassurance: 'Some people are quite worried, because you're putting electrodes on their heads, and they think you can see what they're dreaming or thinking.'
In fact, the laboratory's interest is more physical. In a darkened room stands a motorway simulator, the front section of car facing a wide projection screen. The subjects are always told to arrive at 2pm, in the body's natural mid-afternoon lull, after a short night's sleep or no sleep at all. The projector is switched on and they are asked to drive, while answering questions. An endless road rolls ahead, sunlight glares; and the air is warm.
The young men all deny they are going to fall asleep. Dr Reyner has a video recording of one trying not to. At first the person at the wheel is very upright, wet and bleary eyes determinedly fixed on the windscreen. Then he begins to blink briefly, every now and again; then for longer, and more often, with a slight drop of the head. Each nod grows heavier than the last. The blinks become a 10-second blackout. Every time, he jerks awake as if nothing has happened. But the car, by the second or third occasion, has shot off the carriageway.
A coffee might have helped. Two cups, Dr Reyner says, even after no sleep at all, can make you a safe driver for half an hour or more. She recommends a whole basket of alertness products: tablets, energy drinks, caffeinated chewing gum. Shift workers, she is quite sure, could probably use them.
But apart from these findings, what else do know about human sleep with any kind of certainty? It is known that humans sleep, like other mammals, according to a daily cycle. Once asleep, they switch between four different stages of unconsciousness, from stage one sleep, the shallowest, to stage four, the deepest. When dreams occur, which is usually during the lightest sleep, the brain paralyses the body except for the hands and eyelids, thus preventing injuries.
Beyond this, certainties blur into theories. It is often suggested, for example, that sleep repairs body tissue, or restores muscles, or rests the frontal section of the brain that controls speech and creativity. But all of this may happen more quickly during relaxed wakefulness, so no one is really sure.
However, there is a strong degree of certainty among scientists that women seep for half an hour longer than men, and that older people require less sleep, though they don't know why. When asked what sleep is for, some sleep researchers reply in cosmic terms: 'Sleep is a tactic to travel through time without injury.'
Moreover, people may have had different sleep patterns in the past. A history professor has investigated nocturnal British life between 1500 and 1850 and discovered that sleeping routines were very different. People went to bed at nine or ten, then woke up after midnight, after what they called their 'first sleep', stayed awake for an hour, and then had their 'morning sleep'.
The interlude was a haven for reflection, remembering dreams, or even night-time thieving. The poorest were the greatest beneficiaries of this quiet time, fleetingly freed from the constraints and labours that ruled their day-time existence.
By the 17th century, however, as artificial light became more common, the rich began to switch to the more concentrated, and economically more efficient, mode of recuperation that we follow today. Two centuries later, the industrial revolution pushed back the dusk for everyone except some country-dwellers, by making most people work longer hours in lighted buildings.
Yet beyond Europe and America, the old pattern was widespread until quite recently, and according to a leading anthropologist, in some non-western settings there are still no rigid bedtimes. People go to bed for a few hours, and then get up again. The idea of a night's solid sleep does not apply. For certain tribal societies, human and animal noises and the need to supervise the fire and watch out for predators combine to make continuous sleep impossible. It seems that people all round the world are badly in need of sleep.
