results.src_text:
We changed lives for a day!

Have you ever dreamed about swapping lives with someone else for a day? Perhaps you think it would be more fun to do something quite different for a change? We fixed it for four people - read how it went.
Amanda (23), a young mother with two daughters, swapped lives with her friend Cindy (30), who works as a waitress at a glitzy London restaurant and entertainment complex.

A. Amanda's story

I'd never been inside anywhere remotely like it before. I couldn't believe how dark and noisy it was - there were so many people and such a brilliant atmosphere. It was all a far cry from my home town and, to he honest, I wasn't sure I'd survive! Being a mother is definitely a busy job - but this was something else!
I had just fifteen minutes to learn how to carry a tray of drinks at shoulder height with one hand. The other waitresses made it look so simple, but just as I was getting the hang of it, the drinks started to slide off the tray and crashed on to the floor, splattering cocktails everywhere. I was so embarrassed, but all the other waitresses laughed. Everyone makes a fool of themselves at first!
By opening time at 11.30 am, a queue had already formed outside and I began to feel really nervous. I was worried about how I'd remember all the orders, but that, at least, wasn't a problem because everything was automated.
After a couple of hours my feet really ached and I couldn't get used to the constant loud music. Every time a customer spoke to me I had to say 'Pardon?', which was so embarrassing! By the end of my shift at 5 pm, I was totally exhausted and longed to soak my feet in a bowl of hot water. I couldn't believe it when one of the waitresses told me it had been a 'quiet' day!
I never realised how tiring waitressing would be. I've always thought it was a job for shrinking violets, but in fact you definitely need to be quite bubbly, as well having the ability to keep a cool head and deal with what is known in the trade as a 'high-volume experience' - in other words, lots of customers!
I'm really quite shy and I don't think I could cope on a Saturday night, when it gets chaotically busy. I wasn't too impressed with the pay either. Unfortunately, I must have been a lousy waitress because even the rich Americans didn't tip me a bean!
I must admit I was very glad to get back to my children. It seems quite easy after waitressing!

B. Cindy's story

I was feeling quite apprehensive about being a 'mum' for the day, but I was looking forward to it, too. I'd been warned the girls were cheeky, but in my ignorance I thought I could handle it. Little did I know!
As Amanda left to make her way to the restaurant, I had to get the two girls dressed and fed. After dropping off Sophie at school and Katie at nursery I thought I'd have three hours of peace. Wrong! A note from Amanda reminded me that I still had to make the beds, clean the house and do the washing.
At 1 pm I picked up Katie, whizzed around the supermarket and then took her home for lunch. But it was when I brought Sophie home from school that the real trouble started. They turned the settee into a trampoline and played a game which involved screaming as loudly as they possibly could! I decided to take the laid-back approach, imagining they'd soon get worn out. Wrong again. I thought I had a fair amount of stamina, but they beat me, hands down!
After much persuasion, I managed to get them into bed by about 8 pm, but then the fun and games started! How many glasses of water can a child drink, for heaven's sake? Of course, I realised it was just a ploy so they could come downstairs and watch television, but it was exhausting to spend all evening negotiating deals with them.
I never realised how tiring it could be looking after two small children. You don't get a second to think about yourself - and the sheer sense of responsibility is overwhelming. Even so, I really enjoyed the day.

Rosemary (42) runs a dairy farm. She swapped with Hilary (30), a teacher at a primary school.

C. Rosemary's story

On the farm, I have to get up at 5.30 am so sleeping in until 7 was pure luxury! But I dithered for ages about how to look. I could hardly turn up in overalls and boots, could I?
Looking at a sea of faces -- about 400 pupils -- at assembly, I hoped I melted into the background and that my fresh complexion didn't make me stand out as being straight off the farm.
After that it was time for a maths class. The children worked in small groups, using workcards graded according to difficulty - rather different from when I was at school and we had to recite tables in unison! Then I helped out with a nature project - identifying and feeding species of snails.
By lunchtime I was exhausted and looking forward to an hour's break, but the teachers only have about five minutes to eat their meal. There's so much to do before classes start again. I attended a staff meeting about reports and couldn't avoid getting roped in to help with athletics trials.
Alter lunch there was a silent reading lesson (bliss!) and then a French lesson in the video room. This was great fun because all the children wanted to practise on me, which really showed up my rusty French.
Finally we moved on to the school hall for Physical Education. I was drained by now, but the children seemed to have inexhaustible energy.
The hardest part of the job was standing up in front of the class and speaking - even for just two minutes, it's daunting. Teachers may get more holidays a year, but I think I'll stick to farming, anyway!

D. Hilary's story

I arrived at White House Farm at 8.30 am, bright and early, only to discover that Rosemary had been up for three hours! Rosemary's 280-acre farm has 100 Jersey cows, 15 calves and heifers and about 800 ewes! As well as milk, she manufactures ice-cream, yoghurt and cream, which is sold in shops, restaurants and at tourist attractions. I spent most of the morning in the ice-cream parlour, bottling milk into plastic litre containers, squeezing ice-cream from a machine into cartons and sticking on labels. It was difficult to stop myself dipping my fingers into the goodies! At lunchtime it was time to inspect the sheep. I drove over to one of the fields and picked up a ewe which had fallen over. If the sheep are left for more than 12 hours once they have fallen over they could die, so they have to he checked every day. What a nightmare it must be in winter!
Alter feeding the calves, I started the milking. The process took an exhausting two-and-a-half hours. And Rosemary does this twice a day, starting at 6 am, seven days a week, 365 days a year!
I found it quite a lonely day. I was surprised how much I missed the children - animals don't answer back! The worst aspect of the job is not being able to get away from work. The cows always have to be milked twice a day, so it's really difficult to plan any time off. Rosemary will only get about three days' holiday this year.
Farming seems romantic but the reality is very different. The income is irregular and I'd hate to be at the mercy of the weather.
results.tgt_text:
Nous avons changé des vies pendant une journée !

Avez-vous déjà rêvé d’échanger votre vie avec quelqu’un d’autre le temps d’une journée ? Peut-être pensez-vous qu’il serait plus amusant de faire quelque chose de tout à fait différent pour changer ? Nous l’avons organisé pour quatre personnes — lisez comment cela s’est passé.
Amanda (23 ans), une jeune mère de deux filles, a échangé sa vie avec son amie Cindy (30 ans), qui travaille comme serveuse dans un restaurant et complexe de loisirs chic à Londres.

A. L’histoire d’Amanda

Je n’étais jamais entrée dans un endroit qui ressemblait, même de loin, à celui-là. Je n’en revenais pas de voir à quel point c’était sombre et bruyant — il y avait tant de monde et une ambiance tellement incroyable. C’était à mille lieues de ma ville natale et, pour être honnête, je n’étais pas sûre de m’en sortir ! Être mère est sans aucun doute un travail prenant — mais là, c’était autre chose !
Je n’ai eu que quinze minutes pour apprendre à porter d’une seule main, à hauteur d’épaule, un plateau de boissons. Les autres serveuses donnaient l’impression que c’était très simple, mais au moment même où je commençais à prendre le coup, les boissons ont commencé à glisser du plateau et se sont écrasées sur le sol, éclaboussant des cocktails partout. J’étais morte de honte, mais toutes les autres serveuses ont ri. Tout le monde se ridiculise au début !
À l’heure de l’ouverture, à 11 h 30, une file s’était déjà formée dehors et j’ai commencé à me sentir vraiment nerveuse. J’avais peur de ne pas me souvenir de toutes les commandes, mais au moins ce n’était pas un problème parce que tout était automatisé.
Au bout de quelques heures, j’avais vraiment mal aux pieds et je n’arrivais pas à m’habituer à la musique constamment forte. Chaque fois qu’un client me parlait, je devais dire « Pardon ? », ce qui était vraiment embarrassant ! À la fin de mon service, à 17 heures, j’étais totalement épuisée et je n’aspirais qu’à faire tremper mes pieds dans une bassine d’eau chaude. Je n’en revenais pas quand une des serveuses m’a dit que ça avait été une journée « calme » !
Je n’avais jamais imaginé à quel point le métier de serveuse pouvait être fatigant. J’ai toujours pensé que c’était un travail pour les timides, mais en réalité il faut absolument être assez extravertie, tout en ayant la capacité de garder son sang-froid et de gérer ce qu’on appelle dans le métier une « expérience à fort volume » — autrement dit, beaucoup de clients !
Je suis en fait assez timide et je ne pense pas que je pourrais tenir un samedi soir, quand ça devient un chaos total. Je n’ai pas non plus été très impressionnée par le salaire. Malheureusement, j’ai dû être une serveuse lamentable parce que même les riches Américains ne m’ont pas laissé un sou de pourboire !
Je dois admettre que j’étais très contente de retrouver mes enfants. Cela paraît presque facile après avoir fait le service !

B. L’histoire de Cindy

J’étais assez inquiète à l’idée d’être une « maman » pour la journée, mais j’étais impatiente aussi. On m’avait prévenue que les filles étaient effrontées, mais dans mon ignorance je pensais pouvoir gérer ça. Si seulement j’avais su !
Quand Amanda est partie pour se rendre au restaurant, j’ai dû habiller et faire manger les deux filles. Après avoir déposé Sophie à l’école et Katie à la maternelle, j’ai cru que j’aurais trois heures de tranquillité. Faux ! Un mot d’Amanda me rappelait que je devais encore faire les lits, nettoyer la maison et faire la lessive.
À 13 heures, je suis allée chercher Katie, j’ai filé au supermarché puis je l’ai ramenée à la maison pour le déjeuner. Mais c’est quand j’ai ramené Sophie de l’école que les vrais problèmes ont commencé. Elles ont transformé le canapé en trampoline et ont joué à un jeu qui consistait à crier aussi fort que possible ! J’ai décidé d’adopter une attitude détendue, en imaginant qu’elles finiraient vite par se fatiguer. Encore faux. Je pensais avoir une bonne endurance, mais elles m’ont battue à plate couture !
Après bien des efforts de persuasion, j’ai réussi à les mettre au lit vers 20 heures, mais c’est alors que les ennuis ont commencé ! Combien de verres d’eau un enfant peut-il boire, bon sang ? Bien sûr, j’ai compris que ce n’était qu’un stratagème pour pouvoir redescendre et regarder la télévision, mais c’était épuisant de passer toute la soirée à négocier avec elles.
Je n’avais jamais réalisé à quel point s’occuper de deux jeunes enfants pouvait être fatigant. On n’a pas une seconde pour penser à soi — et l’énorme sens des responsabilités est accablant. Malgré tout, j’ai vraiment aimé cette journée.

Rosemary (42 ans) dirige une ferme laitière. Elle a échangé avec Hilary (30 ans), institutrice dans une école primaire.

C. L’histoire de Rosemary

À la ferme, je dois me lever à 5 h 30, alors dormir jusqu’à 7 heures relevait du pur luxe ! Mais j’ai hésité pendant des siècles sur ma tenue. Je ne pouvais quand même pas arriver en salopette et en bottes, si ?
En regardant une mer de visages — environ 400 élèves — lors de l’assemblée, j’espérais me fondre dans le décor et que mon teint frais ne me trahisse pas comme quelqu’un arrivant tout droit de la ferme.
Après cela, c’était l’heure d’un cours de mathématiques. Les enfants travaillaient en petits groupes, en utilisant des fiches classées selon le niveau de difficulté — assez différent de mon époque, où nous devions réciter les tables de multiplication tous ensemble ! Ensuite, j’ai aidé à un projet sur la nature — identifier et nourrir différentes espèces d’escargots.
À l’heure du déjeuner, j’étais épuisée et j’attendais avec impatience une heure de pause, mais les enseignants n’ont qu’environ cinq minutes pour manger leur repas. Il y a tellement à faire avant la reprise des cours. J’ai assisté à une réunion du personnel sur les bulletins et je n’ai pas pu éviter d’être réquisitionnée pour aider aux sélections d’athlétisme.
Après le déjeuner, il y a eu une séance de lecture silencieuse (le bonheur !) puis un cours de français dans la salle vidéo. C’était très amusant parce que tous les enfants voulaient s’exercer avec moi, ce qui a vraiment mis en évidence mon français rouillé.
Enfin, nous sommes allés dans le gymnase pour l’éducation physique. J’étais vidée à ce stade, mais les enfants semblaient avoir une énergie inépuisable.
Le plus difficile dans ce métier, c’était de se tenir debout devant la classe et de parler — même pendant seulement deux minutes, c’est intimidant. Les enseignants ont peut-être plus de vacances par an, mais je crois que je vais quand même m’en tenir à l’agriculture !

D. L’histoire d’Hilary

Je suis arrivée à White House Farm à 8 h 30, bien tôt, pour découvrir que Rosemary était levée depuis trois heures déjà ! La ferme de Rosemary, qui s’étend sur 280 acres, compte 100 vaches Jersey, 15 veaux et génisses, et environ 800 brebis ! En plus du lait, elle fabrique de la glace, du yaourt et de la crème, vendus dans des magasins, des restaurants et des lieux touristiques. J’ai passé la plus grande partie de la matinée dans l’atelier de glaces, à mettre le lait en bouteilles plastiques d’un litre, à faire sortir la glace d’une machine dans des cartons et à coller des étiquettes. Il était difficile de m’empêcher de tremper les doigts dans toutes ces bonnes choses ! À l’heure du déjeuner, il a fallu aller inspecter les moutons. Je suis allée en voiture jusqu’à l’un des champs et j’ai relevé une brebis qui était tombée. Si les moutons restent plus de 12 heures couchés après être tombés, ils peuvent mourir, alors il faut les vérifier tous les jours. Quel cauchemar cela doit être en hiver !
Après avoir nourri les veaux, j’ai commencé la traite. Le processus a duré deux heures et demie, ce qui était épuisant. Et Rosemary fait cela deux fois par jour, à partir de 6 heures du matin, sept jours sur sept, 365 jours par an !
J’ai trouvé que c’était une journée assez solitaire. J’ai été surprise de voir à quel point les enfants me manquaient — les animaux ne répondent pas ! Le pire aspect de ce travail, c’est de ne jamais pouvoir s’en éloigner. Les vaches doivent toujours être traites deux fois par jour, donc il est vraiment difficile de prévoir du temps libre. Rosemary n’aura qu’environ trois jours de vacances cette année.
L’agriculture semble romantique, mais la réalité est tout autre. Les revenus sont irréguliers et je détesterais être à la merci du temps.
results.back_text:
We Changed Lives for a Day!

Have you ever dreamed of swapping your life with someone else’s for a day? Perhaps you think it would be more fun to do something completely different for a change? We arranged it for four people—read how it went.
Amanda (23), a young mother of two girls, swapped lives with her friend Cindy (30), who works as a waitress in a chic restaurant and leisure complex in London.

A. Amanda’s story

I had never set foot in a place even remotely like that. I couldn’t believe how dark and noisy it was—there were so many people and such an incredible atmosphere. It was a million miles away from my hometown and, to be honest, I wasn’t sure I’d be able to cope! Being a mother is certainly a demanding job—but this was something else!
I had only fifteen minutes to learn how to carry a tray of drinks at shoulder height with one hand. The other waitresses made it look very easy, but just as I was starting to get the hang of it, the drinks began sliding off the tray and crashed onto the floor, splashing cocktails everywhere. I was mortified, but all the other waitresses laughed. Everyone makes a fool of themselves at first!
By opening time, at 11:30, a queue had already formed outside and I started to feel really nervous. I was afraid I wouldn’t remember all the orders, but at least that wasn’t a problem because everything was computerized.
After a few hours, my feet were really hurting and I couldn’t get used to the constantly loud music. Every time a customer spoke to me, I had to say, “Sorry?” which was really embarrassing! By the end of my shift, at 5 p.m., I was completely exhausted and all I wanted was to soak my feet in a bowl of hot water. I couldn’t believe it when one of the waitresses told me it had been a “quiet” day!
I had never imagined how tiring waitressing could be. I had always thought it was a job for shy people, but in reality you absolutely have to be outgoing, while also being able to keep your cool and handle what they call in the trade a “high-volume experience”—in other words, lots of customers!
I’m actually quite shy and I don’t think I could cope on a Saturday night, when it becomes total chaos. I wasn’t very impressed by the pay either. Unfortunately, I must have been a terrible waitress because even the rich Americans didn’t leave me a penny in tips!
I have to admit, I was very glad to get back to my children. It seems almost easy after waiting tables!

B. Cindy’s story

I was quite worried about being a “mum” for the day, but I was excited too. I’d been warned that the girls were cheeky, but in my ignorance I thought I could handle it. If only I had known!
When Amanda left to go to the restaurant, I had to get both girls dressed and fed. After dropping Sophie off at school and Katie at nursery, I thought I’d have three hours of peace and quiet. Wrong! A note from Amanda reminded me that I still had to make the beds, clean the house and do the laundry.
At 1 p.m., I went to pick up Katie, rushed to the supermarket and then brought her home for lunch. But it was when I brought Sophie home from school that the real problems started. They turned the sofa into a trampoline and played a game that involved screaming as loudly as possible! I decided to take a relaxed approach, imagining they would soon tire themselves out. Wrong again. I thought I had good stamina, but they beat me hands down!
After a great deal of persuasion, I managed to get them into bed at about 8 p.m., but that was when the trouble started! How many glasses of water can a child drink, for heaven’s sake? Of course, I realized it was just a trick so they could come back downstairs and watch television, but it was exhausting spending the whole evening negotiating with them.
I had never realized how tiring it could be to look after two young children. You don’t have a second to think about yourself—and the enormous sense of responsibility is overwhelming. Even so, I really enjoyed the day.

Rosemary (42) runs a dairy farm. She swapped with Hilary (30), a primary school teacher.

C. Rosemary’s story

On the farm, I have to get up at 5:30, so sleeping until 7 o’clock was pure luxury! But I spent ages wondering what to wear. I couldn’t exactly turn up in overalls and boots, could I?
As I looked out at a sea of faces—about 400 pupils—during assembly, I hoped I would blend in and that my fresh complexion wouldn’t give me away as someone straight from the farm.
After that, it was time for a maths lesson. The children worked in small groups, using worksheets graded by level of difficulty—quite different from my day, when we all had to recite the times tables together! Then I helped with a nature project—identifying and feeding different species of snails.
By lunchtime, I was exhausted and looking forward to an hour’s break, but teachers only get about five minutes to eat their meal. There is so much to do before lessons start again. I attended a staff meeting about reports and couldn’t avoid being roped in to help with athletics trials.
After lunch, there was a silent reading session (bliss!) and then a French lesson in the video room. It was great fun because all the children wanted to practise with me, which really highlighted how rusty my French was.
Finally, we went to the gym for PE. I was worn out by then, but the children seemed to have endless energy.
The hardest thing about this job was standing in front of the class and speaking—even for just two minutes, it’s intimidating. Teachers may get more holidays each year, but I think I’ll stick to farming!

D. Hilary’s story

I arrived at White House Farm at 8:30, bright and early, only to find that Rosemary had already been up for three hours! Rosemary’s farm, which covers 280 acres, has 100 Jersey cows, 15 calves and heifers, and about 800 ewes! As well as milk, she makes ice cream, yogurt and cream, which are sold in shops, restaurants and tourist attractions. I spent most of the morning in the ice-cream workshop, putting milk into one-litre plastic bottles, dispensing ice cream from a machine into cartons and sticking on labels. It was hard not to dip my fingers into all that delicious stuff! At lunchtime, we had to go and inspect the sheep. I drove to one of the fields and got up a ewe that had fallen over. If sheep stay down for more than 12 hours after falling, they can die, so they have to be checked every day. What a nightmare that must be in winter!
After feeding the calves, I started milking. The process took two and a half hours, which was exhausting. And Rosemary does this twice a day, starting at 6 a.m., seven days a week, 365 days a year!
I found it quite a lonely day. I was surprised by how much I missed the children—the animals don’t answer back! The worst aspect of this job is never being able to get away from it. The cows always have to be milked twice a day, so it is really hard to plan any time off. Rosemary will only get about three days of holiday this year.
Farming sounds romantic, but the reality is very different. The income is irregular and I would hate to be at the mercy of the weather.

Little Chefs

For one group of children aged between ten and fifteen, Saturdays are spent learning the art of serious cooking. Their weekly lessons in small classes are so popular that there is a waiting list of 30 children who want to do the course. Parents pay PS280 for the course where their children can have fun and learn how to make good food.
Class member Bill, aged ten, says, 'I love my mum's cooking and now I can do it better than her. The teachers make us laugh, especially when we sit down with them to share the food we've made.'
Flora is twelve, and she's having problems preparing onions. 'I love cooking. I did a meal for ten friends which they really enjoyed. Then my mum suggested I take up a hobby, instead of doing nothing at weekends. I was happy staying at home, so I wasn't too keen at first. I'm really glad I decided to come, though.'
Their teacher, Philippe, says, 'It's great fun. Children pay attention and remember things better than adults, although the kitchen isn't always as tidy when they're cooking! As adults, we're always learning more about food. If parents interest their children in cooking while they are young, they'll have enough skill to make food for themselves when they leave home.'

Les Petits Chefs

Pour un groupe d’enfants âgés de dix à quinze ans, les samedis sont consacrés à l’apprentissage de l’art de la cuisine sérieuse. Leurs cours hebdomadaires en petits groupes sont si populaires qu’il y a une liste d’attente de 30 enfants qui veulent suivre la formation. Les parents paient 280 livres sterling pour le cours, où leurs enfants peuvent s’amuser et apprendre à préparer de bons plats.

Bill, un élève de dix ans, dit : « J’adore la cuisine de ma mère et maintenant je peux cuisiner mieux qu’elle. Les professeurs nous font rire, surtout quand nous nous asseyons avec eux pour partager les plats que nous avons préparés. »

Flora a douze ans et elle a des difficultés à préparer les oignons. « J’adore cuisiner. J’ai préparé un repas pour dix amis, qu’ils ont vraiment apprécié. Puis ma mère m’a suggéré de me trouver un passe-temps, au lieu de ne rien faire le week-end. J’étais heureuse de rester à la maison, donc au début, cela ne m’enthousiasmait pas beaucoup. Mais je suis vraiment contente d’avoir décidé de venir. »

Leur professeur, Philippe, dit : « C’est très amusant. Les enfants sont attentifs et retiennent mieux les choses que les adultes, même si la cuisine n’est pas toujours aussi bien rangée quand ils cuisinent ! En tant qu’adultes, nous en apprenons toujours davantage sur la nourriture. Si les parents intéressent leurs enfants à la cuisine quand ils sont jeunes, ils auront suffisamment de compétences pour se préparer à manger eux-mêmes quand ils quitteront la maison. »

results.src_text:
CARTOON FILMS 

Cartoon films have very few limits. If you can draw something, you can make it move on the cinema screen. The use of new ideas and advanced computer programs means that cartoons are becoming exciting again for people of all ages. 
By the end of the 1970s, the cinema world had decided that cartoons were only for children. 
But soon afterwards, one or two directors had some original new ideas. They proved that it was possible to make films in which both adults and children could share the fun. 
However, not every cartoon film was successful. The Black Cauldron, for example, failed, mainly because it was too frightening for children and too childish for adults. Directors learnt from this mistake, and the film companies began to make large amounts of money again.

results.src_text:
Simon Costello knew that the purchase of the house in Pembroke Square had been a mistake within a year of his and Lois's moving in. A possession which can only be afforded by the exercise of stringent and calculated economy is best not afforded at all. But at the time it had seemed a sensible, as well as a desirable, move. He had had a run of successful cases and they were coming in with reassuring regularity. Lois had returned to her job at the advertising agency within two months of the birth of the twins, and had been given a rise which took her salary to thirty-five thousand. It was Lois who had argued the more strongly for a move, but he had put up little resistance to arguments which at the time had seemed compelling: the flat wasn't really suitable for a family, they needed more room, a garden, separate accommodation for an au pair. All these, of course, could have been achieved in a suburb or in a less fashionable part of London than Pembroke Square, but Lois was ambitious for more than additional space. Mornington Mansions had never been an acceptable address for an up-and-coming young barrister and a successful businesswoman. She never said it without a sense that even speaking the words subtly diminished her standing, socially and economically.
Lois had decided that a necessary economy was for one of them to travel by public transport. Her firm was on the other side of London; obviously Simon must be the one to economise. The overcrowded tube journey, stayed in a mood of envious resentment, had become an unproductive thirty minutes of brooding on present discontents. He would recall his grandfather's house in Hampstead where he had stayed as a boy, the smell of dinner from the kitchen, his grandmother's insistence that the returning breadwinner, tired from his exhausting day in court, should be given peace, a little gentle cosseting, and relief from every petty domestic anxiety. She had been a 'lawyer's wife', indefatigable in legal good causes, elegantly present at all lawyers' functions, apparently content with the sphere of life which she had made her own. Well, that world had passed for ever. Lois had made it plain before their marriage that her career was as important as his. It hardly needed saying, this was, after all, a modern marriage. The job was important to her and important to them both. The house, the au pair, their whole standard of living depended on two salaries. And now what they were precariously achieving could be destroyed by that self-righteous, interfering Venetia.
Venetia must have come straight from the court to their offices and she had been in a dangerous mood. Something or someone had upset her. But the word 'upset' was too weak, too bland for the intensity of furious disgust with which she had confronted him. Someone had driven her to the limit of her endurance. He cursed himself. If he hadn't been in his room, if he'd only left a minute earlier, the encounter wouldn't have taken place, she would have had the night to think it over, to consider what, if anything, she ought to do. Probably nothing. The morning might have brought sense. He remembered every word of her angry accusations.
'I defended Brian Cartwright today. Successfully. He told me that when you were his counsel four years ago you knew before trial that he had bribed three of the jury. You did nothing. You went on with the case. Is that true?'
'He's lying. It isn't true.'
'He also said that he passed over some shares in his company to your fiancee. Also before trial. Is that true?'
'I tell you, he's lying. None of its true.'
The denial had been as instinctive as an arm raised to ward off a blow and had sounded unconvincing even to his own ears. His whole action had been one of guilt. The first cold horror draining his face was succeeded by a hot flush, bringing back shameful memories of his headmaster's study, of the terror of the inevitable punishment. He had made himself look into her eyes and had seen the look of contemptuous disbelief. If only he'd had some warning. He knew now what he should have said: 'Cartwright told me after the trial but I didn't believe him. I don't believe him now. That man will say anything to make himself important.'
But he had told a more direct, more dangerous lie, and she had known that it was a lie. Even so, why the anger, why the disgust? What was that old misdemeanour to do with her? Who had sent Venetia Aldridge to be guardian of the conscience of their legal practice? Or of his, come to that? Was her own conscience so clear, her behaviour in court always immaculate? Was she justified in destroying his career? And it would be destruction. He wasn't sure what exactly she could do, how far she was prepared to go, but if this got about, even as a rumour, he was done for.

Simon Costello sut, dans l’année qui suivit son installation avec Lois, que l’achat de la maison de Pembroke Square avait été une erreur. Un bien que l’on ne peut s’offrir qu’au prix d’une économie rigoureuse et calculée vaut mieux ne pas être acquis du tout. Mais, à l’époque, cela avait semblé une décision aussi sensée que souhaitable. Il avait enchaîné plusieurs affaires couronnées de succès et de nouveaux dossiers arrivaient avec une régularité rassurante. Lois avait repris son poste dans l’agence de publicité deux mois seulement après la naissance des jumeaux, et avait obtenu une augmentation qui portait son salaire à trente-cinq mille. C’était Lois qui avait plaidé le plus fermement pour un déménagement, mais il n’avait guère opposé de résistance à des arguments qui, sur le moment, lui avaient paru convaincants : l’appartement ne convenait pas vraiment à une famille, ils avaient besoin de plus d’espace, d’un jardin, d’un logement séparé pour une jeune fille au pair. Bien sûr, tout cela aurait pu se trouver en banlieue ou dans un quartier moins huppé de Londres que Pembroke Square, mais Lois ambitionnait plus qu’un simple supplément d’espace. Mornington Mansions n’avait jamais été une adresse acceptable pour un jeune avocat prometteur et une femme d’affaires accomplie. Elle ne la prononçait jamais sans avoir le sentiment que le simple fait d’en dire les mots diminuait subtilement son rang, socialement et économiquement.

Lois avait décidé qu’une économie nécessaire consistait à ce que l’un d’eux se déplace en transports en commun. Son entreprise se trouvait de l’autre côté de Londres ; évidemment, ce devait être Simon qui ferait des économies. Le trajet en métro bondé, effectué dans un état d’esprit de ressentiment envieux, était devenu une demi-heure stérile de rumination sur ses mécontentements présents. Il se rappelait la maison de son grand-père à Hampstead où il avait séjourné enfant, l’odeur du dîner venant de la cuisine, l’insistance de sa grand-mère pour que celui qui faisait vivre la famille, fatigué par son éprouvante journée au tribunal, puisse avoir la paix, un peu de douce sollicitude, et soit soulagé de toute petite anxiété domestique. Elle avait été une « femme d’avocat », infatigable dans les bonnes causes juridiques, présente avec élégance à toutes les réceptions du monde judiciaire, apparemment satisfaite de la sphère d’existence qu’elle s’était créée. Eh bien, ce monde avait disparu à jamais. Lois avait clairement fait comprendre avant leur mariage que sa carrière comptait autant que la sienne. Cela allait presque sans dire ; après tout, c’était un mariage moderne. Son travail était important pour elle, et important pour eux deux. La maison, la jeune fille au pair, tout leur niveau de vie dépendait de deux salaires. Et maintenant, ce qu’ils parvenaient à maintenir tant bien que mal risquait d’être détruit par cette Venetia, moralisatrice et indiscrète.

Venetia devait être venue directement du tribunal à leurs bureaux, et elle était d’une humeur dangereuse. Quelque chose ou quelqu’un l’avait bouleversée. Mais le mot « bouleversée » était trop faible, trop fade pour rendre l’intensité du dégoût furieux avec lequel elle l’avait affronté. Quelqu’un l’avait poussée à la limite de ce qu’elle pouvait supporter. Il se maudit. S’il n’avait pas été dans son bureau, s’il était seulement parti une minute plus tôt, cette confrontation n’aurait pas eu lieu, elle aurait eu la nuit pour y réfléchir, pour se demander ce qu’elle devait faire, si tant est qu’elle dût faire quoi que ce soit. Probablement rien. Le matin lui aurait peut-être apporté un peu de bon sens. Il se rappelait chaque mot de ses accusations furieuses.

« J’ai défendu Brian Cartwright aujourd’hui. Avec succès. Il m’a dit que, lorsque vous étiez son avocat il y a quatre ans, vous saviez avant le procès qu’il avait soudoyé trois jurés. Vous n’avez rien fait. Vous avez poursuivi l’affaire. Est-ce vrai ? »

« Il ment. Ce n’est pas vrai. »

« Il a aussi dit qu’il avait cédé des actions de sa société à votre fiancée. Là encore, avant le procès. Est-ce vrai ? »

« Je vous dis qu’il ment. Rien de tout cela n’est vrai. »

Le démenti avait été aussi instinctif qu’un bras levé pour parer un coup, et il avait sonné peu convaincant jusque à ses propres oreilles. Toute son attitude avait été celle d’un homme coupable. À la première horreur glacée qui lui avait vidé le visage avait succédé un brusque afflux de chaleur, lui ramenant les souvenirs honteux du bureau de son proviseur, de la terreur du châtiment inévitable. Il s’était forcé à soutenir son regard et y avait vu une expression d’incrédulité méprisante. Si seulement il avait été prévenu. Il savait à présent ce qu’il aurait dû dire : « Cartwright me l’a dit après le procès, mais je ne l’ai pas cru. Je ne le crois pas davantage aujourd’hui. Cet homme est capable de dire n’importe quoi pour se donner de l’importance. »

Mais il avait proféré un mensonge plus direct, plus dangereux, et elle avait su que c’était un mensonge. Malgré cela, pourquoi cette colère, pourquoi ce dégoût ? En quoi cet ancien méfait la concernait-il ? Qui avait chargé Venetia Aldridge d’être la gardienne de la conscience de leur cabinet ? Ou de la sienne, d’ailleurs ? Sa propre conscience était-elle donc si pure, sa conduite au tribunal toujours irréprochable ? Était-elle fondée à détruire sa carrière ? Et ce serait bien une destruction. Il ne savait pas exactement ce qu’elle pouvait faire, jusqu’où elle était prête à aller, mais si cela venait à se savoir, ne fût-ce qu’à l’état de rumeur, il était perdu.

A trumpet isn't just for Christmas...

It is strange how many musicians, even leading ones, come from homes without music. Out of the blue, Hakan Hardenberger, the only son of totally unmusical parents in a country district of southern Sweden, has at the age of 30 established himself as unique among the world's trumpet-players today.
His records are continually opening up new repertory, not just concertos by long-neglected composers of the baroque and classical periods, but new works too. When you meet him, bright-eyed and good-looking, he seems even younger than his years, as fresh and open in his manner as the sound of the trumpet.
Recently in one of London's premier concert halls he played the Hummel Trumpet Concerto, something of a party-piece for him, while on television a whole feature was devoted to his work and development, filmed both here and in Sweden.
Born near Malmo, he owes his career to the accident of a Christmas present when he was only eight.
His father, unmusical but liking Louis Armstrong's playing, had the idea of giving his only son a trumpet. Being a serious man, he didn't pick a toy trumpet, but took advice and bought a genuine grown-up instrument.
The success of the gift was instant. The boy never stopped playing. His mother managed to contact the second trumpet-player in the Malmo Symphony Orchestra, whom she persuaded to give her son lessons.
Bo Nilsson was an up-and-coming musician, and at once spotted natural talent. Hardenberger consistently blesses his luck to have got such a teacher right from the start, one who was himself so obsessed with the trumpet and trumpet-playing that he would search out and contact players all over the world, and as a 'trumpet fanatic' was 'always looking for another mouthpiece'.
There the mature Hardenberger has to draw a line between himself and his teacher. 'The trumpet is so primitive an instrument,' he explains, 'that you can't build a trumpet that is acoustically perfect. Whatever you do, it will have imperfections. Besides, you can't find two mouthpieces exactly the same. To me it is a matter of getting to know the imperfections and making a relationship with them.'
From the very start Hardenberger seems to have had the gift of finding the right compromise, and making that relationship. Without any sense of boasting, he explains that even in his boyhood years the characteristic Hardenberger sound was already recognisable, 'the first thing I acquired'.
And unlike the great British contender among virtuoso trumpet-players, John Wallace, who developed originally from a brass-band background and then through working in orchestras, Hardenberger has always thought of himself as a solo artist pure and simple.
From early boyhood he had as a role-model the French trumpeter, Maurice Andre, another player who bypassed the orchestra. The boy bought all his records, and idolised him.
His parents gave him every chance to practise, and went along with his ambition to make trumpet-playing a career. It was then a question of where, at 15, he should be sent to study. America, Bo Nilsson's first choice, was thought to be too far away and too dangerous, which meant that he went instead at the age of 16 to study in Paris with Pierre Thibaud. Thibaud confirmed his prejudice against going into an orchestra, saying that 'Playing in the orchestra is like digging in the garden.'
He was objective enough about himself to know that he played the trumpet better than others of his age, but it was only at the end of the first competition he entered, at the age of 17 during his first year in Paris, that he came to realise that in addition he had a particular gift of communicating.
Thibaud suggested that he should enter the competition just for experience. Hardenberger learned the pieces for the first round only, but he won through to the second. Luckily he already knew most of the pieces in that round too, but on getting through to the final he was faced with a concerto that had already daunted him. He didn't win first prize that time, but he enjoyed the performance, realising that though he 'played like a pig', people did listen to him.
Quoted like that, Hardenberger's realism about his work and his career may sound arrogant, but that would be a totally false impression. Thoughtfully he refuses to try and analyse what such a gift of communication might consist of, as 'You risk destroying it in trying to explain. The power of the music lies in the fact that it can always move people.'

Une trompette ne sert pas seulement à Noël...

Il est étrange de voir combien de musiciens, même parmi les plus grands, viennent de foyers sans musique. Sorti de nulle part, Hakan Hardenberger, fils unique de parents totalement dépourvus de sens musical dans une région rurale du sud de la Suède, s’est imposé à l’âge de 30 ans comme une figure unique parmi les trompettistes du monde actuel.

Ses disques ouvrent sans cesse de nouveaux répertoires, non seulement avec des concertos de compositeurs longtemps négligés des périodes baroque et classique, mais aussi avec des œuvres nouvelles. Quand on le rencontre, le regard vif et de belle prestance, il paraît encore plus jeune que son âge, aussi frais et spontané dans sa manière que le son de la trompette.

Récemment, dans l’une des plus grandes salles de concert de Londres, il a joué le Concerto pour trompette de Hummel, une sorte de morceau de bravoure pour lui, tandis qu’à la télévision une émission entière était consacrée à son travail et à son évolution, filmée à la fois ici et en Suède.

Né près de Malmö, il doit sa carrière au hasard d’un cadeau de Noël reçu alors qu’il n’avait que huit ans.

Son père, sans être musicien mais appréciant le jeu de Louis Armstrong, eut l’idée d’offrir une trompette à son fils unique. Homme sérieux, il ne choisit pas une trompette-jouet, mais demanda conseil et acheta un véritable instrument d’adulte.

Le succès du cadeau fut immédiat. Le garçon ne cessa plus de jouer. Sa mère réussit à prendre contact avec le deuxième trompette de l’Orchestre symphonique de Malmö, qu’elle persuada de donner des leçons à son fils.

Bo Nilsson était un musicien en pleine ascension, et il repéra immédiatement un talent naturel. Hardenberger ne cesse de bénir sa chance d’avoir eu un tel professeur dès le départ, quelqu’un qui était lui-même si passionné par la trompette et l’art d’en jouer qu’il recherchait et contactait des instrumentistes dans le monde entier et qui, en véritable « fanatique de la trompette », était « toujours à la recherche d’une autre embouchure ».

C’est là que le Hardenberger mûr établit une distinction entre lui-même et son professeur. « La trompette est un instrument si primitif, explique-t-il, qu’on ne peut pas fabriquer une trompette acoustiquement parfaite. Quoi qu’on fasse, elle aura des imperfections. En plus, on ne trouve pas deux embouchures exactement identiques. Pour moi, il s’agit de connaître ces imperfections et de nouer une relation avec elles. »

Dès le début, Hardenberger semble avoir eu le don de trouver le bon compromis et d’établir cette relation. Sans aucune vantardise, il explique que, même dans ses années d’enfance, le son caractéristique de Hardenberger était déjà reconnaissable, « la première chose que j’ai acquise ».

Et contrairement au grand rival britannique parmi les trompettistes virtuoses, John Wallace, qui s’est d’abord formé dans les brass bands avant d’évoluer en travaillant dans des orchestres, Hardenberger s’est toujours considéré comme un artiste soliste, purement et simplement.

Dès son plus jeune âge, il prit pour modèle le trompettiste français Maurice André, un autre musicien qui avait contourné l’orchestre. Le garçon acheta tous ses disques et l’idolâtra.

Ses parents lui donnèrent toutes les possibilités de s’exercer et soutinrent son ambition de faire de la trompette sa carrière. La question fut alors de savoir où, à 15 ans, il devait aller étudier. L’Amérique, premier choix de Bo Nilsson, fut jugée trop lointaine et trop dangereuse, ce qui fit qu’il partit à 16 ans étudier à Paris avec Pierre Thibaud. Thibaud confirma son préjugé contre l’idée d’entrer dans un orchestre, en disant que « jouer dans un orchestre, c’est comme bêcher le jardin ».

Il était assez lucide sur lui-même pour savoir qu’il jouait mieux de la trompette que les autres de son âge, mais ce n’est qu’à la fin du premier concours auquel il participa, à 17 ans durant sa première année à Paris, qu’il prit conscience qu’il possédait en plus un don particulier pour communiquer.

Thibaud lui suggéra de se présenter au concours uniquement pour acquérir de l’expérience. Hardenberger n’apprit que les morceaux du premier tour, mais il se qualifia pour le second. Heureusement, il connaissait déjà la plupart des morceaux de cette manche aussi, mais en arrivant en finale, il se trouva face à un concerto qui l’avait déjà intimidé. Il ne remporta pas le premier prix cette fois-là, mais il prit plaisir à jouer, réalisant que même s’il « jouait comme un cochon », les gens l’écoutaient tout de même.

Citée ainsi, la lucidité de Hardenberger sur son travail et sa carrière peut paraître arrogante, mais ce serait une impression totalement fausse. Avec réflexion, il refuse d’essayer d’analyser en quoi peut consister un tel don de communication, car « on risque de le détruire en cherchant à l’expliquer. La force de la musique réside dans le fait qu’elle peut toujours émouvoir les gens. »

The Actor's Craft

Derision and contempt are sprayed at actors from time to time. Much of this disdain is fuelled by the actors themselves when they're compelled by their film/theatre companies to talk about their craft (and themselves) in interviews. They should give the dancer Pavlova's reply to the man who asked her what she meant when she was dancing: 'If I could tell you,' she said, 'I wouldn't dance it.' But instead they all too easily fall into ponderous cliches, silly truisms or into the prurient jaws of the gossip machine. We should all pay heed to what Paul Scofield said in a letter to a friend of mine: 'I have found that an actor's work has life and interest only in its execution. It seems to wither away in discussion and become emptily theoretical and insubstantial. It has no rules (except perhaps audibility). With every play and every playwright the actor starts from scratch, as if he or she knows nothing and proceeds to learn afresh every time growing with the relationships of the characters and the insights of the writer. When the play has finished its run, he's empty until the next time. And its the emptiness which is, I find, apparent in any discussion of theatre work.'

A review of Hamlet

Adrian Lester's Hamlet is poised precariously between boyhood and manhood, and it is a performance of thrilling simplicity and assurance. His handling of the text and his physical and psychological self-control take him, in one leap, from brilliantly promising to frontline player: an actor with the intelligent confidence to be almost self-effacing. Lester plays an edgy, tetchy young man who feeds on a banked-down sense of anger, agile, watchful and driven, he deploys a sense of acid wit and generous humour that makes him both formidable and lovable. Although played down, the virtuosity of this performance is unmistakable. Observe Lester's body, the way his arms hang stiffly, giving you a sense of a figure waiting to be animated. Handy's portrayal of Horatio gives you a similar feeling of a body being moved by an inner force that he both knows and does not know. So what is acting? What is behaviour? Is the former an imitation or an evocation of the latter? Who and what animates these bodies, morally and physically? That is the central question about the life of the theatre.

One director's approach to rehearsal

The first stage of this director's rehearsal process is known as 'dropping in', a procedure which goes something like this. The stage manager projects the script onto a screen. The actors sit quietly while someone else is speaking, finding out what effect the words are having. When if is their turn to speak, they glance of the screen, digest the first phrase, think about what it means to them, wait to find the impulse - the reason to speak - then speak. For example, the line is, 'Queuing all night, the rain, do you remember?; Breathe. Let the thought drop in with your breath. A memory, a vision, an impression. Some people will imagine a queue, maybe at a bus stop on the way to rehearsals or for a rock concert in their youth. Having visualised the scene, find the impulse to speak it - what this director calls 'The pathway to the line'. Impulses can come from without or within. Look in the eyes of the other actor listening. Consider your character's situation. This director talks of 'dropping in' as a means of finding out what is going on. Don't pre-plan or pre-judge. Dare to go down there with an empty mind and trust that something will happen to you.

The Perfect Theatre

The perfect theatre should make you feel as if your presence has made a difference. Going to the theatre, going to any live performance, is an event and the staff need to have a sense of that, too. It's terribly alienating if you feel that its just any old job for the people working front of house.
The theatre itself needs to create a relationship between the performer and the audience - no one in the audience should feel that they're getting an unreasonably prejudiced view of the actor. It's important that they're not too far away, they can hear, they can see, they can feel in some sense in contact with what's going on on stage. The proportions of an auditorium are important. They have to respond to the human voice and the scale of the human body. If an auditorium dwarfs the human body, there's something wrong with it because you can't deny the human form at the heart of drama. A lot of theatres in the late nineteenth century got it right because they managed to shape an auditorium that somehow embraces the stage.
I like theatres that have a sense of the past in them. Like worn stone steps in a church, you get the sense of layers of human presence. From the point of view of the plays, you can't have something for everybody. You cant second-guess an audience because they don't know what they're going to want to see. When you visit the theatre, you want something done in a way you can't imagine, otherwise you may as well have stayed at home.

Le métier d’acteur

On couvre les acteurs, de temps à autre, de dérision et de mépris. Une grande part de ce dédain est alimentée par les acteurs eux-mêmes lorsqu’ils sont contraints par leurs compagnies de cinéma ou de théâtre à parler de leur art — et d’eux-mêmes — dans des entretiens. Ils feraient mieux de donner la réponse de la danseuse Pavlova à l’homme qui lui demandait ce qu’elle voulait dire quand elle dansait : « Si je pouvais vous le dire, dit-elle, je ne le danserais pas. » Mais au lieu de cela, ils tombent trop facilement dans des clichés pompeux, des truismes ridicules, ou dans les mâchoires prurientes de la machine à ragots. Nous devrions tous prêter attention à ce que Paul Scofield a dit dans une lettre à un ami à moi : « J’ai constaté que le travail d’un acteur n’a de vie et d’intérêt que dans son exécution. Il semble se flétrir dans la discussion et devenir vainement théorique et inconsistant. Il n’a pas de règles (sauf peut-être l’audibilité). Avec chaque pièce et chaque dramaturge, l’acteur repart de zéro, comme s’il ou elle ne savait rien, et entreprend de réapprendre à chaque fois, grandissant avec les relations entre les personnages et les intuitions de l’auteur. Quand la pièce a terminé sa série de représentations, il est vide jusqu’à la fois suivante. Et c’est ce vide qui, je trouve, apparaît dans toute discussion sur le travail théâtral. »

Une critique de Hamlet

Le Hamlet d’Adrian Lester se tient en équilibre précaire entre l’adolescence et l’âge d’homme, et c’est une interprétation d’une simplicité et d’une sûreté exaltantes. Sa maîtrise du texte ainsi que son contrôle physique et psychologique l’élèvent, d’un seul bond, du rang de promesse brillante à celui d’acteur de premier plan : un acteur doté de l’assurance intelligente qui permet d’être presque effacé. Lester joue un jeune homme nerveux, irritable, nourri d’une colère contenue ; agile, vigilant et poussé en avant, il déploie un esprit caustique et un humour généreux qui le rendent à la fois redoutable et attachant. Bien que discrètement jouée, la virtuosité de cette interprétation est indéniable. Observez le corps de Lester, la manière dont ses bras pendent avec raideur, vous donnant l’impression d’une figure qui attend d’être animée. L’interprétation d’Horatio par Handy vous donne une sensation semblable d’un corps mû par une force intérieure qu’il connaît et ne connaît pas tout à la fois. Alors, qu’est-ce que jouer ? Qu’est-ce que le comportement ? Le premier est-il une imitation ou une évocation du second ? Qui et quoi anime ces corps, moralement et physiquement ? Telle est la question centrale de la vie du théâtre.

L’approche d’un metteur en scène face aux répétitions

La première étape du processus de répétition de ce metteur en scène est connue sous le nom de « dropping in », une procédure qui ressemble à peu près à ceci. Le régisseur projette le texte sur un écran. Les acteurs restent assis tranquillement pendant que quelqu’un d’autre parle, découvrant l’effet que les mots produisent. Quand vient leur tour de parler, ils jettent un coup d’œil à l’écran, assimilent la première phrase, réfléchissent à ce qu’elle signifie pour eux, attendent de trouver l’impulsion — la raison de parler — puis parlent. Par exemple, la réplique est : « Faire la queue toute la nuit, la pluie, tu te souviens ? » Respirez. Laissez la pensée s’installer avec votre souffle. Un souvenir, une vision, une impression. Certains imagineront une file d’attente, peut-être à un arrêt de bus en allant aux répétitions ou pour un concert de rock dans leur jeunesse. Ayant visualisé la scène, trouvez l’impulsion pour la dire — ce que ce metteur en scène appelle « le chemin vers la réplique ». Les impulsions peuvent venir de l’extérieur ou de l’intérieur. Regardez dans les yeux de l’autre acteur qui écoute. Pensez à la situation de votre personnage. Ce metteur en scène parle du « dropping in » comme d’un moyen de découvrir ce qui se passe. Ne planifiez pas à l’avance, ne jugez pas à l’avance. Osez descendre là-dedans l’esprit vide et faites confiance au fait que quelque chose vous arrivera.

Le théâtre parfait

Le théâtre parfait devrait vous donner le sentiment que votre présence a fait une différence. Aller au théâtre, aller à n’importe quelle représentation en direct, est un événement, et le personnel doit en avoir conscience lui aussi. C’est terriblement aliénant si l’on a l’impression que ce n’est qu’un boulot comme un autre pour les gens qui travaillent à l’accueil.
Le théâtre lui-même doit créer une relation entre l’interprète et le public — personne dans la salle ne devrait avoir le sentiment de recevoir une vision déraisonnablement biaisée de l’acteur. Il est important que les spectateurs ne soient pas trop éloignés, qu’ils puissent entendre, voir, sentir en quelque sorte qu’ils sont en contact avec ce qui se passe sur scène. Les proportions d’une salle sont importantes. Elles doivent répondre à la voix humaine et à l’échelle du corps humain. Si une salle écrase le corps humain, c’est qu’il y a quelque chose qui ne va pas, car on ne peut pas nier la forme humaine qui est au cœur du drame. Beaucoup de théâtres de la fin du XIXe siècle avaient trouvé la bonne formule parce qu’ils étaient parvenus à donner à une salle une forme qui, d’une certaine manière, embrasse la scène.
J’aime les théâtres qui portent en eux un sentiment du passé. Comme des marches de pierre usées dans une église, on y perçoit des couches de présence humaine. Du point de vue des pièces, on ne peut pas avoir quelque chose pour tout le monde. On ne peut pas deviner par avance ce que voudra un public, parce qu’il ne sait pas lui-même ce qu’il aura envie de voir. Quand on va au théâtre, on veut voir quelque chose fait d’une manière qu’on ne peut pas imaginer, sinon autant être resté chez soi.

The Actor’s Profession

Actors are, from time to time, showered with ridicule and contempt. A large part of this disdain is fueled by the actors themselves when they are compelled by their film or theater companies to talk about their art—and themselves—in interviews. They would do better to give the answer of the dancer Pavlova to the man who asked her what she meant when she danced: “If I could tell you,” she said, “I wouldn’t dance it.” But instead, they fall too easily into pompous clichés, ridiculous truisms, or into the prurient jaws of the gossip machine. We should all pay attention to what Paul Scofield said in a letter to a friend of mine: “I have found that an actor’s work has life and interest only in its performance. It seems to wither in discussion and become vainly theoretical and insubstantial. It has no rules (except perhaps audibility). With each play and each playwright, the actor starts again from scratch, as if he or she knew nothing, and sets out to relearn each time, growing with the relationships between the characters and the author’s insights. When the play has finished its run, he is empty until the next time. And it is this emptiness that, I find, appears in all discussion of theatrical work.”

A Review of Hamlet

Adrian Lester’s Hamlet stands in precarious balance between adolescence and manhood, and it is a performance of exhilarating simplicity and assurance. His command of the text, as well as his physical and psychological control, lifts him in a single bound from the rank of brilliant promise to that of a leading actor: an actor endowed with the intelligent confidence that makes it possible to be almost self-effacing. Lester plays a nervous, irritable young man, fed by suppressed anger; agile, alert, and driving forward, he displays a caustic wit and generous humor that make him both formidable and appealing. Though quietly played, the virtuosity of this performance is undeniable. Watch Lester’s body, the way his arms hang stiffly, giving you the impression of a figure waiting to be animated. Handy’s performance as Horatio gives you a similar sense of a body moved by an inner force that he both knows and does not know at once. So what is acting? What is behavior? Is the former an imitation or an evocation of the latter? Who and what animate these bodies, morally and physically? That is the central question of the life of the theater.

A Director’s Approach to Rehearsals

The first stage of this director’s rehearsal process is known as “dropping in,” a procedure that goes roughly like this. The stage manager projects the text onto a screen. The actors sit quietly while someone else speaks, discovering the effect the words produce. When their turn comes to speak, they glance at the screen, take in the first line, reflect on what it means to them, wait to find the impulse—the reason to speak—and then speak. For example, the line is: “Queuing all night, in the rain, remember?” Breathe. Let the thought settle with your breath. A memory, a vision, an impression. Some will imagine a line of people, perhaps at a bus stop on the way to rehearsals or for a rock concert in their youth. Having visualized the scene, find the impulse to say it—what this director calls “the path to the line.” Impulses can come from outside or from within. Look into the eyes of the other actor who is listening. Think about your character’s situation. This director speaks of “dropping in” as a way of discovering what is happening. Do not plan ahead, do not judge ahead of time. Dare to go down into it with an empty mind and trust that something will happen to you.

The Perfect Theater

The perfect theater should give you the feeling that your presence has made a difference. Going to the theater, going to any live performance, is an event, and the staff must be aware of that too. It is terribly alienating if one feels that it is just another job for the people working front of house.
The theater itself must create a relationship between performer and audience—no one in the auditorium should feel that they are being given an unreasonably skewed view of the actor. It is important that spectators should not be too far away, that they can hear, see, somehow feel that they are in contact with what is happening on stage. The proportions of an auditorium matter. They must answer to the human voice and the scale of the human body. If an auditorium crushes the human body, then something is wrong, because one cannot deny the human form that lies at the heart of drama. Many late nineteenth-century theaters had found the right formula because they had succeeded in giving an auditorium a shape that, in a sense, embraces the stage.
I like theaters that carry within them a sense of the past. Like worn stone steps in a church, they bear the traces of layers of human presence. In terms of plays, you cannot have something for everyone. You cannot guess in advance what an audience will want, because it does not itself know what it will feel like seeing. When you go to the theater, you want to see something done in a way you cannot imagine, otherwise you might as well have stayed home.

It was a hot Saturday in early July. The water and sky were blue in the afternoon sun and there were some big waves for the surfers. A lot of them were in the sea. Nick was there, too. He sat on his surfboard and waited for a good wave. A big wave came - Nick started to swim strongly. His board moved quickly with the wave and Nick stood up on it. He was a very  good surfer. 
There were some Australians on the beach. They were there for the surf . . . and for the big surfing competition at the beach in a week's time. One of them was a tall girl with long dark hair - Janelle. She was from Queensland. She watched Nick and then looked at one of the boys with her. Mike smiled. 'He's very good, and that's a strong wave. It'll be difficult to beat him in the competition.' The second boy, Brian, was small with long hair and cold blue eyes. Janelle was his girlfriend.
'We can beat him easily,' Brian said. 'He's only good because he knows the beach here. I can surf well on any beach. I want to catch some waves.' He walked down to the sea. 'I don't want to go in the water now,' Janelle said. 'Let's go and have a drink at the caf,.' Brian sat on his surfboard and watched Nick in the water. 'Mike and Janelle are wrong,' he thought. 'He's not very good.'

Living in the valley

We had been living in our valley for sixteen months when we first realised the dangers that could exist in the surrounding hills and threaten our very survival.
It was the year when the storms came early, before the calendar even hinted at winter, even before November was out. Until that time, we had felt safe and sheltered in our valley below the protecting hills.
Soon snow began to fall. Within a day it lay some 15 centimetres deep. It almost completely blocked our lane and made the streamside path slippery and dangerous. But on the neighbouring heights the snow was much deeper and stayed for longer. Up there the wind blasted fiercely. Deep in our valley we felt only sudden gusts of wind; trees swayed but the branches held firm.
And yet we knew that there was reason for us to worry. The snow and wind were certainly inconvenient but they did not really trouble us greatly. It was the river, the Ryburn, which normally flowed so gently, that threatened us most. It reminded us of what could have occurred if circumstances had been different, if the flow of water from the hills had not, many years before, been controlled, held back by a series of dams.
In a short time the snow started to melt. Day after day, we watched furious clouds pile up high over the hills to the west. Sinister grey clouds extended over the valleys. They twisted and turned, rising eastwards and upwards, warning of what was to come. We had seen enough of the sky; now we began to watch the river, which every day was becoming fuller and wilder.
The snow was gradually washed away as more and more rain streamed from the clouds, but high up in the hills the reservoir was filling and was fast approaching danger level. And then it happened - for the first time in years the reservoir overflowed. There in the heights it was like the Niagara Falls, as the water surged over the edge of the dam and poured into the stream below. 
The river seemed maddened as the waters poured almost horizontally down to its lower stretches. Just a couple of metres from our cottage, the stream seemed wild beneath the bridge. It was far deeper than we'd ever seen it so near our home, lunging furiously at its banks. For three days we prayed that it would stay below its wall. Fortunately, our prayers were answered as the dam held and the waters began to subside.
On many occasions through the centuries before the dam was built, the river had flooded the nearby villages in just such a rage. Now, though, the dam restricts the flow of the river and usually all is well; the great mass of water from the hills, the product of snow and torrential rain, remains behind its barrier with just the occasional overflow. We can thus enjoy, rather than fear, the huge clouds that hang over the valley, and can be thrilled by the tremendous power which we know the river possesses. Thanks to this protection we can feel our home in the valley is still secure and safe.

Wonen in de vallei

We woonden al zestien maanden in onze vallei toen we ons voor het eerst realiseerden welke gevaren er in de omliggende heuvels konden schuilen en ons voortbestaan zelfs konden bedreigen.
Het was het jaar waarin de stormen vroeg kwamen, nog voordat de kalender zelfs maar op de winter wees, nog voordat november voorbij was. Tot die tijd hadden we ons veilig en beschut gevoeld in onze vallei onder de beschermende heuvels.
Al snel begon de sneeuw te vallen. Binnen een dag lag er ongeveer 15 centimeter. Onze landweg raakte daardoor bijna helemaal geblokkeerd en het pad langs de beek werd glad en gevaarlijk. Maar op de naburige hoogten lag de sneeuw veel dieper en bleef zij langer liggen. Daarboven loeide de wind hevig. Diep in onze vallei voelden we alleen plotselinge windstoten; bomen zwaaiden heen en weer, maar de takken hielden stand.
En toch wisten we dat we reden hadden om ons zorgen te maken. De sneeuw en de wind waren zeker lastig, maar ze bezorgden ons eigenlijk niet al te veel problemen. Het was de rivier, de Ryburn, die normaal zo rustig stroomde, die ons het meest bedreigde. Zij herinnerde ons eraan wat er had kunnen gebeuren als de omstandigheden anders waren geweest, als de waterstroom uit de heuvels niet al vele jaren eerder onder controle was gebracht, tegengehouden door een reeks dammen.
Al snel begon de sneeuw te smelten. Dag na dag zagen we woeste wolken zich hoog boven de heuvels in het westen opstapelen. Dreigende grijze wolken spreidden zich uit over de valleien. Ze kronkelden en draaiden, stegen oostwaarts en omhoog, en waarschuwden voor wat zou komen. We hadden genoeg naar de lucht gekeken; nu begonnen we de rivier in de gaten te houden, die met de dag voller en woester werd.
De sneeuw werd geleidelijk weggespoeld terwijl er steeds meer regen uit de wolken neerstreamde, maar hoog in de heuvels vulde het stuwmeer zich en naderde het snel het gevarenniveau. En toen gebeurde het — voor het eerst in jaren stroomde het stuwmeer over. Daar hoog in de bergen was het als de Niagarawatervallen, terwijl het water over de rand van de dam kolkte en in de stroom daaronder neerstortte.
De rivier leek buiten zinnen terwijl het water bijna horizontaal naar de lager gelegen gedeelten stroomde. Slechts een paar meter van ons huisje leek de beek onder de brug woest. Hij was veel dieper dan we hem ooit zo dicht bij ons huis hadden gezien en beukte razend tegen zijn oevers. Drie dagen lang baden we dat hij onder zijn muur zou blijven. Gelukkig werden onze gebeden verhoord, want de dam hield stand en het water begon te zakken.
Vele malen in de eeuwen voordat de dam werd gebouwd, had de rivier in precies zo'n woede de nabijgelegen dorpen overstroomd. Nu echter beperkt de dam de stroom van de rivier en gaat het meestal goed; de enorme massa water uit de heuvels, voortgebracht door sneeuw en stortregen, blijft achter de barrière, op af en toe een overstroming na. Daardoor kunnen we genieten van, in plaats van bang te zijn voor, de enorme wolken die boven de vallei hangen, en kunnen we onder de indruk raken van de geweldige kracht waarvan we weten dat de rivier die bezit. Dankzij deze bescherming kunnen we het gevoel hebben dat ons huis in de vallei nog steeds zeker en veilig is.

We are being bombarded with advertisements all the time and a lot of them are targeted at young people. Smaller children, apart from spending their own pocket money, can also influence what their parents buy, so many TV ads are created with kids in mind. 
For example, adverts for drinks feature cartoon animals. Then, as two-year-olds are being pushed around the shop by their parents in a trolley, they recognise the drink from the advert and ask the adults to buy it. As children grow older, some products are marketed to them as 'must-have' items, implying that children won't be liked by their friends if they don't get them. 
As a result, kids are desperate to get the product and parents can be made to feel guilty if they don't buy it for their child. Teenagers are incredibly critical of adverts, so products aimed at them have to be advertised much more cleverly. As teens are driven by the desire to be part of the 'coolest' group in their school, products need to be given a cool feel. 
For example, advertisers give away stickers which direct teens to a difficult-to-find website with more information about a product. In this way, naturally rebellious teens feel that they have been invited to an exclusive club and can be sold expensive products. 
As teens hate being influenced by adults, marketers let them persuade each other that a certain product is cool. Since the late nineties, 'street teams' of teenagers have been employed by clothing and record companies to spread the word about a product among young people.

Lexington, who had always done everything his aunt had told him, put the money in his pocket, put on a pair of shoes and a clean shirt, and went down the mountain to the village where the doctor lived.
'Old Glosspan?' the doctor said. 'Is she dead?'
'Certainly she's dead,' the boy answered. 'If you come home with me now I'll dig her up and you can see for yourself.'
'How deep did you bury her?' the doctor asked. 'Two or three metres down, I think.' 
'And how long ago?' 'Oh, about eight hours.' 'Then she's dead,' the doctor announced. 'Here's the certificate.'
Lexington now left for the city of New York to find Mr Samuel Zuckermann. He travelled on foot, and he slept under bushes, and he lived on berries and wild plants, and it took him sixteen days to reach the city.
'What a place this is!' he cried, as he stood staring around him. 'There are no chickens or cows anywhere and none of the women looks like Aunt Glosspan at all.'
Lexington had never seen anyone like Mr Zuckermann before, either. He was a small man with a large nose, and when he smiled, bits of gold flashed at you from lots of different places inside his
mouth. In his office, he shook Lexington warmly by the hand and congratulated him on his aunt's death.
'I suppose you know that your dearly loved aunt was a woman of great wealth?' he said.
'Do you mean the cows and the chickens?'
'I mean five hundred thousand dollars,' Mr Zuckermann said.
'How much?'
'Five hundred thousand dollars, my boy. And she's left it all to you.'

"There's something out there! It threw an orange at me!" Elliott said. "Ooooo!" said Tyler, a friend of Elliott. "An orange! Very dangerous!" Elliott's mom, Mary, took a light, and then she and the boys went into the yard. "What did you see?" Mary asked Elliott. "Something there," he answered. He pointed to the end of the yard. Elliott's brother, Michael, said, "Look, something walked across the ground here!" The extra-terrestrial looked at them from the dark. There were five Earth children, and a tall, beautiful person. Strange sounds came from her mouth. He couldn't understand them. Was she their mother? His heart-light started to shine, so he put his hand over it. She was the most beautiful of Earth people. 
The extra-terrestrial looked and looked. "Stupid heart-light," he said-but it shone more and more. The Earth people went back into the kitchen. Later in the night, three of the children left the house. They were Elliott's friends, Greg, Tyler, and Steve. Then, the lights went out and the house was quiet. The extra-terrestrial walked across the yard to the plants. It was very dark now, so he couldn't see. He hit his head and fell back on the ground.
He cried out loudly. Suddenly, the kitchen door opened and Elliott ran out into the yard with his dog, Harvey. He shone a light into the plants and saw the extraterrestrial. Elliott shouted-and fell over. The extra-terrestrial started to run.
"Don't go!" Elliott said.

Elliotts moeder, Mary, pakte een zaklamp, en daarna gingen zij en de jongens de tuin in. 'Wat heb je gezien?' vroeg Mary aan Elliott. 'Iets daar,' antwoordde hij. Hij wees naar het einde van de tuin. Elliotts broer, Michael, zei: 'Kijk, hier is iets over de grond gelopen!' De buitenaardse keek vanuit het donker naar hen. Er waren vijf aardse kinderen, en een lang, mooi persoon. Er kwamen vreemde geluiden uit haar mond. Hij kon ze niet begrijpen. Was zij hun moeder? Zijn hartlicht begon te schijnen, dus legde hij zijn hand erover. Zij was de mooiste van de aardse mensen.
De buitenaardse keek en keek. 'Stomme hartlicht,' zei hij, maar het scheen steeds feller. De aardse mensen gingen terug naar de keuken. Later in de nacht verlieten drie van de kinderen het huis. Het waren Elliotts vrienden, Greg, Tyler en Steve. Daarna gingen de lichten uit en was het stil in huis. De buitenaardse liep door de tuin naar de planten. Het was nu erg donker, dus hij kon niets zien. Hij stootte zijn hoofd en viel achterover op de grond.
Hij riep hard. Plotseling ging de keukendeur open en rende Elliott met zijn hond, Harvey, de tuin in. Hij scheen met een licht in de planten en zag de buitenaardse. Elliott schreeuwde en viel om. De buitenaardse begon te rennen.
'Ga niet weg!' zei Elliott.

"There's something there! It threw an orange at me!" said Elliott. "Ooooo!" said Tyler, a friend of Elliott's. "An orange! Very dangerous!" Elliott's mother, Mary, picked up a flashlight, and then she and the boys went into the garden. "What did you see?" Mary asked Elliott. "Something there," he replied. He pointed to the end of the garden. Elliott's brother, Michael, said, "Look, something walked across the ground here!" The alien watched them from the darkness. There were five earthly children, and one tall, beautiful person. Strange sounds came from her mouth. He could not understand them. Was she their mother? His heartlight began to shine, so he put his hand over it. She was the most beautiful of the earthly people.
The alien watched and watched. "Stupid heartlight," he said, but it kept shining brighter and brighter. The earthly people went back to the kitchen. Later in the night, three of the children left the house. They were Elliott's friends, Greg, Tyler, and Steve. Then the lights went out and the house was quiet. The alien walked through the garden to the plants. It was very dark now, so he could not see anything. He bumped his head and fell backward onto the ground.
He cried out loudly. Suddenly the kitchen door opened and Elliott ran into the garden with his dog, Harvey. He shone a light on the plants and saw the alien. Elliott screamed and fell over. The alien began to run.
"Don't go away!" said Elliott.

Growing up in Los Angeles, Vanessa Van Petten got into trouble so often that her mother and father began buying parenting advice books. 
During one of her frequent groundings, Van Petten glanced through several of the books and spotted what she considered two major problems. 
First, the books provided useless advice. More importantly, they were written by adults with no input from teenagers. That's when Van Petten decided to take matters into her own hands. 
At the age of sixteen, she wrote a book for parents from the teenage perspective: You're Grounded: How to Stop Fighting and Make the Teenage Years Easier. 
By the age of twenty-one, she had created RadicalParenting.com, an online community for parents and teens. That's where, with two full-time employees, Van Petten's 120 bloggers aged twelve to twenty answer questions from parents. The site generates revenue through advertising and sponsored links to other websites. 
Vanessa's advice: 
Get advice and help: 'Everyone said I was too young to start a company but I used online resources, read books, attended conferences and got advice from people I know. That's how I learnt about the business so quickly.' 
Reach new audiences: 'Social media is a great way to get in touch with new users - that's why we went on sites for mums and personally emailed videos to big users in each community.' 
Do something that works: 'Most importantly, we offered advice that actually works. Parents increasingly began spreading our quirky and sometimes controversial articles by word of mouth. We want to build a brand that is not only interesting but also life-changing.'
