Art on TV

Why is it that television so consistently fails when it comes to programmes about the visual arts? Painting and sculpture should be natural subjects for the camera, which has the ability to show a whole work of art, then move in close to examine the details. Yet I can think of few series on television that have managed to convey both the pleasure and complexity of looking at them.
A good example of what goes wrong can be seen in Robert Hughes’s eight part survey of American art, American Visions. Hughes is a critic you can trust, he has a personality that commands attention and he has been given nearly eight hours in which to introduce British audiences to a school of art that British galleries have totally ignored. I had expected the series to focus on great works of art. What I got instead was one about the way American history and culture are reflected in its art and architecture.

Dealing in Metals

For 20 years I worked as an international metals dealer and gained something of a reputation as a speculator. Metals are regulated far less than other markets. With a bit of luck, a willingness to take a risk and a good understanding of how the market works, it’s possible to make a lot of money. Risk-taking is part and parcel of the industry. The buccaneering culture fits nicely with a free-market global economy. But now the free-trade economists who claimed the market itself would maintain the price of scarce metals have found the opposite is happening. More minerals are being extracted and the cost of raw materials is decreasing. Taking inflation into account, the prices of most metals are about half of what they were 20 years ago. Recently, I was asked to look into allegations made against one of the multinational conglomerates that benefit from these cheap raw materials.

Extract from a Holiday Brochure

Abaco and its off-shore cays are part of the 700 islands of the Bahamas that stretch from Florida past the Tropic of Cancer, to Cuba. Each one has its own personality, each one has something to offer.
The key to getting anywhere in the islands and cays of Abaco is a boat. If you don’t get one thrown in with the room don’t worry. Be happy. There are ferries galore. And water-taxis. Or, there are plenty of boats to rent if you prefer to go under your own steam.
But sailing is the most popular mode of transport here. Abaco is nicknamed ‘The Sailing Capital of the World' for good reason.
Those calm, naturally protected waters are also a paradise for fishing, diving, snorkelling and swimming. The cays and their beaches stretch for 200 miles like a string of pearls. It’s not only at sea that gems can be found. At night it's the lights of the restaurants and cafes of Hope Town and Green Turtle Cay that sparkle.

Waarom is het dat televisie zo consequent faalt als het gaat om programma’s over de beeldende kunst? Schilderkunst en beeldhouwkunst zouden natuurlijke onderwerpen voor de camera moeten zijn, die het vermogen heeft om een volledig kunstwerk te tonen en vervolgens dichtbij te komen om de details te bekijken. Toch kan ik maar weinig televisieseries bedenken die erin geslaagd zijn zowel het plezier als de complexiteit van het kijken ernaar over te brengen.
Een goed voorbeeld van wat er misgaat, is te zien in Robert Hughes’ achtdelige overzicht van de Amerikaanse kunst, American Visions. Hughes is een criticus die je kunt vertrouwen, hij heeft een persoonlijkheid die de aandacht trekt en hij heeft bijna acht uur gekregen om het Britse publiek kennis te laten maken met een kunststroming die door Britse galerieën volledig is genegeerd. Ik had verwacht dat de serie zich zou richten op grote kunstwerken. Wat ik in plaats daarvan kreeg, was er een over de manier waarop de Amerikaanse geschiedenis en cultuur in haar kunst en architectuur worden weerspiegeld.

Handel in metalen

Twintig jaar lang werkte ik als internationaal metaalhandelaar en verwierf ik enigszins een reputatie als speculant. Metalen worden veel minder gereguleerd dan andere markten. Met een beetje geluk, de bereidheid om risico te nemen en een goed begrip van hoe de markt werkt, is het mogelijk veel geld te verdienen. Risico nemen is een wezenlijk onderdeel van de sector. De roekeloze cultuur past goed bij een vrije-markt wereldeconomie. Maar nu hebben de vrijhandelseconomen die beweerden dat de markt zelf de prijs van schaarse metalen zou handhaven, ontdekt dat het tegenovergestelde gebeurt. Er worden meer mineralen gewonnen en de kosten van grondstoffen dalen. Rekening houdend met inflatie liggen de prijzen van de meeste metalen op ongeveer de helft van wat ze twintig jaar geleden waren. Onlangs werd mij gevraagd onderzoek te doen naar beschuldigingen die waren geuit tegen een van de multinationale conglomeraten die profiteren van deze goedkope grondstoffen.

The History of Farming 

Before people started farming, they went to the forest to look for plants or fruit they could eat. This meant that people were moving all the time to find food. But about 12,000 years ago, in the Middle East, people began to grow food. These people were the first farmers. Farming made it possible for people to stay in one place and slowly their villages got bigger. 
Some people in the villages became free to do other work, like making clothes, because the farmers could grow food for everyone. Unfortunately, farming was difficult when the weather was bad and then some people did not get enough food to eat. 
Today, farmers can grow more food and it travels thousands of kilometres from where it is grown to our homes.

De geschiedenis van de landbouw

Voordat mensen landbouw gingen bedrijven, gingen ze naar het bos om planten of fruit te zoeken die ze konden eten. Dit betekende dat mensen voortdurend onderweg waren om voedsel te vinden. Maar ongeveer 12.000 jaar geleden begonnen mensen in het Midden-Oosten voedsel te verbouwen. Deze mensen waren de eerste boeren. Landbouw maakte het mogelijk voor mensen om op één plek te blijven en langzaam werden hun dorpen groter.

Sommige mensen in de dorpen kregen de vrijheid om ander werk te doen, zoals kleren maken, omdat de boeren voedsel voor iedereen konden verbouwen. Helaas was landbouw moeilijk als het weer slecht was, en dan kregen sommige mensen niet genoeg te eten.

Tegenwoordig kunnen boeren meer voedsel verbouwen en het reist duizenden kilometers van de plek waar het wordt verbouwd naar onze huizen.

Watering the Desert
 It can rain at any time between November and March in Marrakesh, Morocco. It doesn’t happen frequently and when it does, the city’s water pipes can’t manage the sudden floods, which turn the streets into rivers. But, as many winters have remained dry in recent times, when the rain does come, it is welcomed by the local people. 
Marrakesh’s parks and gardens exist, not because of the rain, but thanks to a network of underground channels, dug in the 11th century, which bring in water from the mountains all year round. Basically dry places, which receive their water in this way, are known as oases. 
Further south from Marrakesh, the traveller arrives at Skoura. Here every available piece of land is made into small squares by the water channels and used to grow food. The Atlas mountains, snow-covered in winter, provide a delightful background.
results.tgt_text:
De woestijn bewateren

Tussen november en maart kan het in Marrakesh, Marokko, op elk moment regenen. Dat gebeurt niet vaak en als het wel gebeurt, kunnen de waterleidingen van de stad de plotselinge overstromingen niet aan, waardoor de straten in rivieren veranderen. Maar omdat veel winters de laatste tijd droog zijn gebleven, wordt de regen, wanneer die valt, door de plaatselijke bevolking verwelkomd.

De parken en tuinen van Marrakesh bestaan niet dankzij de regen, maar dankzij een netwerk van ondergrondse kanalen, gegraven in de 11e eeuw, die het hele jaar door water uit de bergen aanvoeren. In wezen droge plaatsen, die op deze manier van water worden voorzien, staan bekend als oases.

Verder naar het zuiden van Marrakesh komt de reiziger aan in Skoura. Hier wordt elk beschikbaar stukje land door de waterkanalen in kleine vierkanten verdeeld en gebruikt om voedsel te verbouwen. Het Atlasgebergte, in de winter met sneeuw bedekt, vormt een prachtig decor.

I stopped the car in a cloud of dust, and we walked up the steps and into the saloon. 
Well if I'd wanted to do a bit of time-travelling, I couldn't have done much better; walking through that door was like walking back eighty years in time. Inside, the old Western saloon was still intact, with its big long wooden bar, and enormous mirrors on the walls. Apart from the electric light, the juke box, and the tables set for dinner, it was almost perfect. 
And there in the corner sat the prospector, with his wife. If he'd been wearing a red gown, I'd have taken him for Father Christmas, but he wasn't. This old-timer wasn't in Atlantic City to bring presents, but to find gold. 

He said his name was Brad, and he'd been looking for gold in Atlantic City for some time now. Yes, he'd found some too; not enough to make him a millionaire, but enough to make him happy. 
When the Gold Rush ended in Atlantic City, he told me, it was not actually because there was no more gold, but because gold was too hard to find, or not valuable enough. 
Today, gold is a lot more valuable than it was a hundred years ago, and modern techniques allow people to find gold more easily. And that was why Brad and his wife were in Atlantic City, digging for gold. 
They were not the only ones, said Brad; quite a few of the "concessions" are now being worked, and some old mines are being opened up again. In some places, mining for gold has become commercially profitable again; but in most cases, the miners, like Brad, are just amateurs.

GETTING FIT 

Exercise is essential for mind, body and spirit. It's one of the best ways to maintain a perfect balance when all around you everything seems more and more unbalanced and the world becomes ever more fast and furious. 
Don't groan because this is yet another article about fitness. The reason why there are so many is that it is seriously good for you. There are plenty of reasons why you should exercise and very few - for most of us why you shouldn't. Exercise improves muscle tone and provides quick changes in body shape. It improves muscle power and promotes good posture - the way in which you hold your body when sitting or standing. It helps prevent those muscle imbalances which can lead to injuries. It provides quick improvement in specific problem areas such as thighs, stomach and upper arms. It improves the condition of the heart and lungs and blood circulation. 
Probably all these reasons have been thrown at you time and time again, so maybe you are bored by them and have switched off. All right then, this should make you sit up and take notice. Did you know that exercise helps to ease depression and tiredness, and that it helps to regulate sleep patterns? Also that exercise is instrumental in controlling stress? Not only this, but exercise can help to relieve certain medical conditions. 
By now you should be influenced a little by these arguments. If not, common sense alone should tell you that exercise is good for you. 
There are plenty of types of exercise you can do aerobics, calisthenics, jogging, working out with free weights, working on weight machines. There is one point you should note - training too hard and with too much weight may cause injury, so start slowly and carefully. If you're not sure, you should consult your doctor on what's good for you personally. 
No amount of exercise will improve your body shape if you don't have good posture. This practically determines how you look and feel. Not only is a stiff or sagging body unattractive, it also lacks energy and is more likely to suffer from minor health complaints. 
If your body tends to slouch, imagine that the top of your head is connected to a helium balloon, which is trying to pull you up into the sky. This will help you to lift the chest for fuller and easier breathing. At the same time, it lengthens the abdomen, making the body look much slimmer. If the chest is well balanced when you are standing, you can see your ankles. 
Stretching the muscles improves flexibility and ease of movement, and helps you to maintain correct posture and to prevent muscle tears and injuries caused by overuse. If done four or five times a week, it will guarantee a more flexible,fitter body. So stretching should play an important part in your exercise routine, which should be performed both slowly and precisely. 
The best exercise, therefore, involves a good warm-up, stretching exercises, an energetic workout and definitely a cool down period.
results.tgt_text:
FIT WORDEN

Lichaamsbeweging is essentieel voor geest, lichaam en ziel. Het is een van de beste manieren om een perfect evenwicht te bewaren wanneer alles om je heen steeds onevenwichtiger lijkt te worden en de wereld almaar sneller en hectischer wordt.
Kreun niet, want dit is alweer een artikel over fitness. De reden waarom er zo veel zijn, is dat het echt heel goed voor je is. Er zijn tal van redenen waarom je zou moeten bewegen en voor de meesten van ons maar heel weinig redenen waarom je dat niet zou moeten doen. Beweging verbetert de spierspanning en zorgt snel voor veranderingen in de lichaamsvorm. Het vergroot de spierkracht en bevordert een goede houding - de manier waarop je je lichaam houdt wanneer je zit of staat. Het helpt die spieronevenwichtigheden te voorkomen die tot blessures kunnen leiden. Het zorgt snel voor verbetering van specifieke probleemzones zoals dijen, buik en bovenarmen. Het verbetert de conditie van hart en longen en de bloedsomloop.
Waarschijnlijk zijn al deze redenen al keer op keer op je afgevuurd, dus misschien verveel je je ermee en ben je afgehaakt. Goed dan, misschien zorgt dit ervoor dat je rechtop gaat zitten en oplet. Wist je dat lichaamsbeweging helpt om depressie en vermoeidheid te verlichten, en dat het helpt om het slaappatroon te reguleren? Ook dat lichaamsbeweging van groot belang is bij het beheersen van stress? En niet alleen dat, lichaamsbeweging kan ook helpen om bepaalde medische aandoeningen te verlichten.
Inmiddels zouden deze argumenten je toch een beetje beïnvloed moeten hebben. Zo niet, dan zou het gezonde verstand alleen al je moeten vertellen dat beweging goed voor je is.
Er zijn tal van soorten lichaamsbeweging die je kunt doen: aerobics, gymnastische oefeningen, joggen, trainen met losse gewichten, oefenen op krachttoestellen. Er is wel één punt waar je op moet letten - te hard trainen en met te veel gewicht kan blessures veroorzaken, dus begin langzaam en voorzichtig. Als je het niet zeker weet, moet je je arts raadplegen over wat persoonlijk goed voor je is.
Geen enkele hoeveelheid lichaamsbeweging zal je lichaamsvorm verbeteren als je geen goede houding hebt. Die bepaalt in de praktijk hoe je eruitziet en hoe je je voelt. Een stijf of ingezakt lichaam is niet alleen onaantrekkelijk, het heeft ook minder energie en krijgt eerder last van kleine gezondheidsklachten.
Als je lichaam de neiging heeft om onderuit te zakken, stel je dan voor dat de kruin van je hoofd vastzit aan een heliumballon die je de lucht in probeert te trekken. Dit zal je helpen de borst op te heffen voor vollere en gemakkelijkere ademhaling. Tegelijkertijd verlengt het de buik, waardoor het lichaam veel slanker lijkt. Als de borst goed in balans is wanneer je staat, kun je je enkels zien.
Het rekken van de spieren verbetert de lenigheid en het gemak van bewegen, en helpt je om een correcte houding te behouden en spierscheuren en blessures door overbelasting te voorkomen. Als je dit vier of vijf keer per week doet, garandeert het een soepeler en fitter lichaam. Rekken zou daarom een belangrijk onderdeel van je trainingsroutine moeten zijn, en het moet zowel langzaam als nauwkeurig worden uitgevoerd.
De beste training bestaat daarom uit een goede warming-up, rekoefeningen, een energieke workout en beslist een cooling-downperiode.

This will help lift the chest for fuller and easier breathing. At the same time, it lengthens the abdomen, making the body look much slimmer. If the chest is properly balanced when you are standing, you should be able to see your ankles.
Stretching the muscles improves flexibility and ease of movement, and helps you maintain correct posture and prevent muscle tears and overuse injuries. If you do this four or five times a week, it guarantees a suppler and fitter body. Stretching should therefore be an important part of your exercise routine, and it should be performed both slowly and accurately.
The best workout therefore consists of a good warm-up, stretching exercises, an energetic workout, and definitely a cool-down period.

And certainly Catherine's education could not be described as appropriate for a heroine. In fact, she had an obvious dislike for the classroom and never could learn or understand anything before she was taught; occasionally she even seemed rather stupid. 
Her mother wanted her to learn music and Catherine was sure that she would like to play the piano, so at eight years old she began lessons. But she soon gave up, and the day on which the music teacher was dismissed was one of the happiest days of her young life. Her drawing ability was also disappointing; although she enjoyed drawing animals, all her pictures, from chickens to horses, looked very similar. 
What a strange, incomprehensible character! Incomprehensible because, in spite of such clear signs of a difficult nature, Catherine was seldom unpleasant; she rarely quarrelled and was very kind to her six younger brothers and sisters and quite friendly with the three older ones. But it still must be admitted that she was untidy, noisy and wild and loved nothing better than rolling down her favourite hill at the back of the house. 
At fifteen, Catherine's appearance began to improve; her skin was brighter, her hair was shinier and nicely styled, her eyes shone and her figure was pleasing. Her love of dirt was replaced by an interest in the latest fashions and in the possibility of going to a ball. She was quite thrilled one day to hear her father remark on her personal improvement: 'Catherine is almost pretty today.' To be almost pretty is a great prize to a girl who has been plain for fifteen years.

It was late autumn. The weather was wet and the wind had blown all the leaves from the trees. I was riding my horse across the wet, empty land. I was traveling alone. I was going toward a dark and strange house - the House of Usher.
Why had I come to this lonely place? I knew Roderick Usher - the owner of the house. We were old friends, but we had not met for many years. A few weeks ago, I had received a letter from Roderick.

I am ill - very ill. Please come and visit me. I am going mad! I want your help. We have been friends since we were boys. Please come!
Roderick Usher

I had been riding all day and it was now late. The pale sun was low in the sky when I arrived at the House of Usher.
A large lake of black water surrounded the house. I stopped by the lake and looked at the house. Roderick Usher's house was a large black building. Its many windows were like empty eyes. Suddenly, I felt cold...and a little afraid.
In front of me, a narrow road went across a bridge toward the house. I walked my horse along the narrow road until I reached the walls of the house.
I knocked on the front door and a servant opened it. He took my horse to a stable. Then he led me inside the house.
We climbed many stairs to his master's room. Lamps burned along the walls, but they gave little light. The long corridors and stairways were full of dark shadows.
The servant opened a big, wooden door and I looked inside a large room.

THE HISTORY OF THE LONDON POLICE

Today there are policemen everywhere, but in 1700 London had no policemen at all. A few old men used to protect the city streets at night and they were not paid very much.
About 300 years ago, London was starting to get bigger. The city was very dirty and many people were poor. There were so many thieves who stole money in the streets that people stayed in their homes as much as possible.
In 1750, Henry Fielding started to pay a group of people to stop thieves. They were like policemen and were called 'Bow Street Runners' because they worked near Bow Street.
Fifty years later, there were 120 Bow Street Runners, but London had become very big and needed more policemen. So, in 1829, the first Metropolitan (or London) Police Force was started with 3000 officers. Most of the men worked on foot, but a few rode horses. Until 1920 all the police in London were men.
Today, London police are quite well paid and for the few police officers who still ride horses, the pay is even better than for the others.

Once a select forum of the great and good, the Technology Entertainment and Design (TED) conference now has millions of avid online fans. How did an elite ideas-sharing gathering go mainstream?
Falling animals, misbehaving toddlers and footage of Justin Bieber may populate the bulk of any YouTube most-viewed list.
But amid the viral clips and pop music promos is a series of videos that seems to go against all received wisdom about what online audiences like to consume.
Their tone is sunnily optimistic, go-getting, Californian, with titles like Information Is Food, Crowdsource Your Health and Inventing Is the Easy Part.
They feature luminaries such as Stephen Hawking, JK Rowling and Bono delivering 18-minute lectures about big ideas - technology, culture, the environment, science, social trends.
Yet although there is nary a Lolcat in sight, the YouTube channel of the Technology Entertainment and Design (TED) conference has attracted nearly 112 million views.
The talks have a habit of catching on. TED attendees were given a preview of Al Gore's lecture on climate change lecture, later popularised in An Inconvenient Truth . Biologist Richard Dawkins' 2002 lecture on "militant atheism" laid the groundwork for the arguments set out in hishugely controversial book The God Delusion 
Others have entered the realms of the downright strange, such as whenMicrosoft founder Bill Gates unleashed live mosquitoes into the auditorium during a talk on malaria because "there's no reason why only poor people should have the experience" (the insects were not infected).
It's an impressive level of public interest in an event sneered at by detractors as an expensive talking-shop-cum-networking-event for latte-wielding, iPad clutching, West Coast blue-sky thinkers.

When the Mayor heard about Jack's fall from the sky, he sadly told everybody in  his town. They all looked down at the ground. They didn't scream or shout. They stood and remembered their great friend. "We will never see our dear friend Jack Skellington again," the Mayor said. 
"This is a very sad day for us all." Everybody felt very bad, but nobody was sadder than the Mayor. Sally could hear the Mayor from inside Oogie Boogie's house. He spoke loudly and she tried hard to listen to his words. They sounded very important and very sad. When Sally understood, she cried quietly. Oogie Boogie laughed at her. "Now I'm the scariest person in Halloweentown!" he shouted happily. 
"No more Jack Skellington! Yes!" Sally was in Oogie Boogie's house because she tried to help Santa Claus. Oogie Boogie caught her. He put her on another chair, next to Santa, so she couldn't get away. Oogie Boogie laughed at her, but Sally wasn't afraid.  "You can laugh now," she said to him angrily. "But you'll be sorry!" Oogie laughed again. 
"Very funny, Sally!" he said. But Jack's life didn't end when his sleigh hit the ground. He ran as fast as he could through the woods, with Zero behind him. Then he heard Oogie Boogie's laugh under the ground and stopped suddenly. Ze stonden daar en dachten aan hun grote vriend. "We zullen onze lieve vriend Jack Skellington nooit meer zien," zei de burgemeester.
"Dit is een heel verdrietige dag voor ons allemaal." Iedereen voelde zich heel slecht, maar niemand was verdrietiger dan de burgemeester. Sally kon de burgemeester horen vanuit Oogie Boogies huis. Hij sprak luid en zij deed haar best om naar zijn woorden te luisteren. Ze klonken heel belangrijk en heel verdrietig. Toen Sally het begreep, huilde ze zachtjes. Oogie Boogie lachte haar uit. "Nu ben ik de engste persoon in Halloweentown!" riep hij blij.
"Nooit meer Jack Skellington! Ja!" Sally was in Oogie Boogies huis omdat ze de Kerstman probeerde te helpen. Oogie Boogie had haar gevangen. Hij zette haar op een andere stoel, naast de Kerstman, zodat ze niet kon ontsnappen. Oogie Boogie lachte haar uit, maar Sally was niet bang. "Je kunt nu lachen," zei ze boos tegen hem. "Maar je zult er spijt van krijgen!" Oogie lachte weer.
"Heel grappig, Sally!" zei hij. Maar Jacks leven eindigde niet toen zijn slee de grond raakte. Hij rende zo snel als hij kon door het bos, met Zero achter zich. Toen hoorde hij Oogie Boogies lach onder de grond en stopte plotseling. When the mayor heard about Jack's fall from the sky, he sadly told everyone in his town. They all looked at the ground. They did not scream or shout. They stood there and thought about their great friend. "We will never see our dear friend Jack Skellington again," said the mayor.
"This is a very sad day for all of us." Everyone felt very bad, but no one was sadder than the mayor. Sally could hear the mayor from Oogie Boogie's house. He spoke loudly, and she did her best to listen to his words. They sounded very important and very sad. When Sally understood, she cried softly. Oogie Boogie laughed at her. "Now I am the scariest person in Halloweentown!" he shouted happily.
"No more Jack Skellington! Yes!" Sally was in Oogie Boogie's house because she was trying to help Santa Claus. Oogie Boogie had captured her. He put her on another chair, next to Santa Claus, so that she could not escape. Oogie Boogie laughed at her, but Sally was not afraid. "You can laugh now," she said angrily to him. "But you will regret it!" Oogie laughed again.
"Very funny, Sally!" he said. But Jack's life did not end when his sleigh hit the ground. He ran as fast as he could through the forest, with Zero behind him. Then he heard Oogie Boogie's laugh under the ground and suddenly stopped. He looked through the hole at Oogie Boogie's house, and he could see Santa Claus and Sally on the chairs and the hungry Oogie Boogie by the fire.

The journey from our town to the capital was a journey of about five hours. When I arrived at Mr Jaggers's office the clerk told me that he was in court, and that he had left word I should wait in
his room. He led me to a dark room. After I had waited for a long time Mr Jaggers arrived.
Many people, men and women, who had been waiting for him outside the office, made a rush at him. He addressed himself to two of the men.
'Now, I have nothing to say to you,' said Mr Jaggers, pointing his finger at them. 'I want to know no more than I know. As to the result, it could go either way. I told you that from the start. Have you paid Wemmick?'
'Yes, sir,' said both the men together.
'Very well; then you may go. Now, I won't have it!' said Mr Jaggers, waving his hand at them to put them behind him. 'If you say a word to me, I'll throw up the case.'
'We thought, Mr Jaggers -' one of the men began, pulling off his hat.
'That's what I told you not to do,' said Mr Jaggers. 'You thought! I think for you; that's enough for you. If I want you, I know where to find you; I don't want you to find me. Now I won't have it. I won't hear a word.' 
The two men looked at one another as Mr Jaggers waved them behind him, and fell back and were heard no more.

Charles Darwin (1809-1882) developed a revolutionary theory of evolution that transformed the way we understand the world and we see ourselves. In On the Origin of Species, published in 1859, Darwin described the process of natural selection. 
The 'fittest' animals or plants - those with the characteristics best suited to their environment - are more likely to survive and reproduce. They pass on these desirable characteristics to their offspring. Gradually those features become more common, causing the species to change over time. If the changes are great enough, they can produce an entirely new species. 
The Descent of Man, published in 1871, suggested that humans descended from apes. When Darwin studied medicine, he witnessed an operation performed on a child without anaesthetic. That made him give up medical studies. 
He then studied theology but, instead of becoming a priest, in 1831 he set off on a five-year scientific expedition around the world. There he collected evidence for his future theory. One of the key arguments for natural selection came from the birds that Darwin collected from the Gal pagos Islands. The birds were clearly the same species but some had large strong beaks for eating nuts while others had long thin beaks for finding worms in the ground. 
Darwin realised that all came from a single ancestor but, as they dispersed to different islands, they had adapted to eat the various foods available. Darwin developed the theory of evolution in the 1830s but he didn't announce it then. He knew his ideas were radical so he delayed publishing the theory for about twenty years while he assembled more evidence.

After that, he studied theology, but instead of becoming a priest, he set out in 1831 on a five-year scientific expedition around the world. There he collected evidence for his later theory. One of the main arguments for natural selection came from the birds Darwin collected on the Galápagos Islands. The birds were clearly of the same species, but some had large, strong beaks for eating nuts, while others had long, thin beaks for finding worms in the ground.

Darwin realized that they had all descended from a single ancestor, but that, as they spread across different islands, they had adapted to eat the different food available. Darwin developed the theory of evolution in the 1830s, but did not make it public at the time. He knew that his ideas were radical, so he delayed publishing the theory for about twenty years while he gathered more evidence.

Looking after the countryside 

THE NATIONAL TRUST 

The National Trust is an organisation whose aim is to conserve the British countryside. Gill Page visits the Lleyn Peninsula in North Wales and talks to one of the wardens employed by the Trust to look after the beautiful areas it owns. 

Common sense. That's what a National Trust Warden needs, according to Gareth Roberts. 'And you definitely need to be good at handling people, because you're continually dealing with farmers, visitors, conservationists and building firms.' 
Gareth was born and bred on the Lleyn Peninsula and worked on his parents' farm until he married. About 80 people applied for the post as National Trust Warden for the Lleyn Peninsula. In the end, Gareth's local knowledge and farming experience won him the job, despite his lack of formal training. 
'I find it particularly helpful that I still farm with my parents and that I can deal with farmers on the same level and be aware of their problems. Also, they can't take me in about anything!' he says. His farming life also means he is well able to cope with the physical demands of the job - erecting fences, planting trees, building walls. 
Since he has been with the Trust, Gareth says he has come to understand more about nature conservation. 'When I was a youngster,' he recalls, 'I used to pick and press flowers, collect butterfly larvae and old birds' nests. And I thought to myself recently, where would I find all those flowers, the birds' nests, the grasshoppers now? It's really become clear to me that farming has affected the countryside. It's not the farmers' fault - they were just doing what the government told them.' 
Gareth says that, when he started his job, farmers and conservationists were set against each other. Both sides wanted things done their way.Now they are talking and can see each other's point of view. 'We're at the crossroads and there's just a small step needed to join them together,' says Gareth. 
Conservation is one of the main aspects of Gareth's work, along with public entry to the Trust's land, tree planting and maintenance, and meeting the Trust's tenant farmers. 'My role is to make sure jobs get finished, with as little fuss and as economically as possible. What I enjoy most is seeing projects completed, although about half my time is spent on reports, signing bills and so on.' 
Gareth is certainly keen on his job and despite never being off duty, he obviously enjoys every minute of his work, especially talking to the public. Most of them, anyway. 'It's the attitude of some people I dislike,' he admits. 'They just walk into the area, demand everything, then walk out again as if it's their absolute right. Having to be nice to those people gets on my nerves!' 
But as Gareth says, it's all down to common sense really.So if you've got plenty of that, and you like the idea of an outdoor job, you might think of applying to become a warden like Gareth - but don't expect a job to be available on the Lleyn Peninsula for a good many years!

Zorg voor het platteland

DE NATIONAL TRUST

De National Trust is een organisatie die als doel heeft het Britse platteland te behouden. Gill Page bezoekt het schiereiland Lleyn in Noord-Wales en spreekt met een van de boswachters die door de Trust in dienst zijn genomen om te zorgen voor de prachtige gebieden die zij bezit.

Gezond verstand. Dat is wat een boswachter van de National Trust nodig heeft, volgens Gareth Roberts. ‘En je moet beslist goed met mensen kunnen omgaan, want je hebt voortdurend te maken met boeren, bezoekers, natuurbeschermers en bouwbedrijven.’
Gareth is geboren en getogen op het schiereiland Lleyn en werkte op de boerderij van zijn ouders totdat hij trouwde. Ongeveer 80 mensen solliciteerden naar de functie van boswachter van de National Trust voor het schiereiland Lleyn. Uiteindelijk bezorgden Gareths plaatselijke kennis en ervaring in de landbouw hem de baan, ondanks zijn gebrek aan formele opleiding.
‘Ik vind het vooral handig dat ik nog steeds samen met mijn ouders boer en dat ik met boeren op hetzelfde niveau kan praten en me bewust ben van hun problemen. Bovendien kunnen ze mij niets wijs maken!’ zegt hij. Zijn leven als boer betekent ook dat hij goed in staat is om de fysieke eisen van het werk aan te kunnen – hekken plaatsen, bomen planten, muren bouwen.
Sinds hij bij de Trust werkt, zegt Gareth dat hij meer is gaan begrijpen van natuurbehoud. ‘Toen ik jong was,’ herinnert hij zich, ‘plukte en perste ik bloemen, verzamelde ik rupsen van vlinders en oude vogelnesten. En onlangs dacht ik bij mezelf: waar zou ik al die bloemen, de vogelnesten, de sprinkhanen nu nog vinden? Het is me echt duidelijk geworden dat de landbouw invloed heeft gehad op het platteland. Het is niet de schuld van de boeren – zij deden alleen wat de regering hun opdroeg.’
Gareth zegt dat, toen hij met zijn baan begon, boeren en natuurbeschermers tegenover elkaar stonden. Beide kanten wilden dat dingen op hun manier werden gedaan. Nu praten ze met elkaar en kunnen ze elkaars standpunt inzien. ‘We staan op een kruispunt en er is nog maar een kleine stap nodig om hen samen te brengen,’ zegt Gareth.
Natuurbehoud is een van de belangrijkste aspecten van Gareths werk, samen met openbare toegang tot het land van de Trust, het planten en onderhouden van bomen, en het contact met de pachters van de Trust. ‘Mijn rol is ervoor te zorgen dat het werk afkomt, met zo weinig mogelijk gedoe en zo voordelig mogelijk. Wat ik het leukste vind, is projecten voltooid te zien, hoewel ongeveer de helft van mijn tijd opgaat aan rapporten, het ondertekenen van rekeningen en dergelijke.’
Gareth is duidelijk enthousiast over zijn werk en hoewel hij nooit echt vrij is, geniet hij zichtbaar van elk moment van zijn werk, vooral van het praten met het publiek. Tenminste, de meesten van hen. ‘Het is de houding van sommige mensen waar ik een hekel aan heb,’ geeft hij toe. ‘Ze lopen gewoon het gebied binnen, eisen van alles op, en lopen daarna weer weg alsof het hun absolute recht is. Aardig moeten blijven tegen zulke mensen werkt me op de zenuwen!’
Maar zoals Gareth zegt, komt het uiteindelijk allemaal neer op gezond verstand. Dus als je daar genoeg van hebt, en het idee van een baan in de buitenlucht je aanspreekt, zou je erover kunnen denken om te solliciteren om boswachter te worden zoals Gareth – maar verwacht niet dat er de komende jaren een baan vrijkomt op het schiereiland Lleyn!

Monsieur Firmin was right. All Paris talked about the new Margarita in Faust, the girl with the beautiful voice, the girl with the voice of an angel. People loved her. They laughed and cried and called for more. Daae was wonderful, the best singer in the world!
Behind the stage Meg Giry looked at Annie Sorelli. 'Christine Daae never sang like that before,' she said to Annie. 'Why was she so good tonight?'
'Perhaps she's got a new music teacher,' Annie said.
The noise in the Opera House went on for a long time. In Box 14, Philippe, the Comte de Chagny, turned to his younger brother and smiled.
'Well, Raoul, what did you think of Daae tonight?'
Raoul, the Vicomte de Chagny, was twenty-one years old. He had blue eyes and black hair, and a wonderful smile. The Chagny family was old and rich, and many girls in Paris were in love with the young Vicomte. But Raoul was not interested in them.
He smiled back at his brother. 'What can I say? Christine is an angel, that's all. I'm going to her dressing-room to see her tonight.'
Philippe laughed. He was twenty years older than Raoul, and was more like a father than a brother.
'Ah, I understand,' he said. 'You are in love! But this is your first night in Paris, your first visit to the opera. How do you know Christine Daae?'
'You remember four years ago, when I was on holiday by the sea, in Brittany?' Raoul said. 'Well, I met Christine there. I was in love with her then, and I'm still in love with her today!'

The cop saw the car stop on the bridge but didn't think too much about it. People often stopped their cars on the bridge late at night, when there was not much traffic. The bridge was over the deep river that cut the city neatly in two, and the center of the bridge provided the best view of the city.
Suicides liked the bridge, too. The cop didn't think of that until he saw the man get out of the car, walk slowly along the footpath at the edge, and put a hand on the rail. There was something about that lonely figure, something about the grayness of the night, the fog coming off the river. The cop looked at him and swore, and wondered if he could get to him in time.
He didn't want to shout or blow his whistle because he knew what surprise could do to a probable suicide. Then the man lit a cigarette, and the cop knew he had time. They always smoked all of that last cigarette before they went over the edge.
When the cop was within ten yards of him, the man turned, gave a slight jump, then nodded as if accepting that the moment had passed. He appeared to be in his middle thirties, tall with a long narrow face and thick black eyebrows.
'Looking at the city?' said the cop. 'I saw you here, and thought I'd come and have a talk with you. It can get lonely at this hour of the night.' He patted his pockets, pretending to look for his cigarettes and not finding them. 'Got a spare cigarette on you?' he asked.
The man gave him a cigarette and lit it for him. The cop thanked the man and looked out at the city.

Steve Jobs met engineering student Steve Wozniak through a mutual friend. Jobs was surprised to find Wozniak “knew more about electronics than I did.”
Their first joint venture was building devices that enabled people to make illegal free calls. Wozniak later said it was a “bad idea” to sell them, but it gave the duo “a taste of what we could do with my engineering skills and Jobs’ vision.” They then worked on a game for Atari, where Jobs convinced Wozniak to work round the clock to produce the game in four days – something Wozniak considered to be impossible. Jobs was paid a bonus for delivering on time that he kept secret from Wozniak.
Steve Jobs insisted on attending Reed College, Oregon, an expensive liberal arts university, despite his parents telling him they couldn’t afford it.
However, he soon dropped out. He had an on-off relationship with Chrisann Brennan and lived in a cabin in Los Gatos, California. His passion for good design led him to drop into a calligraphy class back at Reed which later inspired him to include a selection of fonts on his computers. He visited India, shaved his head and wore traditional Indian clothes. Eastern philosophy influenced him. He said: “I saw the craziness of the Western world as well as its capacity for rational thought.”
Jobs and Wozniak formed Apple Computer and built their first machine, the Apple I. It was sold without a case, screen, power supply or keyboard.

It's true - we're all getting too big for our boots

Chris Greener was fourteen when he told his careers teacher he wanted to join the navy when he left school. 'What do you want to be?' asked the teacher. 'The flagpole on a ship?' The teacher had a point - because Chris, though still only fourteen, was already almost two metres tall. Today, at 228 cm, he is Britain's tallest man.
Every decade, the average height of people in Europe grows another centimetre. Every year, more and more truly big people are born. Intriguingly, this does not mean humanity is producing a new super race. In fact, we are returning to what we were like as cavemen. Only now are we losing the effects of generations of poor diet - with dramatic effects. 'We are only now beginning to fulfil our proper potential,' says palaeontologist Professor Chris Stringer. 'We are becoming Cro-Magnons again - the people who lived on this planet 40,000 years ago.'
For most of human history, our ancestors got their food from a wide variety of sources: women gathered herbs, fruits and berries, while men supplemented these with occasional kills of animals (a way of life still adopted by the world's few remaining tribes of hunter- gatherers). One research study found that they based their diet on 85 different wild plants, for example. Then about 9,000 years ago, agriculture was invented - with devastating consequences. Most of the planet's green places have been gradually taken over by farmers, with the result that just three carbohydrate-rich plants - wheat, rice and maize - provide more than half of the calories consumed by the human race today.
This poor diet has had a disastrous effect on human health and physique. Over the centuries we have lived on soups, porridges and breads that have left us underfed and underdeveloped. In one study in Ohio, scientists discovered that when they began to grow corn, healthy hunter-gatherers were turned into sickly, underweight farmers. Tooth decay increased, as did diseases. Far from being one of the blessings of the New World, corn was a public health disaster, according to some anthropologists.
Nevertheless, from then on agriculture spread because a piece of farmed land could support ten times the number of people who had previously lived off it as hunter-gatherers. The fact that most people relying on this system are poorly nourished and stunted has only recently been tackled, even by the world's wealthier nations. Only in Europe, the US and Japan are diets again reflecting the richness of our ancestors' diets.
As a result, the average man in the US is now 179cm, in Holland 180 cm, and in Japan 177 cm. It is a welcome trend, though not without its own problems. Heights may have risen, but the world has not moved on, it seems. A standard bed-length has remained at 190cm since 1860. Even worse, leg-room in planes and trains seems to have shrunk rather than grown, while clothes manufacturers are constantly having to revise their range of products.
The question is: where will it all end? We cannot grow for ever. We must have some programmed upper limit. But what is it? According to Robert Fogel, of University, it could be as much as 193 cm - and we are likely to reach it some time this century.
However, scientists add one note of qualification. Individuals may be growing taller because of improved nutrition, but as a species we are actually shrinking. During the last ice age, 10,000 years ago, members of the human race were slightly rounder and taller - an evolutionary response to the cold. (Large, round bodies are best at keeping in heat.) Since the climate warmed, we appear to have got slightly thinner and smaller, even when properly fed. And as the planet continues to heat up, we may shrink even further. In other words, the growth of human beings could be offset by global warming.

'We beginnen nu pas ons werkelijke potentieel te verwezenlijken,' zegt paleontoloog professor Chris Stringer. Gedurende het grootste deel van de menselijke geschiedenis haalden onze voorouders hun voedsel uit een grote verscheidenheid aan bronnen: vrouwen verzamelden kruiden, vruchten en bessen, terwijl mannen dit aanvulden met af en toe een gedood dier (een manier van leven die nog steeds wordt gevolgd door de weinige overgebleven stammen van jager-verzamelaars in de wereld). Uit een onderzoek bleek bijvoorbeeld dat zij hun dieet baseerden op 85 verschillende wilde planten. Toen werd ongeveer 9.000 jaar geleden de landbouw uitgevonden - met verwoestende gevolgen. De meeste groene gebieden op aarde zijn geleidelijk overgenomen door boeren, met als gevolg dat slechts drie koolhydraatrijke planten - tarwe, rijst en maïs - tegenwoordig meer dan de helft leveren van alle calorieën die de mensheid consumeert.
Dit slechte dieet heeft een rampzalig effect gehad op de gezondheid en lichaamsbouw van de mens. Door de eeuwen heen hebben we geleefd op soepen, pap en brood die ons ondervoed en onderontwikkeld hebben achtergelaten. In een onderzoek in Ohio ontdekten wetenschappers dat toen men maïs begon te verbouwen, gezonde jager-verzamelaars veranderden in ziekelijke boeren met ondergewicht. Tandbederf nam toe, net als ziekten. Verre van een zegen van de Nieuwe Wereld te zijn, was maïs volgens sommige antropologen een ramp voor de volksgezondheid.
Desondanks verspreidde de landbouw zich vanaf dat moment, omdat een stuk landbouwgrond tien keer zoveel mensen kon onderhouden als er voorheen van leefden als jager-verzamelaars. Dat de meeste mensen die van dit systeem afhankelijk zijn slecht gevoed en groeiachterstand hebben, is pas recent aangepakt, zelfs door de rijkere landen van de wereld. Alleen in Europa, de VS en Japan weerspiegelen diëten opnieuw de rijkdom van het dieet van onze voorouders.
Daardoor is de gemiddelde man in de VS nu 179 cm lang, in Nederland 180 cm en in Japan 177 cm. Het is een welkome trend, al gaat die niet zonder eigen problemen. Mensen zijn misschien langer geworden, maar de wereld lijkt niet te zijn meegegroeid. De standaardlengte van een bed is sinds 1860 190 cm gebleven. Nog erger is dat de beenruimte in vliegtuigen en treinen eerder lijkt te zijn afgenomen dan toegenomen, terwijl kledingfabrikanten hun assortiment voortdurend moeten aanpassen.
De vraag is: waar eindigt dit allemaal? We kunnen niet voor altijd blijven groeien. Er moet een geprogrammeerde bovengrens zijn. Maar wat is die? Volgens Robert Fogel, van de universiteit, zou die wel 193 cm kunnen zijn - en waarschijnlijk bereiken we die ergens in deze eeuw.
Wetenschappers voegen daar echter één kanttekening aan toe. Individuen worden misschien langer door verbeterde voeding, maar als soort krimpen we in feite. Tijdens de laatste ijstijd, 10.000 jaar geleden, waren leden van het menselijk ras iets ronder en langer - een evolutionaire reactie op de kou. (Grote, ronde lichamen houden warmte het best vast.) Sinds het klimaat warmer werd, lijken we iets slanker en kleiner te zijn geworden, zelfs wanneer we goed gevoed zijn. En naarmate de planeet verder opwarmt, kunnen we nog verder krimpen. Met andere woorden: de groei van de mens zou tenietgedaan kunnen worden door de opwarming van de aarde.

It is true – we are all getting too big for our boots

Chris Greener was fourteen when he told his careers adviser that he wanted to join the navy when he left school. “What do you want to be?” asked the teacher. “The mast on a ship?” The teacher had a point – because Chris, although only fourteen, was already almost two metres tall. Today, at 228 cm, he is the tallest man in Britain.

Every decade, the average height of people in Europe increases by another centimetre. Every year, more and more really tall people are being born. Intriguingly, this does not mean that humanity is producing a new super-race. In fact, we are returning to how we were as cavemen. Only now are we getting rid of the effects of generations of poor nutrition – with dramatic results. “We are only just beginning to realise our true potential,” says palaeontologist Professor Chris Stringer. “We are becoming Cro-Magnons again – the people who lived on this planet 40,000 years ago.”

For most of human history, our ancestors got their food from a wide variety of sources: women gathered herbs, fruit and berries, while men supplemented this with the occasional killed animal (a way of life still followed by the few remaining hunter-gatherer tribes in the world). One study found, for example, that they based their diet on 85 different wild plants. Then, about 9,000 years ago, agriculture was invented – with devastating consequences. Most green areas on earth were gradually taken over by farmers, with the result that just three carbohydrate-rich plants – wheat, rice and maize – now provide more than half of all the calories humanity consumes.

This poor diet has had a disastrous effect on human health and physique. Over the centuries, we have lived on soups, porridge and bread that have left us undernourished and underdeveloped. In one study in Ohio, scientists discovered that when people began to cultivate maize, healthy hunter-gatherers turned into sickly, underweight farmers. Tooth decay increased, as did disease. Far from being a blessing from the New World, maize was, according to some anthropologists, a public health disaster.

Nevertheless, agriculture spread from that point on, because one area of farmland could support ten times as many people as had previously lived off it as hunter-gatherers. The fact that most people dependent on this system are poorly nourished and stunted has only recently been addressed, even by the richer countries of the world. Only in Europe, the US and Japan do diets once again reflect the richness of our ancestors’ diet.

As a result, the average man in the US is now 179 cm tall, in the Netherlands 180 cm, and in Japan 177 cm. It is a welcome trend, although not without its own problems. People may have become taller, but the world does not seem to have grown with them. The standard bed length has remained 190 cm since 1860. Worse still, legroom on planes and trains seems to have decreased rather than increased, while clothing manufacturers constantly have to adjust their ranges.

The question is: where does all this end? We cannot go on growing forever. There must be a programmed upper limit. But what is it? According to Robert Fogel, from the university, it may be as much as 193 cm – and we will probably reach it sometime in this century.

Scientists do add one reservation, however. Individuals may grow taller through improved nutrition, but as a species we are actually shrinking. During the last ice age, 10,000 years ago, members of the human race were slightly broader and taller – an evolutionary response to the cold. (Large, round bodies retain heat best.) Since the climate became warmer, we appear to have become somewhat slimmer and smaller, even when well nourished. And as the planet continues to warm, we may shrink even further. In other words, human growth may be cancelled out by global warming.

The Cabinet-Maker
Charles Hurst makes a living from perfectly crafted furniture Joanna Watt meets him
Charles Hurst gives the impression of being a man in a hurry. I arrive at his workshop, tucked under a railway arch in East London, and am greeted with a quick handshake and the words: 'Well, fire away then!' Whether this brusqueness is real or a front hiding a shy streak is not immediately apparent. But a glance around the workshop reveals that Hurst is obviously busy, with good reason not to waste a minute of his time.
The arched space is full of half-made pieces of furniture and planks of wood in an amazing array of natural colours. Hurst has been a cabinet-maker for ten years and has built up a very nice reputation for himself. His order book is always full for several months in advance, despite the fact that he does not really promote himself. Word has spread that if you want a decent cupboard or table, bookcase or kitchen units, Hurst is your man.
Of course, finding a furniture-maker is not that taxing a task. Wherever you live in the countryside, the craft is alive and well. But finding a cabinet- maker who prides himself on making beautifully crafted furniture with clean, simple lines is less easy. 'There are few real cabinet-makers now. People call themselves furniture-makers,' Hurst says wearily. As a craftsman who sets himself exacting standards, he is continually disappointed by some contemporary furniture. 'I am amazed by what some furniture-makers get away with, and saddened by what people will put up with.' He rails against shoddy, mass-produced furniture, and craftsmen who churn out second-rate pieces.
Such a quest for perfection is obviously a key to Hurst's success. That and his talent. This man is not coy about his ability. Indeed, his blatant self- confidence is as surprising as his initial brusque manner. 'I have a huge natural ability,' he says, with a deadpan expression. 'I have always been good at making things.' If it were not for the self-deprecating mood into which he slipped towards the end of our interview, I would have believed his conceit to be wholly genuine.
Hurst is self-taught. So how did he learn his craft? 'I asked the right questions and picked it all up,' he says nonchalantly. Almost all of his commissions come from private individuals ('l used to do some commercial work for companies but it was soul-destroying'). Some clients have returned time and again. 'You end up doing the whole of their house. That is very satisfying.' But he is honest enough to admit that relationships with clients do not always run smoothly. 'The most infuriating clients are those who don't know what they want, and then decide they do when it's too late ... my favourite clients are the exacting ones.'
If Hurst has every reason to be pleased with himself, he is also gracious in his praise for others - where it is due. With a sudden shot of modesty, he says: 'There are people far better than me. I can admire other people. After all, I wasn't trained at Parnham' (the leading college of furniture design). However, he is also unremittingly critical of those craftsmen who 'are trying to be artists and take a year to make one piece.' He also has little time for degree shows, in which students exhibit their work but at the same time are 'trying to make fashion statements. That can be pretentious. A piece of furniture is not about making a statement. It has to be something that people really can use.'
Confident Hurst may be, even brusque, but you could never call him or his work pretentious. Indeed, his parting shot displays a welcome down- to-earth approach to his craft and a streak of humility strangely at odds with his earlier self- confidence. 'After all, I am only making furniture,' he says as I make my exit.

De meubelmaker
Charles Hurst verdient zijn brood met perfect vervaardigde meubels. Joanna Watt spreekt hem.

Charles Hurst wekt de indruk een man te zijn die haast heeft. Ik kom aan bij zijn werkplaats, verscholen onder een spoorwegboog in Oost-Londen, en word begroet met een snelle handdruk en de woorden: 'Nou, steek maar van wal dan!' Of deze kortafheid echt is of een façade waarachter verlegenheid schuilgaat, is niet meteen duidelijk. Maar een blik rond de werkplaats laat zien dat Hurst het duidelijk druk heeft, en goede reden heeft om geen minuut van zijn tijd te verspillen.

De gewelfde ruimte staat vol halfafgemaakte meubelstukken en houten planken in een verbazingwekkende verscheidenheid aan natuurlijke kleuren. Hurst is al tien jaar meubelmaker en heeft in die tijd een uitstekende reputatie opgebouwd. Zijn orderboek zit altijd maanden van tevoren vol, ondanks het feit dat hij nauwelijks reclame voor zichzelf maakt. Het nieuws heeft zich verspreid dat als je een degelijke kast of tafel, boekenkast of keukeninrichting wilt, Hurst de man voor jou is.

Natuurlijk is het vinden van een meubelmaker niet zo'n moeilijke opgave. Waar je ook op het platteland woont, het ambacht leeft en bloeit. Maar een meubelmaker vinden die er trots op is prachtig vervaardigde meubels met strakke, eenvoudige lijnen te maken, is minder gemakkelijk. 'Er zijn tegenwoordig nog maar weinig echte meubelmakers. Mensen noemen zichzelf meubelmaker,' zegt Hurst vermoeid. Als vakman die zichzelf strenge normen oplegt, is hij voortdurend teleurgesteld door sommige hedendaagse meubels. 'Ik verbaas me erover waar sommige meubelmakers mee wegkomen, en het stemt me verdrietig wat mensen allemaal accepteren.' Hij fulmineert tegen slecht gemaakte, massaproductiemeubels en vaklieden die tweederangs stukken aan de lopende band produceren.

Zo'n streven naar perfectie is duidelijk een sleutel tot Hursts succes. Dat, en zijn talent. Deze man is niet terughoudend over zijn eigen kunnen. Sterker nog, zijn openlijke zelfvertrouwen is even verrassend als zijn aanvankelijke kortafheid. 'Ik heb een enorm natuurlijk talent,' zegt hij met een uitdrukkingsloos gezicht. 'Ik ben altijd goed geweest in dingen maken.' Als het niet was geweest voor de zelfspottende stemming waarin hij tegen het einde van ons gesprek verviel, zou ik zijn eigendunk voor volledig oprecht hebben gehouden.

Hurst is autodidact. Dus hoe heeft hij zijn vak geleerd? 'Ik stelde de juiste vragen en heb het allemaal opgepikt,' zegt hij nonchalant. Bijna al zijn opdrachten komen van particulieren ('Vroeger deed ik wel commercieel werk voor bedrijven, maar dat was zielsdodend'). Sommige klanten zijn keer op keer teruggekomen. 'Uiteindelijk doe je hun hele huis. Dat is heel bevredigend.' Maar hij is eerlijk genoeg om toe te geven dat de relaties met klanten niet altijd soepel verlopen. 'De meest frustrerende klanten zijn degenen die niet weten wat ze willen, en dan besluiten dat ze het wel weten als het te laat is ... mijn favoriete klanten zijn de veeleisende.'

Als Hurst alle reden heeft om tevreden met zichzelf te zijn, is hij ook gul met lof voor anderen - waar die op zijn plaats is. Met een plotselinge opwelling van bescheidenheid zegt hij: 'Er zijn mensen die veel beter zijn dan ik. Ik kan bewondering hebben voor andere mensen. Ik ben tenslotte niet opgeleid aan Parnham' (de toonaangevende opleiding voor meubelontwerp). Toch is hij ook onverbiddelijk kritisch over die vaklieden die 'artiest proberen te zijn en een jaar doen over één stuk.' Ook heeft hij weinig op met eindexamenexposities, waarop studenten hun werk tonen maar tegelijkertijd 'modieuze statements proberen te maken. Dat kan pretentieus zijn. Een meubelstuk draait niet om het maken van een statement. Het moet iets zijn dat mensen echt kunnen gebruiken.'

Zelfverzekerd mag Hurst zijn, zelfs kortaf, maar pretentieus kun je hem of zijn werk nooit noemen. Sterker nog, zijn slotopmerking getuigt van een verfrissend nuchtere kijk op zijn vak en van een vleugje bescheidenheid die vreemd contrasteert met zijn eerdere zelfvertrouwen. 'Ik maak tenslotte alleen maar meubels,' zegt hij terwijl ik vertrek.

The Elephant Show 

by Daniel Allsop, age 14 

Last summer, I went to Thailand for a beach holiday with my family. One day, we took a trip to a park not far from our hotel. It had beautiful flower gardens but we were only interested in the elephant show. 
We went straight to a large square with seats on three sides. Three elephants came in with their keepers and stood in front of a large piece of white card. Each elephant was given a paintbrush and started to paint on its own card. From time to time, the keepers put a new brush full of paint into each elephant's trunk and took the old one away. Slowly, following their keepers' instructions, the elephants drew pictures on the cards. I couldn't believe what I was seeing! One picture showed a river, one a tree and the third a bunch of flowers. When the keepers held up the paintings, everyone wanted to buy one. We gave the elephants the bananas we brought for our lunch. 
Twenty years ago, elephants worked in the forest. Now, they no longer work there, but the cleverest of these animals live in special centres where visitors can watch them.

De olifantenshow

door Daniel Allsop, 14 jaar

Afgelopen zomer ging ik met mijn familie naar Thailand voor een strandvakantie. Op een dag maakten we een uitstapje naar een park niet ver van ons hotel. Er waren prachtige bloementuinen, maar wij waren alleen geïnteresseerd in de olifantenshow.
We gingen meteen naar een groot plein met aan drie kanten zitplaatsen. Drie olifanten kwamen met hun verzorgers binnen en gingen voor een groot stuk wit karton staan. Elke olifant kreeg een penseel en begon op zijn eigen vel te schilderen. Af en toe stopten de verzorgers een nieuwe, met verf gevulde kwast in de slurf van elke olifant en namen de oude weg. Langzaam tekenden de olifanten, volgens de aanwijzingen van hun verzorgers, afbeeldingen op het karton. Ik kon niet geloven wat ik zag! Op één schilderij stond een rivier, op een ander een boom en op het derde een bos bloemen. Toen de verzorgers de schilderijen omhooghielden, wilde iedereen er een kopen. We gaven de olifanten de bananen die we voor onze lunch hadden meegenomen.
Twintig jaar geleden werkten olifanten in het bos. Nu werken ze daar niet meer, maar de slimste van deze dieren leven in speciale centra waar bezoekers naar hen kunnen komen kijken.

results.src_text:
Paul Simon

Rock and roll in the 1950s was primarily a youth cult, but its lasting importance lay in the seismic impact it had on the middle class and the middle-aged. It also paved the way for the next generation of rock idols, who listened to it awestruck and aware that this strange, unsettling sound would somehow, irrevocably, be linked with their destinies.
For Paul Simon, as for other youngsters in the US, the chief opportunity for hearing this new and invigorating type of music that was sweeping the country was courtesy of Alan Freed's radio show, Moondog Rock'n'Roll Party. Freed's show was required listening for a whole generation of fledgling rock idols. Like the young John Lennon, 3,000 miles away in Liverpool, with his ear glued to Radio Luxembourg - the only European outlet for the new rock and roll - Paul Simon was fascinated by the sounds pouring from Freed's show, and prepared himself for the next big step for a rock and roll obsessed teenager, the switch from listening to others' music to making his own.

Snow

No path was visible, but I thought that I would be all right if I walked with due caution. The wind hammered down from the heights, knocking me over as I slid and slithered on the slippery ice. Suddenly the innocent-looking snow gave way beneath me. I dropped, startled, into a hole some four feet deep. The snow had formed a roof over the gap between two rocks, melting away to leave nothing but a thin crust through which I had plunged. I hauled myself out, shaken and unnerved, wondering what I would have done if the hole had been thirty feet deep. I sat back against the top of a pine tree that protruded from the snow to take stock of the situation. In an hour I had covered about half a mile. It was perfectly clear that I would have to abandon my plan.

Qualitative Research

There are now numerous books which attempt to give guidance to researchers about qualitative research. While much has been written about the collection of data, the books are often silent about the processes and procedures associated with data analysis. Indeed, much mystery surrounds the way researchers analyse their data. Accordingly, we invited a range of social scientists who have engaged in qualitative projects to discuss the approaches that they used. The idea was to share insight and understanding of the process of qualitative data analysis rather than to produce a guidebook for the intending researcher. Such a task involves a process of demystification, of making implicit procedures more explicit. While this may sound straightforward, we have found it far from simple. We have therefore given our contributors the opportunity to present their work in a range of styles, which include autobiographical narratives and more impersonal forms.

Paul Simon

Rock-'n-roll was in de jaren vijftig in de eerste plaats een jeugdcultus, maar het blijvende belang ervan lag in de enorme impact die het had op de middenklasse en de mensen van middelbare leeftijd. Het effende ook het pad voor de volgende generatie rockidolen, die er met ontzag naar luisterden en zich ervan bewust waren dat dit vreemde, verontrustende geluid op de een of andere manier onherroepelijk met hun lot verbonden zou zijn.
Voor Paul Simon was, net als voor andere jongeren in de VS, de belangrijkste gelegenheid om dit nieuwe en verkwikkende soort muziek te horen, die het hele land veroverde, Alan Freeds radioprogramma Moondog Rock'n'Roll Party. Naar Freeds programma moest een hele generatie beginnende rockidolen absoluut luisteren. Net als de jonge John Lennon, 3.000 mijl verderop in Liverpool, met zijn oor gekluisterd aan Radio Luxembourg - het enige Europese kanaal voor de nieuwe rock-'n-roll - was Paul Simon gefascineerd door de klanken die uit Freeds programma stroomden, en bereidde hij zich voor op de volgende grote stap voor een door rock-'n-roll geobsedeerde tiener: de overgang van het luisteren naar andermans muziek naar het maken van zijn eigen muziek.

Sneeuw

Er was geen pad zichtbaar, maar ik dacht dat het wel goed zou gaan als ik met de nodige voorzichtigheid liep. De wind beukte vanaf de hoogten naar beneden en sloeg me omver terwijl ik over het gladde ijs gleed en uitgleed. Plotseling gaf de onschuldig ogende sneeuw onder mij mee. Geschrokken viel ik in een gat van zo'n anderhalve meter diep. De sneeuw had een dak gevormd over de opening tussen twee rotsen en was weggesmolten zodat er niets meer overbleef dan een dunne korst waar ik doorheen was gezakt. Ik hees mezelf eruit, geschokt en van mijn stuk gebracht, en vroeg me af wat ik zou hebben gedaan als het gat tien meter diep was geweest. Ik ging achterover zitten tegen de top van een dennenboom die uit de sneeuw stak om de situatie op te nemen. In een uur had ik ongeveer achthonderd meter afgelegd. Het was volkomen duidelijk dat ik mijn plan zou moeten opgeven.

Kwalitatief onderzoek

Er zijn tegenwoordig talloze boeken die onderzoekers proberen richtlijnen te geven over kwalitatief onderzoek. Hoewel er veel is geschreven over het verzamelen van gegevens, zwijgen deze boeken vaak over de processen en procedures die samenhangen met de analyse van gegevens. Er hangt zelfs veel geheimzinnigheid rond de manier waarop onderzoekers hun gegevens analyseren. Daarom hebben wij een aantal sociale wetenschappers die zich met kwalitatieve projecten hebben beziggehouden, uitgenodigd om de benaderingen te bespreken die zij hebben gebruikt. Het idee was om inzicht in en begrip van het proces van kwalitatieve gegevensanalyse te delen, en niet om een handleiding te produceren voor de aspirant-onderzoeker. Een dergelijke taak brengt een proces van demystificatie met zich mee, van het explicieter maken van impliciete procedures. Hoewel dit eenvoudig klinkt, hebben wij vastgesteld dat het allesbehalve simpel is. Daarom hebben wij onze bijdragers de gelegenheid gegeven hun werk in uiteenlopende stijlen te presenteren, waaronder autobiografische vertellingen en meer onpersoonlijke vormen.

Like the young John Lennon, 3,000 miles away in Liverpool, with his ear glued to Radio Luxembourg—the only European outlet for the new rock ’n’ roll—Paul Simon was fascinated by the sounds pouring from Freed’s program, and was preparing for the next big step for a rock ’n’ roll-obsessed teenager: the transition from listening to other people’s music to making his own.

Snow

There was no visible path, but I thought I would be all right if I walked with due caution. The wind was pounding down from the heights and knocked me over as I slid and slipped across the smooth ice. Suddenly, the innocent-looking snow beneath me gave way. Startled, I fell into a hole about a meter and a half deep. The snow had formed a roof over the gap between two rocks and had melted away so that nothing remained but a thin crust, which I had fallen through. I hauled myself out, shaken and unnerved, and wondered what I would have done if the hole had been ten meters deep. I sat back against the top of a pine tree sticking out of the snow to take stock of the situation. In an hour I had covered about eight hundred meters. It was perfectly clear that I would have to abandon my plan.

Qualitative Research

There are countless books nowadays that try to provide researchers with guidelines on qualitative research. Although much has been written about data collection, these books often say little about the processes and procedures associated with data analysis. Indeed, there is a great deal of mystery surrounding the way researchers analyze their data. We therefore invited a number of social scientists who have been involved in qualitative projects to discuss the approaches they have used. The idea was to share insight into and understanding of the process of qualitative data analysis, not to produce a handbook for the aspiring researcher. Such a task involves a process of demystification, of making implicit procedures more explicit. Although this sounds simple, we have found that it is anything but. We have therefore given our contributors the opportunity to present their work in a variety of styles, including autobiographical narratives and more impersonal forms.

It's true - we're all getting too big for our boots
Chris Greener was fourteen when he told his careers teacher he wanted to join the navy when he left school. 'What do you want to be?' asked the teacher. 'The flagpole on a ship?' The teacher had a point - because Chris, though still only fourteen, was already almost two metres tall. Today, at 228 cm, he is Britain's tallest man.
Every decade, the average height of people in Europe grows another centimetre. Every year, more and more truly big people are born. Intriguingly, this does not mean humanity is producing a new super race. In fact, we are returning to what we were like as cavemen. Only now are we losing the effects of generations of poor diet - with dramatic effects. 'We are only now beginning to fulfil our proper potential,' says palaeontologist Professor Chris Stringer. 'We are becoming Cro-Magnons again - the people who lived on this planet 40,000 years ago.'
For most of human history, our ancestors got their food from a wide variety of sources: women gathered herbs, fruits and berries, while men supplemented these with occasional kills of animals (a way of life still adopted by the world's few remaining tribes of hunter- gatherers). One research study found that they based their diet on 85 different wild plants, for example. Then about 9,000 years ago, agriculture was invented - with devastating consequences. Most of the planet's green places have been gradually taken over by farmers, with the result that just three carbohydrate-rich plants - wheat, rice and maize - provide more than half of the calories consumed by the human race today.
This poor diet has had a disastrous effect on human health and physique. Over the centuries we have lived on soups, porridges and breads that have left us underfed and underdeveloped. In one study in Ohio, scientists discovered that when they began to grow corn, healthy hunter-gatherers were turned into sickly, underweight farmers. Tooth decay increased, as did diseases. Far from being one of the blessings of the New World, corn was a public health disaster, according to some anthropologists.
Nevertheless, from then on agriculture spread because a piece of farmed land could support ten times the number of people who had previously lived off it as hunter-gatherers. The fact that most people relying on this system are poorly nourished and stunted has only recently been tackled, even by the world's wealthier nations. Only in Europe, the US and Japan are diets again reflecting the richness of our ancestors' diets.
As a result, the average man in the US is now 179cm, in Holland 180 cm, and in Japan 177 cm. It is a welcome trend, though not without its own problems. Heights may have risen, but the world has not moved on, it seems. A standard bed-length has remained at 190cm since 1860. Even worse, leg-room in planes and trains seems to have shrunk rather than grown, while clothes manufacturers are constantly having to revise their range of products.
The question is: where will it all end? We cannot grow for ever. We must have some programmed upper limit. But what is it? According to Robert Fogel, of University, it could be as much as 193 cm - and we are likely to reach it some time this century.
However, scientists add one note of qualification. Individuals may be growing taller because of improved nutrition, but as a species we are actually shrinking. During the last ice age, 10,000 years ago, members of the human race were slightly rounder and taller - an evolutionary response to the cold. (Large, round bodies are best at keeping in heat.) Since the climate warmed, we appear to have got slightly thinner and smaller, even when properly fed. And as the planet continues to heat up, we may shrink even further. In other words, the growth of human beings could be offset by global warming.

Het is waar - we worden allemaal te groot voor onze schoenen

Chris Greener was veertien toen hij zijn decaan vertelde dat hij bij de marine wilde toen hij van school af ging. 'Wat wil je worden?' vroeg de leraar. 'De vlaggenmast op een schip?' De leraar had een punt - want Chris was, hoewel nog maar veertien, al bijna twee meter lang. Tegenwoordig is hij met 228 cm de langste man van Groot-Brittannië.

Elk decennium neemt de gemiddelde lengte van mensen in Europa met nog een centimeter toe. Elk jaar worden er meer en meer echt grote mensen geboren. Interessant genoeg betekent dit niet dat de mensheid een nieuw superras voortbrengt. In feite keren we terug naar hoe we waren als holbewoners. Pas nu raken we de gevolgen van generaties van slechte voeding kwijt - met dramatische effecten. 'We beginnen nu pas ons werkelijke potentieel te vervullen,' zegt paleontoloog professor Chris Stringer. 'We worden weer Cro-Magnons - de mensen die 40.000 jaar geleden op deze planeet leefden.'

Gedurende het grootste deel van de menselijke geschiedenis haalden onze voorouders hun voedsel uit een grote verscheidenheid aan bronnen: vrouwen verzamelden kruiden, fruit en bessen, terwijl mannen dit aanvulden met af en toe een gedood dier (een levenswijze die nog steeds wordt gevolgd door de paar overgebleven stammen van jager-verzamelaars in de wereld). Uit een onderzoek bleek bijvoorbeeld dat zij hun dieet baseerden op 85 verschillende wilde planten. Toen werd ongeveer 9.000 jaar geleden de landbouw uitgevonden - met verwoestende gevolgen. De meeste groene gebieden van de planeet zijn geleidelijk overgenomen door boeren, met als gevolg dat slechts drie koolhydraatrijke planten - tarwe, rijst en maïs - tegenwoordig meer dan de helft leveren van de calorieën die de mensheid verbruikt.

Dit slechte dieet heeft een rampzalig effect gehad op de gezondheid en lichaamsbouw van de mens. Door de eeuwen heen hebben we geleefd van soepen, pap en brood die ons ondervoed en onderontwikkeld hebben achtergelaten. In een onderzoek in Ohio ontdekten wetenschappers dat gezonde jager-verzamelaars veranderden in zwakke, ondergewichtige boeren toen zij maïs begonnen te verbouwen. Tandbederf nam toe, evenals ziekten. Volgens sommige antropologen was maïs, verre van een van de zegeningen van de Nieuwe Wereld te zijn, een ramp voor de volksgezondheid.

Toch verspreidde de landbouw zich vanaf dat moment, omdat een stuk landbouwgrond tien keer zoveel mensen kon onderhouden als er voorheen als jager-verzamelaars van konden leven. Het feit dat de meeste mensen die van dit systeem afhankelijk zijn slecht gevoed en klein van stuk zijn, is pas onlangs aangepakt, zelfs door de rijkere landen van de wereld. Alleen in Europa, de VS en Japan weerspiegelen diëten weer de rijkdom van het dieet van onze voorouders.

Daardoor is de gemiddelde man in de VS nu 179 cm, in Nederland 180 cm en in Japan 177 cm. Het is een welkome trend, al is die niet zonder eigen problemen. De lengte mag dan zijn toegenomen, maar de wereld lijkt niet mee veranderd te zijn. Een standaard bedlengte is sinds 1860 190 cm gebleven. Nog erger is dat de beenruimte in vliegtuigen en treinen eerder lijkt te zijn gekrompen dan gegroeid, terwijl kledingfabrikanten hun assortiment producten voortdurend moeten herzien.

De vraag is: waar eindigt dit allemaal? We kunnen niet eeuwig doorgroeien. Er moet een geprogrammeerde bovengrens zijn. Maar wat is die? Volgens Robert Fogel, van de universiteit, zou die wel 193 cm kunnen bedragen - en waarschijnlijk zullen we die ergens deze eeuw bereiken.

Wetenschappers voegen hier echter één voorbehoud aan toe. Individuen worden misschien langer door betere voeding, maar als soort worden we in feite kleiner. Tijdens de laatste ijstijd, 10.000 jaar geleden, waren leden van het menselijk ras iets ronder en langer - een evolutionaire reactie op de kou. (Grote, ronde lichamen houden warmte het best vast.) Sinds het klimaat opwarmde, lijken we iets slanker en kleiner te zijn geworden, zelfs als we goed gevoed zijn. En naarmate de planeet verder opwarmt, kunnen we nog verder krimpen. Met andere woorden: de groei van de mens zou kunnen worden tenietgedaan door de opwarming van de aarde.
